name: Hatchet
description: A light, short-hafted axe small enough to be thrown as well as swung in melee. Common as a utility tool for chopping wood and clearing brush, it doubles readily as a weapon in a pinch. Known by many names worldwide, including the Norman francisca and the Japanese nata. Its compact size makes it easy to carry and conceal, though its short reach and light head limit the damage it can deal compared to a full axe.

name: Axe
description: A wedge-shaped iron blade mounted on a wooden handle, found in nearly every culture as both a tool and a weapon. Long enough to be swung two-handed if desired, though the one-handed grip is most common. Effective at delivering powerful cutting blows, an axe can split shields, armor, and limbs alike. Variants include the epsilon axe of Sumer and the Japanese masakari. Its weight is concentrated in the head, making it unwieldy for parrying but devastating on the attack.

name: Pick
description: A curved digging tool with one or two pointed or wedged ends mounted on a long handle, used to break up hard or compacted soil and rock before it can be shoveled away. Early picks made of wood, bone, or antler are less effective and prone to breaking against true stone, while later all-metal picks deliver full striking power and durability, becoming the standard tool of professional miners and excavators.

name: Pickaxe
description: A heavy digging tool combining a pointed pick head with a flat or wedge-shaped blade on the opposite side of its iron head, mounted on a long wooden haft. The pick end breaks up hard-packed earth, clay, or soft rock, while the opposing blade chops through roots or pries loose debris, letting a worker clear ground considerably faster than with a simple shovel or pick alone. Common among miners, sappers, and laborers from TL2 onward, its weight and reach also make it a serviceable improvised weapon in a pinch, though it is slow and unwieldy to swing.

name: Maul
description: A heavy, two-handed hammer with a large blunt head, used for everything from driving stakes and splitting wood to crushing armor and bone in combat. Its tremendous mass delivers devastating blunt-force trauma, capable of denting plate armor and shattering shields, though its weight makes it slow and unwieldy compared to lighter weapons, requiring real strength to wield effectively.

name: Warhammer
description: A long, two-handed version of the pick, often fitted with a heavy hammer head opposite the armor-piercing spike, making it a combination weapon. The hammer face delivers crushing blows capable of denting armor and breaking bones, while the spike on the reverse can punch through plate when a more precise strike is needed. A favored weapon of European knights for fighting other heavily armored opponents.

name: Mining Hammer
description: A heavy-headed metal hammer designed for breaking rock, sometimes featuring a slightly pointed end for splitting stone along seams. Used in conjunction with chisels and picks, mining hammers come in small and large sizes for different tasks underground or in quarries. Their substantial weight and metal heads also make them dangerous improvised weapons, striking with crushing force when swung in anger.

name: Smithing Hammer
description: A lighter, more precisely balanced hammer than those used in mining, employed by blacksmiths to shape heated metal on an anvil. Smithing hammers came in many head shapes for specialized purposes—grooved heads for drawing wire, rounded faces for general shaping, or pointed ends for detail work—making the hammer one of the smith's most personalized and frequently used tools.

name: Club
description: Any balanced wooden club, whether purpose-made as a weapon of good quality or simply a sturdy branch or table leg pressed into service. Known by many names worldwide, including the cudgel and the Irish shillelagh. Virtually every culture has some equivalent, and most languages have a word for this most basic of weapons. Cheap, durable, and requiring no special skill to obtain, it remains the default weapon of the desperate and the poor.

name: Blackjack
description: A small, weighted truncheon made from cloth or soft leather, packed with sand, shot, or similar material. Designed to deliver a stunning beating without leaving obvious bruising, making the injury hard to detect on casual examination. Every culture has its own version under names like 'cosh' or 'sap.' Favored by thieves, enforcers, and anyone needing to incapacitate a target quietly and without obvious evidence of an attack.

name: Baton
description: A short, balanced club usually made of wood or metal. Simple, sturdy, and requiring no special maintenance, the baton serves as a versatile blunt weapon and a symbol of authority for guards and officials across many cultures.

name: Arm Splint
description: A set of flat wooden strips, thick enough to provide rigidity, placed against a broken arm and tied or strapped in place to immobilize it while the bone mends. Anyone trained in First Aid can apply a splint to form a rigid framework for a limb, though properly setting the bone first requires surgical skill. Splints represent one of the oldest and most universal medical interventions, requiring only basic carpentry materials and cordage, and remain in use essentially unchanged across all tech levels covered by this volume.

name: Leg Splint
description: A larger set of flat wooden strips, thick enough for rigidity, bound against a broken leg to hold the fractured bone in alignment while it heals. Heavier and longer than an arm splint due to the size of the limb involved, it serves the same essential function: providing a rigid external framework so a crippling injury can recover properly. Like its arm counterpart, it requires only simple woodworking and binding materials, making it available to even the most primitive societies practicing basic field medicine.

name: Pry-Bar
description: A 30-inch metal crowbar optimized for forcing open doors and snapping padlocks, smaller and more portable than the heavy bars used in mining and tunneling. Its leverage significantly aids efforts to force open barred doors, and in a pinch it can be wielded as an improvised mace-like weapon. A smaller 20-inch version is easier to hide under clothing but provides less leverage, functioning more like a light club if used in a fight. Both versions are common tools for burglars, scrap-metal scavengers, and anyone needing to force open a stuck or locked door.

name: Mace
description: The classic medieval European war mace, fitted with flanges specifically designed to punch through plate armor and helmets. Its head, mounted on a handle long enough for comfortable two-handed use, concentrates tremendous force into a small area. A favored weapon of knights and clergy (who were sometimes forbidden from drawing blood with edged weapons), it remained effective even against the heaviest armor of its era.

name: Flail
description: A two-handed weapon consisting of iron bars, spiked balls, or similar heavy weights attached to a long haft by a chain or cord, found wherever grain flails are used as agricultural tools. Includes the Japanese chi-giriki. The chain's flexibility lets the striking head swing around shields and parries to land devastating blows, but makes the weapon extremely difficult for the wielder to control precisely or use defensively.

name: Morningstar
description: A one-handed flail consisting of a handle connected by a chain to a spiked striking head, designed to deliver crushing and puncturing blows that flow around a target's shield or parry. Some historical sources also apply this name to a simple mace with a spiked head rather than a true chained flail. The chain's flexibility makes the weapon notoriously difficult to parry, rewarding aggressive offense over careful defense.

name: Sickle
description: A farming tool repurposed as a weapon, typically given a straighter blade than an agricultural sickle to allow both hooking and impaling attacks alongside its natural cutting motion. Versions of the weaponized sickle appear worldwide, including the Indonesian arit, the Dacian falx, and the Japanese kama. Cheap and ubiquitous, it could be picked up by peasant rebels or used by trained martial artists as a hooking, slashing, and thrusting weapon all in one.

name: Scythe
description: A two-handed farming implement used to harvest grain and mow grass, rarely a dedicated weapon but weaponized versions exist. Its long, curved blade can deliver powerful cutting strokes and, when reversed, an impaling thrust, while the back of the blade can hook an opponent's weapon or limb. An iconic improvised weapon of peasant uprisings throughout history.

name: Glaive
description: A European polearm consisting of a pointed cleaver-like blade mounted on a long haft, evolved from the heavy spear in ancient times for both cutting and thrusting attacks at range. Includes the French fauchard and the Scottish jedwart stave and Lochaber axe.

name: Bill
description: A heavy European polearm with a bladed, hooked head originally designed for unseating horsemen, the hook allowing the wielder to snag a rider's limb, weapon, or harness. Includes the English forest bill and the French guisarme. Its hooking capability gives it tactical options beyond simple cutting and thrusting.

name: Halberd
description: A heavy European polearm topped with an axe-like head featuring both a back-spike for the Hook technique and an axial spike for spear-like thrusts. A devastating combination weapon capable of cutting, hooking, and stabbing, it was a mainstay of infantry formations facing armored cavalry and other infantry alike. Includes the Swiss voulge. Its versatility made it one of the most feared infantry weapons of the medieval period.

name: Javelin
description: A light spear specifically balanced for throwing rather than thrusting, used by skirmishers, hunters, and light infantry across nearly every culture. Some javelins are fitted with a leather thong wound around the shaft near the point of balance; the thrower's fingers hook through a loop in the thong, imparting a spin that stabilizes flight and increases both range and accuracy, at a slight increase in cost. Javelins can also be launched from an atlatl for even greater distance, making them a versatile weapon for both melee and ranged combat.

name: Fishing Spear
description: A thin, spear-like implement used to strike fish near the surface of the water, often featuring a forked point or a cluster of barbed prongs to improve the odds of a successful strike despite the visual distortion caused by light refraction at the water's surface. While its design resembles a javelin, its balance is optimized for thrusting and jabbing rather than throwing, making it a poor choice if pressed into use as a thrown weapon.

name: Pilum
description: The signature throwing spear of the Ancient Roman legions, plural pila, distinguished by a long iron shank ending in a hardened point but with the portion just behind it left soft and unhardened. On striking a shield or target, this soft iron bends, preventing the enemy from pulling the weapon free easily or hurling it back, and if it strikes a shield it can deform and stick fast, dragging the shield down and penalizing its use. A pilum that hits becomes a useless bent rod until straightened. The barbed Frankish angon is a closely related derivative weapon.

name: Harpoon
description: A barbed hunting spear, found in virtually every coastal and riverine culture, with a line attached to the shaft so the wielder or a boat crew can retrieve it and its catch after a throw. Unlike a true entangling weapon, the harpoon is not meant to bind a target; pulling hard on the line tends to yank the barbed head back out rather than hold fast. In melee it handles clumsily, more like an awkward heavy spear than a balanced weapon, but its primary purpose is to strike large prey such as fish, seals, or whales from a distance and keep them tethered.

name: Spear
description: A pole topped with a pointed stabbing head, prized for its sheer versatility: usable in one hand or two, often suitable for throwing, and effective against nearly any opponent.

name: Lance
description: A heavy cavalry spear sturdy enough to deliver the full kinetic energy of a charging horse and armored rider, equipped with stirrups and a high-backed saddle for stability. Unlike an infantry spear, it typically has a grip and handguard suited for the unique stresses of a mounted charge. Specialized tournament lances are deliberately blunt and designed to shatter harmlessly on impact, used for jousting rather than war.

name: Pike
description: An extremely long spear designed for use in dense infantry formations. The listed pike represents a five-yard weapon, though shorter four-yard and longer six-yard versions exist with correspondingly adjusted reach, weight, and strength requirements. Pikes were the backbone of 'pike and shot' formations, providing a defensive wall of points against cavalry while gunners provided ranged firepower.

name: Cutlass
description: A short, single-edged sword with a distinctive open-framed basket hilt, favored by sailors and pirates for its compact size and effectiveness in the tight confines of a ship. Versions lacking the basket hilt exist and handle more like a plain shortsword. The mass-produced cutlasses associated with large naval powers were relatively cheap and common, making them an iconic weapon of maritime combat and boarding actions.

name: Broadsword
description: The term for what medieval European warriors simply called an 'arming sword' — a straight, double-edged, pointed blade roughly 30 to 40 inches long, designed for both cutting and thrusting. The name was coined later by writers to distinguish robust military swords from narrower civilian blades. Nearly every ironworking culture developed an equivalent, often called simply 'the sword' in the local tongue, including the Scandinavian longsax and the Roman spatha.

name: Large Falchion
description: A broadsword-sized version of the falchion, a heavy, often curved, single-edged blade that favors powerful cutting strokes over precise thrusts. The widened, forward-curving tip concentrates mass for devastating chopping blows, much like a machete scaled up for war. Includes the largest parangs and the Chinese ring sword. Its unbalanced heft makes it harder to parry quickly but rewards committed, slashing attacks against lightly armored foes.

name: Thrusting Broadsword
description: A variant of the broadsword built with a sharper point optimized for thrusting attacks while retaining solid cutting capability, representing the more historically accurate form of the classic 'arming sword.' Traditionally straight, double-edged, and well-balanced, it served as the primary sidearm of knights and men-at-arms for centuries, equally capable of punching through gaps in armor or delivering powerful slashes to unarmored opponents.

name: Bastard Sword
description: A sword with a blade long enough for two-handed use but a grip that also allows comfortable one-handed wielding, often called a 'hand-and-a-half sword' in later eras. Includes smaller versions of the Japanese nodachi. Its versatility lets a warrior switch between a shield-and-sword stance and a powerful two-handed grip as the situation demands. The pointed thrusting variant was the historically standard form, valued for piercing gaps in plate armor.

name: Estoc
description: An edgeless European thrusting sword with a triangular, circular, or diamond cross-section blade, purpose-built to pierce gaps and weak points in plate armor. Also called a 'tuck' in England, its rigid, needle-like blade sacrifices all cutting ability for maximum penetrating power, making it the specialized anti-armor sword of the late medieval period when full plate harness made conventional cutting swords increasingly ineffective.

name: Longsword
description: A German two-handed thrusting sword, lighter than a greatsword but with a long grip and blade designed for powerful two-handed thrusts as well as cuts. It can be used two-handed or in a defensive one-handed grip; to facilitate the latter, only the topmost six inches of blade were traditionally sharpened, allowing the wielder to grip the blade itself for added leverage in close-quarters techniques.

name: Thrusting Bastard Sword
description: A bastard sword variant featuring a sharper point optimized for thrusting attacks, representing the historically standard form of this versatile weapon. Combining a long, two-handed-capable grip with a blade suited for punching through armor gaps, it gave warriors the flexibility to switch between one-handed sword-and-shield combat and a powerful two-handed thrusting stance as the battlefield demanded.

name: Cavalry Saber
description: A curved sword optimized for one-handed use from horseback, resembling a fencer's saber in profile but built heavier and wielded more like a broadsword. Its curve favors slashing strikes delivered while riding past an opponent, where the horse's momentum adds tremendous force to even a glancing cut. A symbol of cavalry officers for centuries, it balances cutting power with enough weight to survive repeated impacts in melee.

name: Edged Rapier
description: A long, one-handed sword with a narrow blade primarily built for thrusting but given enough of an edge and weight to deliver respectable cuts as well. Early rapiers were often built this way before the type evolved toward purely thrust-oriented designs. Despite the modern myth that rapiers are flimsy, this is simply a longer, thinner cut-and-thrust sword suited to a civilian duelist facing lightly armored opponents.

name: Garrote
description: Any length of cord, wire, or rope used to strangle an opponent, one of the simplest and most universal weapons of stealth and assassination. Utterly silent and easily concealed, it relies on surprise and leverage rather than physical force, making it deadly even in the hands of a weaker attacker against an unprepared victim. Its minimal weight and unobtrusive appearance let it be hidden virtually anywhere on the body.

name: Large Knife
description: A purpose-built fighting knife, larger and heavier than an everyday utility blade but smaller than a shortsword, rarely suited for throwing. Examples include the European ballock knife (or bollocks dagger), the Korean dan gun, the Persian kard, and the Japanese chisel-pointed tanto. Designed primarily for combat rather than camp chores, it offers solid cutting and thrusting capability in a package still small enough for easy carry and concealment.

name: Small Knife
description: The lightest class of fighting knife, sometimes balanced well enough to be thrown effectively. Examples include the Indian bhuj, the Japanese kozuka, and the Indonesian pisau. Easily concealed in boots, sleeves, or belts, a small knife serves as a practical backup weapon, a multipurpose tool, and in skilled hands, a deadly thrown projectile, making it one of the most universally carried implements in any low-tech society.

name: Wooden Stake
description: A simple sharpened wooden stake, little more than a pointed stick but capable of inflicting a nasty puncture wound when driven home. Includes regional variants like the Indonesian liangtjat and paku. While crude and far from ideal, a wooden stake is better than going unarmed entirely, and its ubiquity means one can usually be fashioned from available materials in moments. Famously associated with dispatching supernatural creatures in folklore.

name: Dagger
description: A short, point-only knife in the strict sense, though the term is often used loosely for any small blade from a stiletto to a long knife. Historically, a true dagger was double-edged with a crosspiece and pommel — essentially a tiny sword — including weapons like the Japanese hishi. Lightweight, easily concealed, and deadly in a thrusting attack, the dagger is the quintessential close-quarters and assassination weapon across nearly every culture.

name: Long Knife
description: The largest class of fighting knife, with a total length between 15 and 23 inches, only marginally less substantial than a shortsword but still wielded with knife techniques. Examples include the longest versions of the dirk, kard, and tanto. Capable of both effective cuts and thrusts at slightly greater reach than smaller knives, a long knife bridges the gap between a sidearm blade and a true sword.

name: Rondel Dagger
description: A heavy European dagger fitted with broad disc-shaped guards at both the pommel and handguard. The disc pommel allows the off-hand to drive the blade home with extra force, helping the narrow point punch through gaps in mail or plate armor. If the wielder wears gauntlets, the discs lock the weapon in place point-down, resisting disarm attempts. A favored 'mercy weapon' for finishing downed armored opponents.

name: Stiletto
description: A thin, rigid Italian dagger designed to slip between the links of mail armor and through the joints of plate harness. Its narrow blade is purpose-built for finding and exploiting weak points, making it especially effective against armored opponents at close range. Easily concealed due to its slender profile, the stiletto became infamous as an assassin's weapon in addition to its battlefield armor-piercing role.

name: Main-Gauche
description: A stiff knife with a large basket hilt and broad crosspiece, designed primarily as a parrying weapon to be used in the off-hand alongside a rapier. Its substantial guard can catch and deflect incoming blades, while its rigid blade allows for solid thrusting counterattacks. Not balanced for throwing, the main-gauche exemplifies the paired-weapon fighting styles popular among European duelists.

name: Oar
description: A large boat oar pressed into service as an improvised polearm, used as a weapon of necessity by sailors and shipwrecked travelers worldwide. Includes purpose-made fighting variants like the Okinawan eku and the Maori taiaha. Its long wooden shaft provides decent reach for a crushing weapon, even if it lacks the balance and edge of a dedicated polearm.

name: Light Edged Rapier
description: A lighter, shorter evolution of the edged rapier, retaining a usable cutting edge while moving toward the purely thrust-focused designs that would eventually become the smallsword. Faster and easier to handle than its heavier predecessors, it represents a transitional weapon bridging the gap between cut-and-thrust military rapiers and elegant civilian dueling swords.

name: Light Rapier
description: A later-era rapier well on its way to becoming a smallsword, sacrificing cutting capability entirely for greater speed and a finer point. Designed purely for thrusting in civilian duels, it represents the refinement of the rapier toward the fast, precise fencing weapons that would dominate aristocratic dueling culture in subsequent generations.

name: Rapier
description: A long, one-handed sword with a stiff, narrow blade built specifically for stabbing rather than parrying, meaning rapierists often carried a secondary weapon like a main-gauche or a cloak for defense. Despite a modern myth of fragility, the rapier isn't flimsy — it's simply longer and thinner than a cut-and-thrust military sword of similar weight, reflecting its role as a civilian dueling weapon against lightly armored opponents.

name: Saber
description: A light, one-handed cut-and-thrust sword built for fencing, including weapons like the Thai krabi. Combining a usable edge with a thrusting point and refined balance, the saber became the dueling and military sidearm of choice in many European armies, valued for its speed and versatility compared to heavier cutting swords.

name: Shortsword
description: A one-handed cut-and-thrust sword between 18 and 24 inches long, representing a weapon built for war. Examples include the European cuttoe and hanger, the Roman gladius, the Thai daab, the Indonesian pedang, the Scandinavian seax, and the Japanese wakizashi. Blades made as general-purpose tools rather than dedicated weapons are cheaper but less effective in combat. Its compact size makes it ideal for close-quarters fighting and as a sidearm.

name: Falchion
description: A medieval European term applied broadly to almost any single-edged sword, but most often describing one with a flared, heavy, and/or forward-curving tip that favors cutting over thrusting. Nearly every ironworking culture developed an equivalent valued by both soldiers and civilians for butchering, brush-clearing, and combat alike. Examples include the Philippine bolo, Korean dan sang gum, pre-Roman Iberian falcata, Indonesian parang, Roman sica, and the general 'sickle sword.' Blunt examples exist and deal crushing rather than thrusting damage.

name: Small Falchion
description: A knife-to-shortsword-sized version of the falchion, retaining the type's characteristic flared or curving cutting edge in a more compact package. Suited for one-handed use by those who want a falchion's chopping power without the size and weight of a full shortsword-class weapon, it serves well as both a personal sidearm and a practical utility blade.

name: Short Staff
description: A balanced stick between 25 and 36 inches long, traditionally made of fire-hardened rattan for training or hardwood for actual combat, often used in pairs. Includes the Korean chung bong, the Filipino escrima stick, and the Indonesian tongkat. A lighter cane suitable for use with rapier or smallsword techniques is also covered by these statistics, doubling as both a gentleman's walking accessory and a discreet weapon.

name: Smallsword
description: A one-handed thrusting sword that is speedy on both attack and defense, but whose light weight and short reach are real liabilities against heavier weapons. Representing the refinement of rapier fencing into its purest thrusting form, the smallsword became the standard sidearm and dueling weapon of European gentlemen, prized for elegance and speed rather than raw stopping power.

name: Long Staff
description: A long wooden pole, between roughly eight and nine feet, used two-handed for sweeping strikes and thrusts at extended reach. Traditional medieval European quarterstaves and the English pikestaff fall into this category, as does any broken polearm reduced to its shaft. Its extra length grants reach advantages over a standard quarterstaff at the cost of being somewhat more cumbersome to maneuver.

name: Quarterstaff
description: A balanced five to seven foot wooden pole, wielded two-handed, often gripped in the center for maximum versatility. Praised worldwide for its defensive utility and ability to deliver combat-winning blows, it includes the Japanese bo, Korean jang bong, Indian kettukari and panthiruchan, Thai bamboo plong, Okinawan rokushakubo, and Indonesian toya. Soldiers trained in staff fighting as a backup skill in case their polearm lost its head, making the quarterstaff one of the most broadly taught weapons in history.

name: Greatsword
description: A true two-handed European sword, typically featuring a ricasso — an unsharpened, often leather-wrapped section of blade just above the hilt — ending in two protruding spikes (parierhaken) that protect the wielder's hands and can be gripped for close-range techniques. A sharp-tipped version is the thrusting greatsword. Includes large nodachi and the German zweihänder. Its massive size makes it a devastating but unwieldy weapon requiring significant strength and training.

name: Thrusting Greatsword
description: A two-handed greatsword fitted with a sharper point optimized for thrusting attacks while retaining the type's substantial cutting capability. Also associated with the Scottish claymore depending on the historical period. Its combination of immense reach, cutting power, and a usable thrusting point made it a formidable weapon against both unarmored opponents and gaps in heavy armor, though its size demands considerable strength and space to wield.

name: Light Whip
description: A length of cord or light braided material lacking the weighting and studding of a full whip, used primarily for entangling rather than dealing significant damage. Its lighter construction makes it easier to handle and control for snaring an opponent's limb or weapon, but its strikes carry far less force, making it a specialist tool for grapplers and those seeking to disable rather than injure.

name: Whip
description: A length of braided leather, weighted and studded along its length, that allows the wielder to deliver stinging lashes or snare an opponent's limb or weapon at a distance. Found in cultures worldwide, the whip's extreme flexibility makes it almost impossible to parry effectively, for attacker and defender alike, and its reach lets a skilled user strike from well outside an opponent's normal range.

name: Short Bow
description: A compact wooden self bow, often made from little more than a sturdy bough, representing one of the earliest and simplest bow designs. Though some examples are surprisingly strong, the short bow generally trades power and range for portability, making it favored by hunters, skirmishers, and mounted users who need a lighter weapon. It is strung by hand and shoots arrows placed against the bowstring, requiring a Ready maneuver to nock before each shot. Its modest rated strength requirement makes it accessible to younger or weaker archers.

name: Regular Bow
description: A longer and more powerful self bow than the short bow, made entirely of a single wood such as ash, elm, or yew. It represents the standard hunting and war bow used across much of the ancient and medieval world before composite construction became common. Strung under tension between its two ends, it propels arrows with greater force and range than its shorter cousin, at the cost of being bulkier to carry and use, especially on horseback or in tight quarters.

name: Longbow
description: The pinnacle of single-material bow technology, famed as the weapon of English archers who dominated battlefields like Agincourt. At least six feet long, it is typically made of yew, whose natural elastic properties approach those of composite materials. Drawing a longbow to its full extent requires considerable arm strength and years of practice to master, but it rewards the archer with excellent range and penetrating power, capable of punching through armor at distance when massed in volleys by trained companies of bowmen.

name: Reflex Bow
description: An extreme form of composite bow whose limbs curve entirely away from the archer when unstrung, storing exceptional energy when drawn. Built from layered horn, wood, and sinew glued together, reflex bows give superior range and damage compared to self bows of similar size, making them prized by mounted archers and elite infantry. The added complexity and exotic materials make them expensive and labor-intensive to produce, often taking craftsmen years to season and laminate properly before a bow is battle-ready.

name: Straight Composite Bow
description: A composite bow shaped much like a conventional self bow but built from glued layers of horn, wood, and sinew rather than a single piece of timber. This lamination lets the bow exceed the draw length and power of a similarly sized wooden bow without breaking. Roughly comparable in power to a longbow but considerably less bulky, it was favored by charioteers and cavalry across Eurasia, including the Japanese dai-kyu, since its compact form suits use from horseback or a moving platform.

name: Crossbow
description: A flexion-powered ranged weapon consisting of a bow mounted crosswise on a stock, with the string drawn back by hand and held by a trigger mechanism until released. The familiar Western crossbow developed mainly during the Middle Ages, though a Chinese version dates back to roughly 600 B.C. Unlike a bow, a crossbow can be held at full draw indefinitely while the user aims, trading rate of fire for ease of use and the ability to deliver bow-equivalent power with comparatively little training.

name: Repeating Crossbow
description: A Chinese crossbow variant, known as the chukonu or zhuge nu, fitted with an overhead ammunition hopper holding ten bolts. The shooter operates it by working a lever handle backward and forward, which cocks the bow and feeds a fresh bolt automatically, allowing a shot every other second without manual reloading between bolts. Its rated strength is limited to that of its user, and its bolts hit comparatively softly, but its rapid follow-up fire made it a useful weapon for suppressing enemies at close range, especially from fortifications.

name: Composite Crossbow
description: Developed in Europe around 1100 A.D., this crossbow replaces the simple wooden self bow of the standard crossbow with a layered composite prod of horn, wood, and sinew glued together, much like a composite bow. The result is a noticeably more powerful weapon for a similar size and draw, capable of delivering significant punch through armor. Composite crossbows require a stronger user or mechanical aid to draw fully, but their improved energy storage made them a major step up in lethality over earlier wooden-prod designs.

name: Pistol Crossbow
description: A diminutive crossbow from China, scaled down small enough to be wielded and fired with one hand. Its compact size makes it easy to conceal in a sleeve, a boot, or even built into the heel of a stirrup, giving an assassin or bodyguard a hidden ranged option. While far weaker than a full-sized crossbow, it retains the same drawn-string trigger mechanism, and its tiny darts can still be lethal at close range, particularly if poisoned, making it a favorite tool of spies and palace guards.

name: Prodd
description: Originating in Europe and the Middle East, the prodd (or 'prod') is technically the name for any crossbow's bow assembly, but as a weapon in its own right it refers to a bird-hunting crossbow that fires lead pellets instead of bolts. Used by fowlers and small-game hunters, it delivers a crushing rather than piercing blow suited to killing birds without ruining their plumage or meat. Specialized prodds were also adapted in the Near East to lob small naphtha-based incendiary grenades instead of pellets, trading accuracy for a fire-based area effect.

name: Slurbow
description: A European and Ottoman refinement of the composite crossbow, distinguished by a built-in arrow guide — a grooved channel that lets it launch one or several small, unfeathered darts instead of full-sized bolts. The slurbow can be loaded with either two medium darts or five smaller ones at once, releasing them in a single shot for a shotgun-like spread. This versatility made it useful against lightly armored or massed targets, though the multiple lightweight projectiles individually hit less hard than a standard bolt.

name: Throwing Stick
description: Any sufficiently heavy, well-balanced stick suitable for throwing at game or an opponent, representing one of the simplest and oldest ranged weapons available to humans. Lacking the aerodynamic refinement of a boomerang, a throwing stick relies on raw mass and a straightforward overhand or sidearm throw to deliver a crushing blow. Cheap, plentiful, and requiring no crafting beyond selecting and trimming a suitable branch, it served as an accessible backup weapon or hunting tool for peoples without access to more specialized ranged arms.

name: Large Throwing Knife
description: A knife sized and balanced specifically for hurling rather than fighting, lacking the substantial handle and handguard of a combat knife and giving a penalty when used in melee. The large size variant carries more mass for a harder-hitting throw at the cost of being bulkier to conceal and carry in numbers. If used in melee despite its poor balance, it should be treated as an ordinary large knife but with reduced effectiveness, reflecting its sharpened-for-throwing rather than fighting-oriented design.

name: Small Throwing Knife
description: A compact knife purpose-built for throwing, smaller and lighter than the large throwing knife and correspondingly easier to carry several at once or hide about the body. Its light weight and lack of a proper handle make it a poor choice for melee, where it should be treated as a small knife used at a disadvantage. Its small size means each individual throw delivers less damage than a larger blade, but its concealability and the ability to carry a handful for rapid successive throws make it popular among assassins and duelists alike.

name: Arrow
description: The standard ammunition for any bow, a slender wooden shaft tipped with a point and fletched with feathers or similar vanes at the rear to stabilize its flight. War arrows are commonly barbed by default, making them painful and damaging to remove. Archers had access to numerous variants beyond the basic arrow: blunt heads for hunting fowl or training, leaf- or crescent-shaped cutting heads, fire arrows with fused gunpowder tubes, fire-cage arrows carrying an incendiary payload, lightweight flight arrows optimized for distance, and humming bulb arrows that whistle for signaling.

name: Crossbow Bolt
description: The short, heavy projectile fired by a crossbow, similar in concept to an arrow but shorter and stiffer to suit the crossbow's flatter trajectory and different power delivery. Bolts are typically tipped with a hardened point for piercing armor and may be fletched with small vanes for stability over their shorter flight path. Like arrows, they are consumable ammunition that must be recovered or replaced after use, and dedicated bolts are required for crossbows just as arrows are required for bows; the two are not interchangeable.

name: Padded Cloth Armor
description: A simple armor of heavy felt about a quarter-inch thick, or a stuffed quilt with two cloth layers sandwiching rags, tow, horsehair, rock salt, dried grass, or straw. Sometimes sheepskin with wool worn inside substitutes for similar effect. This is the most basic and widespread form of body armor, cheap to produce and comfortable to wear under heavier protection. It offers only modest resistance to blows but is lightweight, breathable, and easy to maintain compared to metal alternatives.

name: Layered Cloth Armor, Light
description: A semi-rigid defense made from multiple layers of quilted cloth, exemplified by the Greek linothorax, European padded jack, Indian peti, and the hair-and-fiber armor of South America and the Pacific Islands. The light version uses fewer layers of lighter fabric than medium or heavy variants, giving moderate protection for its weight. Layered cloth provides better protection than leather of similar weight, with quality depending on fabric grade and quilting spacing.

name: Layered Cloth Armor, Medium
description: A semi-rigid cuirass of quilted cloth with more layers than the light version, providing solid protection while remaining far cheaper and lighter than metal armor. Worn historically across many cultures as either standalone protection for common soldiers or as a base layer beneath mail and plate. The number of layers and fabric weight determine its defensive value, with medium representing a substantial but still wearable thickness of padding.

name: Layered Cloth Armor, Heavy
description: The thickest and most protective form of quilted cloth armor, built from many dense layers of fabric and padding. While heavier and bulkier than the light or medium versions, it rivals leather and even some metal armors in protection at a fraction of the cost. Common among cultures with limited access to metal, heavy layered cloth was a mainstay of low-tech militaries and provided surprisingly effective defense against cuts and blunt blows alike.

name: Cane Armor
description: Armor woven from flexible cane rods or rattan, sometimes laced to a tree-bark lining, shaped into cuirasses, helmets, or greaves. Common among the Inca of Peru and across many Pacific Islands, with occasional use in Europe. Cane armor is lightweight and surprisingly resilient against blows, but its organic construction makes it combustible — it can catch fire if burning damage penetrates its defense, a significant hazard near torches or incendiary weapons.

name: Horn Armor
description: Armor crafted from antler, ivory, hoof, turtle shell, or baleen, materials that can be molded into scales or plates when heated in water. Popular in resource-poor regions like the Asian steppes and Arctic, famous examples include Mycenaean boar's-tusk helms and Sarmatian horse-hoof scale armor. Horn is light, tough, and takes a good edge against blows, making it a viable substitute for metal armor where ores and smithing knowledge were scarce.

name: Straw Armor
description: A heavy but cheap defense woven from straw mats, offering surprisingly decent protection at minimal cost despite being bulky and uncomfortable to wear. Historical accounts describe straw-mat breastplates absorbing musket shot well enough to prevent serious injury. Like cane and other plant-fiber armors, straw is combustible and will burn if struck by fire that penetrates its protection, but its low cost made it accessible to even the poorest soldiers and militia.

name: Wood Armor
description: Armor formed from solid carved wooden plates fitted to the body, or assembled from wooden slats and rods tied together with cord or rawhide and hung loosely from the shoulders. This construction is semi-ablative, gradually losing protective value as it absorbs repeated blows and splinters. Wood armor was used by cultures with abundant timber but limited metalworking, providing a rigid, if heavy and somewhat fragile, defense against weapons.

name: Leather Armor, Medium
description: Flexible armor made from medium-weight hides such as bear, aurochs, buffalo, or large crocodile. Used from Europe to Indonesia, it remains supple enough for freedom of movement while offering reasonable protection against cuts and blows, though it resists piercing attacks less effectively. Medium leather armor was a common choice for warriors who needed mobility, often worn as a standalone cuirass or as a backing layer for scale and other reinforced armors.

name: Leather Armor, Heavy
description: Armor cut from thick hides of massive animals such as elephant, hippopotamus, and rhinoceros, once widespread across Asia until overhunting of rhinoceros for armor contributed to its decline (coastal Chinese clans later substituted whaleskin). Heavy leather offers solid protection against cuts and blunt blows, though it remains weaker against piercing attacks. Its bulk and weight make it less flexible than lighter hides, but it provided an effective, metal-free defense for soldiers across many cultures.

name: Layered Leather Armor, Light
description: A cuirass built from a few stacked layers of leather, lighter and more flexible than the medium and heavy versions, used to absorb impact and resist impaling better than a single thick hide. Layered leather armor appeared in Bronze Age China and was later adopted by Asian nomads, Eastern Europeans, and South American cultures. The light variant remains supple enough for mobile fighters while still providing meaningfully better protection than plain leather.

name: Layered Leather Armor, Medium
description: A rigid cuirass formed from multiple thicker layers of leather, providing solid protection against cuts and impaling by distributing impact across the layers. This construction was widespread from Bronze Age China through medieval Asia, Eastern Europe, and South America. The medium grade represents a balance between the mobility of the light version and the heavy protection of the thickest layered leather cuirasses.

name: Layered Leather Armor, Heavy
description: The thickest form of layered leather cuirass, built from many stacked hide layers into a rigid shell that resists cuts, blunt trauma, and impaling attacks better than any single-layer leather armor. Heavy and cumbersome, it was favored where leather was abundant but metal was scarce. Leather scale armor, made from overlapping leather plates, can also be treated using these heavy layered leather statistics.

name: Hardened Leather Armor, Medium
description: Known as cuir-bouilli, this leather is softened in hot water, molded to shape, then dried or slowly baked and finally waterproofed with wax, resin, or lacquer. The result is a hard, water- and shatter-resistant material excellent for deflecting weapons, with improved resistance to impaling compared to untreated leather. First documented in Western Europe near the end of the 12th century but used centuries earlier in Asia, hardened medium leather forms solid cuirasses or segmented panel armor.

name: Hardened Leather Armor, Heavy
description: The heavy-grade version of cuir-bouilli, hardened leather soaked, molded, dried, and lacquer-sealed into a tough rigid shell offering superior protection against cuts and impaling compared to medium hardened leather. Used for solid cuirasses or for segmented panel armor assembled from narrower hardened strips. Its waterproofing makes it more durable in wet conditions than untreated hides, though it remains lighter than equivalent metal armor.

name: Rawhide Armor
description: Essentially untanned leather, statistically treated as hardened leather armor but with two key weaknesses: it only provides its protective DR while dry, losing all defensive value if soaked until thoroughly dried and reshaped, and it has only half the structural durability of properly hardened leather. Coating it with oil, wax, lacquer, or resin can stave off moisture damage, but only true tanning or a very dry climate prevents its gradual deterioration over time.

name: Leather of Quality Armor
description: Armor made from superior hides prized for exceptional toughness: kangaroo leather with three times cowhide's tensile strength, abrasion-resistant sharkskin, lightweight yet tough giraffe hide, or select cuts of horse hide, sometimes further improved with advanced tanning. These exotic and rare materials provide better protection than ordinary leather of the same weight, making leather-of-quality cuirasses prized possessions for warriors who could obtain such hides, often via long-distance trade.

name: Jade Armor
description: A ceremonial suit assembled from polished jade plates wired together in lamellar fashion, created by the ancient Chinese as funerary goods believed to preserve the body of the deceased. Despite its ritual origin, jade is extraordinarily tough and could serve in actual combat, offering protection comparable to stone lamellar armor while also conferring social prestige — wearing such an exquisite suit improves how others react to the bearer, reflecting its association with wealth and the divine.

name: Bone Armor
description: Armor fashioned from dead animal bone, including the bone-splint breastplates of the American Plains Indians and the animal-skull helmets used by some South American and African tribes. Though too brittle for prolonged use, bone armor was crafted when better materials were unavailable. It is treated as horn armor but is semi-ablative, gradually wearing away and losing protective value as it absorbs repeated impacts, eventually shattering under sustained punishment.

name: Scale Armor, Light
description: Armor made of small overlapping metal plates laced in rows to a cloth or leather backing garment, one of the oldest known forms of metallic body armor. The light grade uses thinner, less-overlapped plates than medium or heavy scale, giving a balance of mobility and protection. Scale armor's flexible backing allows decent movement while the metal scales deflect cuts, though the construction gives somewhat reduced resistance to crushing blows.

name: Scale Armor, Medium
description: The most common grade of scale armor, with thicker and more overlapped metal plates laced to a cloth or leather backing than the light version. This balance of protection and mobility made medium scale a mainstay of armies across Eurasia for millennia. The plates' thickness and overlap determine protection level, and medium scale represents the typical equipment of professional soldiers in many metal-using cultures.

name: Scale Armor, Heavy
description: The thickest and most protective grade of scale armor, typically worn only on the chest due to its weight, though panels could extend to guard the shoulders, abdomen, and thighs. Heavy scale's densely overlapped plates give superior protection against cuts and thrusts, rivaling early plate armor, at the cost of significant bulk. A variant called Chinese mountain scale uses star-shaped scales that lock together on impact for additional rigidity.

name: Lamellar Armor
description: Armor of small overlapping plates laced directly to each other without need for a separate backing garment, distinguishing it from scale armor's cloth-backed construction. The famous o-yoroi of Japan's samurai exemplifies this style. Lamellar shares the same defensive statistics as scale armor of equivalent grade (light, medium, or heavy), offering flexible yet substantial protection assembled from many small individually-replaceable plates, popular across Central Asia and East Asia.

name: Jack of Plates
description: European-style jacks consist of overlapping metal plates, similar to scale armor, sandwiched between two layers of lightly padded fabric and held in place with cord; Oriental jacks instead sew individual plates into pockets within the garment. Either construction closely resembles ordinary quilted cloth from the outside, making this armor fairly easy to conceal beneath civilian clothing despite its solid metal protection — a useful trait for bodyguards or travelers wary of displaying armor.

name: Mail Armor, Light
description: A fabric of small interlocking metal rings, each riveted closed and linked through four neighbors in the prevalent 'four-in-one' pattern. Light mail uses fairly large links of light-gauge wire, and was historically more often layered beneath other armor than worn alone. Mail is flexible and offers freedom of movement, but as flexible armor it remains susceptible to blunt trauma even when it stops a blade or point. Probably the most successful body armor ever devised, mail saw continuous use for nearly 2,000 years.

name: Mail Armor, Fine
description: Made from small links of light wire, fine mail flows through the fingers like metallic cloth yet resists all but the heaviest sword cuts and spear thrusts. The earliest examples date to the Roman period. Its fine, dense weave gives better protection per pound than light or heavy mail and makes it especially suited for jazerant construction, where it is sewn inside layers of padding for concealed armor. Like all mail, it remains vulnerable to crushing impact.

name: Mail Armor, Heavy
description: Mail woven from large links of heavy-gauge wire, historically worn as primary armor by Roman, Viking, and Norman warriors rather than layered beneath other protection. Heavy mail offers the best protection of the standard mail grades, stopping cuts and most thrusts effectively, though like all mail it suffers reduced resistance to crushing blows. Its substantial weight and the riveted ring construction made it a status symbol as well as a practical defense for elite warriors for two millennia.

name: Butted Mail Armor
description: A cheaper variant of heavy mail in which the wire links are bent into rings but never riveted closed. This makes manufacture far faster and easier but significantly weakens resistance to impaling attacks, since weapon points can pry open the unsecured rings. Historically rare except as ceremonial armor in most cultures, butted mail has become popular among modern re-enactors for its ease of construction, though it offers noticeably less protection than properly riveted mail of the same weight.

name: Banded Mail Armor
description: Light mail reinforced with horizontal strips of leather woven through every other row, stiffening the weave and improving resistance to blunt trauma compared to plain mail. This rare construction is unsuitable for joints and limbs that require flexibility, so it is normally reserved for rigid neck collars. The leather banding negates mail's usual penalty against crushing damage, trading some of mail's flexibility for sturdier, more rigid protection at the cost of additional weight.

name: Jazerant Armor
description: A mail shirt sandwiched between two layers of light padding and/or fine leather, with the mail sewn inside the padding rather than worn over it — making jazerant the most common form of concealed armor. The name derives from the Arabic kazaghand, first recorded in 12th-century Middle Eastern use. Jazerant can be built around any regular mail grade, typically fine mail, retaining that mail's weight and protection while presenting as an ordinary padded garment to casual observation.

name: Mail and Plates Armor
description: Also called combined mail, this armor incorporates vertical rows of overlapping metal plates into a mail garment, appearing in India, Russia, and the Middle East around the 14th century. The added plates give noticeably better resistance to crushing damage than heavy mail alone, while retaining much of mail's flexibility at the joints and edges. This hybrid construction represents a transitional step between pure mail and the segmented and plate armors that would eventually supersede it.

name: Jousting Mail
description: A specialized form of mail mentioned in medieval accounts, apparently designed for tournaments where jousts were conducted with fully sharpened war lances. It isn't entirely clear how jousting mail differed from ordinary field mail, but it was evidently more rigid and considerably heavier, providing superior protection. As with later jousting plate, its construction hampers the wearer's mobility, imposing a penalty to combat skills other than Lance.

name: Segmented Plate Armor, Light
description: Armor made from large horizontal metal bands curved around the body and overlapped to permit some articulation, the best-known example being the Roman lorica segmentata. The light grade uses thinner bands than the medium or heavy versions. Segmented plate is much easier to fashion than solid plate, since the individual sections are smaller and require less precise tailoring — segments are connected by lace, wire, or rivets, or riveted to a canvas or leather foundation.

name: Segmented Plate Armor, Medium
description: The mid-grade of segmented plate, made from larger or thicker overlapping horizontal bands than the light version, curved to follow the body and connected for articulation. This is the construction of the famous Roman lorica segmentata, an early example of mass-produced munitions armor issued to soldiers who couldn't afford mail or bronze cuirasses. Quick to assemble once the bands are forged, segmented plate offered legions a good balance of protection, cost, and manufacturing speed.

name: Segmented Plate Armor, Heavy
description: The heaviest grade of segmented plate armor, using thick overlapping horizontal bands for maximum protection while retaining some articulation at the joints between segments. Such armor saw use beyond Rome, appearing in the Middle East and Asia as well; the earliest known example is the bronze Dendra panoply of Greece, circa 1400 B.C. Heavy segmented plate rivals solid cuirasses in protection while being considerably easier to manufacture and repair in the field.

name: Brigandine, Light
description: Well-tailored, close-fitting armor made of small overlapping metal plates riveted to the inside of a cloth or leather garment, with only the rivet heads visible on the outside. First appearing in Europe in the mid-14th century and evolving from the coat of plates, brigandine became fashionable courtly wear while still providing excellent battlefield protection. The light grade uses fewer or thinner plates, and brigandines were often flamboyantly decorated with gilded rivets in attractive patterns rather than concealed.

name: Brigandine, Medium
description: The heavier grade of brigandine, with more or thicker overlapping plates riveted inside the foundation garment for substantially improved protection over the light version. Brigandine was civilian as well as military wear, emulated even in faux brigandine garments that mimicked the look without any actual plates (sometimes mistakenly called 'studded armor', though such imitation garments provide no real protection). Genuine medium brigandine, however, offered protection comparable to early plate armor and remained popular into the 16th century.

name: Proofed Paper Armor
description: Heavy armor made from laminated barkcloth (often called 'paper armor') combined with several layers of silk to proof it against light firearms. Ordinary laminated barkcloth, called jigap in Korea, was issued as cheap disposable armor to common soldiers and excels at distributing impact and trapping weapon points, but the silk-reinforced proofed version achieves dramatically higher protection. Like other paper and barkcloth armors, it remains combustible and can catch fire if burning damage penetrates its defense.

name: Plate Armor, Light
description: The lightest grade of solid plate armor, made from shaped iron or steel plates specifically curved to cause blows to glance off harmlessly. Full plate first appeared in Western Europe in the late 1300s and, when custom-fitted and properly articulated, could be surprisingly light and comfortable while allowing a full range of movement. Light plate covers the torso with thinner plates than the medium or heavy grades, balancing mobility with solid metal protection.

name: Plate Armor, Medium
description: A mid-weight suit of solid plate, using thicker plates than the light grade for substantially improved protection at moderate additional weight. By the 15th century, plate armorers used pieces of varying thickness across the body, with lighter plates on less-vulnerable areas like the ribs, forearms, and shins, and heavier plates on the head and chest. Medium plate represents the well-articulated, well-balanced harness typical of a knight equipped for general battlefield use.

name: Plate Armor, Heavy
description: The thickest and most protective standard grade of plate armor, offering superior defense at the cost of significant weight and reduced mobility. Anything heavier than this is generally reserved for specialized jousting harnesses or the heaviest proofed armor and is usually worn only on the head or chest, since a complete suit of such thickness would be too cumbersome to articulate. Heavy plate represents the upper limit of practical full-body protection achievable before TL5.

name: Bronze Plate Armor
description: Full suits of solid bronze plate armor available even at TL1, predating the iron plate armors of later tech levels. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin — roughly 8-10% tin was typical for armor — and properly cast and work-hardened bronze performs as well as iron for protective purposes. During the Iron Age, bronze remained the most common metal for plate armor because iron had to be forged from small billets unsuited to large plates; bronze was eventually reserved for elite troops as iron became more available.

name: Copper Armor
description: Armor made from unalloyed copper, used by very early TL1 societies, most notably for helmets — Sumerian copper helmets are among the earliest known helmet examples. Copper's metallurgical properties make it poorly suited to armor: it is soft, dents easily, and doesn't hold an edge or resist impact as well as bronze or iron. Despite this, copper armor was produced at full cost for the protection it offered, representing the earliest stage of metal armor before bronze became the material of choice.

name: Pot Helm
description: Also called a skullcap or cervelliere, this is the simplest of helmets, protecting only the top of the skull while leaving the face and neck completely exposed. Iconographic evidence places the earliest helmets in Sumer at the start of the second millennium B.C., with copper giving way to bronze as the preferred material. Cost and weight are calculated as a fraction of equivalent torso armor of the same material; cloth padding can be added for a small additional DR bonus.

name: Bascinet
description: A helmet more comprehensive than the pot helm, commonly depicted on Norman cavalry, extending down to cover the entire head except part of the face — covering the skull fully and the rear of the face area but leaving the front of the face open. It covers the ears, giving the wearer a degree of Hard of Hearing, but has only a small chance of incidentally protecting the face from a frontal blow. Padding can be added beneath for additional DR.

name: Full Helm
description: A helmet covering the entire skull and face like the Greek 'Corinthian' helm, leaving only the eyes exposed through narrow slits that are very difficult to target accurately. While offering excellent head protection, the wearer suffers from Hard of Hearing and has no peripheral vision, making situational awareness in combat difficult. This trade-off between maximum protection and sensory limitation made the full helm iconic of heavily armored hoplite and similar warriors.

name: Coif
description: Head protection made of mail, sometimes attached directly to a mail shirt like a hood, covering the same areas as the bascinet plus the neck. A coif only causes Hard of Hearing if layered with padding underneath. It is often worn over a padded liner for comfort and additional DR, and beneath a rigid helmet for layered protection. A coif can also extend down to cover the upper chest and shoulders, adding partial torso protection at increased cost and weight.

name: Greathelm
description: A large helm worn over another, smaller helmet, more common in tournaments than on the battlefield. Some versions, such as the great bascinet, bolt onto torso armor and provide enough interior space for the head to move freely. The greathelm offers excellent protection including the neck, but severely limits hearing and peripheral vision (Tunnel Vision). It is an exception to normal layering rules since it sits over a rigid inner helmet rather than requiring a flexible underlayer.

name: Parrying Buckler
description: A small buckler reinforced for parrying, providing a bonus to Block rolls in addition to its modest defense bonus. Bucklers are wielded with a central handgrip and can be readied in one second and dropped as a free action, but it's difficult to put full weight behind a buckler in a shield rush. This compact shield is favored by duelists and lightly-armed fighters who prioritize speed and a free off-hand over the heavier protection of a full shield.

name: Small Shield, Light
description: A small shield, rarely longer than the forearm, giving minimal defense bonus but excellent maneuverability — the wielder suffers only a minor DX penalty in close combat. Middle Eastern archers sometimes carried such shields while firing arrows 'under' them in a horizontal position, and other fighters wielded a knife in the same hand. The light version is built from a single layer of hide over a light wooden frame, keeping weight to a minimum.

name: Small Shield, Heavy
description: The heavier variant of the small shield, built with additional wood and hide layers or metal reinforcement for improved durability and protection compared to the light version, while still remaining compact — rarely longer than the forearm. It retains the maneuverability advantages of small shields, allowing fighters to wield a weapon or even fire a bow while carrying it, at the cost of somewhat more weight than its light counterpart.

name: Medium Shield, Light
description: A medium-sized shield covering the wielder from chin to thighs, constructed of a single layer of hide over a light wooden or wicker frame. Both light and heavy variants of the medium shield were used in some form by nearly every culture until the end of the Middle Ages, in many different shapes, though circular designs were by far the most common. The light version trades some durability for reduced weight and easier handling.

name: Medium Shield, Heavy
description: The heavier construction of the medium shield, built from multiple layers of hide stitched together or wood faced with leather and metal, covering the wielder from chin to thighs. This sturdier build was common in formation fighting from the Sumerians onward across many cultures. It withstands more punishment than the light medium shield and provides a slightly better defense bonus, at the cost of additional weight that the wielder must carry and maneuver.

name: Large Shield, Light
description: A large shield, lighter models made of a single layer of hide stretched over a light wooden or wicker frame, or of several hide layers stitched together. Such shields cover the warrior from chin to shins and could be oval, rectangular, scalloped, hexagonal, or figure-eight shaped, curved to wrap slightly around the body. They usually incorporate a guige (neck strap) to take some weight off the arm, and were used by the Sumerians and many cultures afterward.

name: Large Shield, Heavy
description: Heavier wooden large shields covered with leather and/or metal, common in formation fighting and used by many cultures after their introduction by the Sumerians. Covering from chin to shins and curved to wrap around the body, the heavy large shield provides excellent battlefield coverage and durability. This is the baseline 'heavier model' assumed for most shield types described in Low-Tech, with DR 4 construction of wood, hide, and metal strapped to the arm.

name: Comanche Shield
description: A medium shield made of two layers of hide laced around a wooden hoop and stuffed with feathers, hair, grass, or even paper salvaged from pioneers' books. This construction is treated as Fragile (Combustible), meaning it can be destroyed more easily and may catch fire. It is carried over the shoulder on a neck strap (guige) while riding, making it a practical defense for mounted warriors of the Great Plains.

name: Dueling Buckler
description: The smallest of bucklers, consisting of little more than a metal boss with a handgrip, used by German duelists who called it a 'hut' (hat). It provides no meaningful defense bonus but grants a bonus to Block rolls and gives DR to the shield hand itself. Any ordinary buckler that has been destroyed in combat can still be wielded as a dueling buckler, making it a last-resort defense as much as a purpose-built one.

name: Heater Shield
description: By the end of the 13th century, the heater shield replaced the larger kite shield as Europe's standard, tapering to a point at the bottom but offering no particular benefit over other shapes besides perhaps being a little easier to manage on horseback. Functionally treated as a medium shield, the heater is the iconic shape most associated with knightly heraldry, its flat upper face providing an ideal surface for displaying a coat of arms.

name: Kite Shield
description: During the 11th century, this long, teardrop-shaped shield took over from the round shield as Europe's most popular design, remaining dominant into the 13th century when it was used by both cavalry and infantry. The kite shield reaches down to protect the leading leg in formation and can cover the rider's left leg on horseback. Built like a heavy large shield but tapering toward the bottom, it weighs somewhat less than a comparable rectangular large shield.

name: Dueling Long Shield
description: Depicted in Renaissance fencing manuals such as Talhoffer's Fechtbuch and the Codex Wallerstein, dueling long shields are designed for trial by combat: long, narrow shields mounted on vertical poles with spikes at either end, sometimes with cutouts enabling hooking attacks. These shields are weapons in themselves, usable with the Shield skill at a penalty or the Staff skill at a greater penalty, representing a highly specialized judicial-combat implement rather than a battlefield defense.

name: Pavise
description: A large standing shield carried by one man and designed to protect one or two people, such as an archer or crossbowman plus the pavise's bearer (the paviser). Some versions had folding legs to stand unassisted, or rows of large nails projecting from the face so that abandoned pavises left face-up on the ground would deter pursuit, functioning like caltrops. Classed as cover rather than a true shield, it provides no defense bonus but excellent stationary protection during sieges.

name: Monankon
description: A one-armed torsion catapult, simpler than the ballista, with a single massive arm and sling pouch that hurls stones. The arm swings up and strikes a padded crossbar, flinging the projectile in a high arc. The later Roman version was nicknamed 'onager' for its mule-like kick. Used for siege bombardment of fortifications, it requires a large crew, a sturdy frame, and a torsion spring of twisted sinew or hair cord. Its violent recoil and immense size make it a fearsome but immobile engine of war.

name: Ballista
description: A torsion-powered, two-armed engine resembling a giant crossbow, mounted on a frame and used to hurl heavy bolts or bundled stones with a flat, direct trajectory. Built by the Greeks and refined by Romans, ballistae came in many calibers from one-pound field pieces to massive 180-pound wall-breakers. Twin torsion springs of twisted sinew store energy drawn back by winch or windlass. Crews load bolts or stone bundles for devastating impaling or crushing hits against troops, walls, or ships at long range.

name: Carroballista
description: The oldest known field artillery piece, a stone-throwing ballista permanently mounted on a wheeled carriage with harness for two draft animals and storage for a hundred bolts. Fielded by the later Roman legions, it could be towed onto the battlefield and brought into action quickly, giving infantry mobile fire support. Despite its bulk it is light enough for soldiers to haul by hand in a pinch. It fires impaling bolts with good accuracy at moderate range, making it useful against massed enemy formations or fortified positions.

name: Beam Sling
description: Also called a mangonel or traction trebuchet, this is the principal heavy siege weapon of China and the Middle East. A massive lever pivots on a frame; the short arm is hauled down by a team of men pulling ropes, flinging the long arm's sling-held projectile in a high indirect arc. Sizes are rated by crew size, from 15 to 100 men, with weighted versions adding counterweights to the short arm for greater range. Slow to operate but capable of hurling huge stones to crush walls and fortifications.

name: Trebuchet
description: The classic medieval counterweight catapult, designed to smash castle walls with massive stones. A long pivoting beam has a heavy counterweight fixed to its short end and a sling on its long end; releasing a restraint lets the counterweight fall, whipping the sling around to launch the projectile in a high indirect arc. Built in large and small versions, trebuchets require enormous frames, treadmills to raise the counterweight, and large crews. They were the premier siege weapon of the European Middle Ages until gunpowder artillery replaced them.

name: Trebuchet, Hinged
description: An advanced refinement of the basic trebuchet in which the counterweight hangs from hinges rather than being fixed rigidly to the beam. This lets the counterweight swing freely and descend in a nearly vertical path as it falls, wasting far less energy on horizontal motion and dramatically increasing the weapon's range compared to a fixed-counterweight design. Built in large and small versions like its simpler cousin, the hinged trebuchet represents the pinnacle of mechanical siege engine development before gunpowder bombards rendered such engines obsolete.

name: Gastraphetes, Double
description: A scaled-up version of the personal gastraphetes ('belly bow'), this large two-armed flexion weapon shoots two long bolts simultaneously and requires mechanical winches to draw. Invented in Syracuse in the 4th century B.C., it was among the earliest pieces of mechanical artillery, predating torsion-powered designs. Mounted on a tripod, it delivers powerful impaling hits at long range with good accuracy. Its double-bolt volley made it especially effective against massed infantry or for picking off multiple targets in a single shot.

name: Gastraphetes, Mountain
description: A lighter, mobile variant of the gastraphetes shooting a single shorter bolt, fitted with an unusual asymmetrical mount that allows it to be set up and leveled on sloping or uneven ground. This made it valuable for mountain warfare and irregular terrain where standard artillery frames could not be stably emplaced. Like its larger cousin it is flexion-powered, drawing energy from a great bow rather than torsion springs, and requires a mechanical winch to cock. Crews used it for direct-fire support against troops and light fortifications.

name: Petrobolos
description: An early flexion-powered stone-throwing engine, also called a lithobolos, predating torsion artillery. It uses a great bow whose stored elastic energy in bent wood launches stones in a relatively flat trajectory for crushing damage against walls, gates, and massed troops. Available in light and heavy models, the heavier versions require substantial crews and tripod mounts. As one of the earliest forms of mechanical artillery developed in Syracuse, the petrobolos represents the transitional step between simple bows and true torsion catapults.

name: Polybolos
description: The 'automatic weapon' of the ancient world, a torsion-powered bolt-thrower fitted with a hopper of bolts mounted above the firing mechanism. Turning a crank handle draws the bowstring via a chain-driven mechanism, drops a bolt from the hopper, and releases the shot — the earliest known use of both cams and flat chains. Capable of firing twenty bolts in rapid succession with brief pauses to re-tension, the polybolos was designed to intimidate enemy infantry with sustained fire, though some generals feared its rate of fire would waste ammunition.

name: Scorpion
description: A torsion-powered, two-armed bolt-thrower nicknamed for its sting and scorpion-like appearance, essentially a stone-throwing ballista adapted to fire long bolts with a low, flat arc of fire. Scorpions are rated by the length of the shaft they propel, ranging from small 27-inch models to massive 72-inch siege versions. Mounted on tripods, they deliver precise, hard-hitting impaling attacks at considerable range. Their narrow torsion-spring window of view requires a Vision roll before aiming, but they remained standard Roman and Greek anti-personnel and anti-fortification weapons for centuries.

name: Arbalest
description: A large medieval mechanical artillery piece resembling an oversized crossbow, powered by a built-in winch that supplies the drawing force. While 'arbalest' is sometimes used loosely for ordinary crossbows, here it denotes a much larger weapon requiring a tripod mount and crew assistance to operate. It fires heavy impaling bolts at very long range with excellent accuracy. Arbalests were used in fortification defense and siege work, offering a flexion-powered alternative to torsion-based ballistae with simpler construction and maintenance.

name: Springald
description: A bizarre hybrid siege weapon combining a one-armed throwing mechanism, like a monankon or trebuchet, with the direct-fire role of a bolt-thrower. A thick wooden arm resembling half a bow is winched back under tension and released, snapping forward to strike and drive a heavy bolt out through a guide hole. Springalds were primarily defensive weapons, mounted in fortifications to repel besiegers at relatively short range with powerful impaling hits, their rectangular base making them awkward to traverse quickly.

name: Cheiroballistra
description: A compact, two-armed, torsion-powered bolt-thrower made of iron rather than wood, small and light enough for a single soldier to operate — even from horseback. Developed by the later Roman Empire as an advanced refinement of earlier ballista designs, it draws the string inward toward the center rather than out to the sides, giving the string a sharp V-shape that channels force forward efficiently. The wide-set torsion springs grant a better field of view than older scorpions, allowing aimed shots without a preliminary Vision roll. Roman cavalry trained to cock, load, and fire it on the move.

name: Greek Fire
description: A closely-guarded incendiary mixture invented by the Syrian refugee Kallinikos in 673 A.D. and kept secret by the Byzantine Empire until its formula was lost around the 1200s. Likely based on naphtha, it burns fiercely even on the surface of water, making it devastating against enemy ships — pouring water on it only spreads the flames, earning it the nickname 'marine fire.' Typically delivered via fire-siphon or thrown in ceramic flasks, Greek fire functions like a Molotov cocktail, clinging to targets and inflicting sustained burning damage that is extremely difficult to extinguish.

name: Naphtha
description: A distilled petroleum product developed by Near Eastern alchemists who pioneered methods of refining crude oil into 'naft.' Functionally similar to ordinary oil for damage purposes, naphtha is highly flammable and burns for an exceptionally long time once ignited — far longer than earlier pitch-based mixtures. It was the key ingredient in many incendiary weapons of the era, including the zarraq al-naft hand-pumps used by Arab forces, and represents one of the first true refined fuels used in warfare, centuries before its modern petrochemical descendants.

name: Incendiary Flask
description: A light ceramic vessel that shatters on impact, or a wooden one that burns through, used to deliver incendiary mixtures such as early pitch combustibles, naphtha, or Greek fire onto a target. Small pint-sized flasks could be thrown by hand or launched from a light ballista, spreading flaming liquid over the impact area and anything nearby. Simple, cheap, and effective, the incendiary flask was the low-tech precursor to the Molotov cocktail, used by besiegers and defenders alike to set fortifications, ships, and siege equipment ablaze.

name: Fire-Siphon
description: A Byzantine shipboard weapon for spraying Greek fire onto enemy vessels, based on earlier Roman pumping engines and immortalized in accounts of an 11th-century sea battle. Built directly into a warship's hull with its nozzle projecting outward, the fire-siphon requires a two-man crew to operate the pump and takes time to build pressure before the fuel begins to emerge. Once flowing, it produces a continuous jet of burning liquid that can engulf an enemy ship's deck and rigging, making it one of history's first true flamethrowers.

name: Cheirosiphon
description: The handheld descendant of the shipboard fire-siphon, appearing on Byzantine battlefields by the early 10th century and adopted by Arab forces as the zarraq al-naft. Resembling a large squirt gun with an attached fuel tank, it sprays Greek fire or naphtha and uses a length of slow match mounted near the nozzle to ignite the fuel as it emerges.
