After a preparation period to build pressure, it can deliver a single powerful jet or spray a wide area, making it effective against both individual targets and groups of attackers on open ground or aboard ships.

name: Incendiary Sphere
description: A Chinese siege weapon available from the early 1100s, this perforated metal ball is packed with several pounds of low-grade black powder and meant to be hurled from a beam sling. Once lit, the powder burns for two minutes, spraying flame out through the holes and igniting a wide area around the impact point. Metal hooks studding its surface let it catch on enemy fortifications, siege ladders, or ship rigging, anchoring it in place so its fire keeps burning where it does the most damage.

name: Bombard
description: Among the earliest true gunpowder artillery, the bombard is a heavy, short-barreled gun firing large or huge stone balls, built like a wooden barrel from metal bars bound with hoops, with a separate breech piece. Too heavy and awkward for gun carriages, bombards were built into vehicles, buildings, or massive wooden frames, making them essentially immobile fixed weapons. Despite this, their enormous stone projectiles could batter down castle walls and city gates that had resisted mechanical artillery for centuries, marking the beginning of gunpowder's dominance in siege warfare.

name: Crapaudeau
description: A long-barreled, small-caliber breechloading gun firing small stones, representing one of the more refined early European gunpowder weapons. Lighter and more precise than the massive bombards, the crapaudeau's extended barrel improves both accuracy and range while its breechloading design speeds reloading compared to muzzle-loaded cannon of the same era. It served as a mid-sized fortification and field defense gun, bridging the gap between massive immobile bombards and the smaller, more mobile guns that would follow.

name: Veuglaire
description: A fairly small breechloading gun with a barrel about twelve times its caliber in length, firing stone shot somewhat larger than the crapaudeau's. The veuglaire occupied a middle ground in the early gunpowder artillery lineup, offering more punch than the lightest guns while remaining manageable for fortification crews. Its breechloading design, typical of European guns before the standardization of muzzle-loading cannon, allowed reasonably quick reloading for defensive fire from castle walls or ship decks.

name: Swivel-Gun
description: A small cannon mounted on a pintle that allows it to be swung freely to engage targets from a ship's gunwale or a city wall, entering use as a relatively low-powered breechloader at TL3 and refined into a more powerful TL4 weapon. Swivel-guns gave ships and fortifications a quick-response weapon for repelling boarding attempts or skirmishing with nearby vessels without the lengthy aiming process required by larger fixed cannon. Their light weight and pivoting mount made them indispensable secondary armament on warships and merchant vessels alike.

name: Gonne
description: One of the earliest personal firearms, a miniature bronze cannon mounted on the end of a wooden pole and fired using a simple cannonlock — a touchhole ignited with a handheld slow match or hot wire. Known as a midfa in Arabia and a pao ('eruptor') in China, the gonne usually fires lead balls but some illustrations show bolt-like projectiles. Mounting it on a pole both helped aim the weapon and kept the user's hands away from a barrel that might burst. Gonnes saw use on Hussite war wagons and represent the direct ancestors of the matchlock arquebus.

name: Mr. Facing-Both-Ways Gonne
description: A Chinese variant gonne fitted with a barrel at each end of a long pole, allowing the weapon to be flipped around with a Ready maneuver for a second shot after the first barrel is discharged. The added weight and length make the weapon more awkward to carry and wield than a standard gonne, but the extra mass also helps dampen the felt recoil of firing. This design reflects early experimentation with multi-shot capability before reliable revolving or multi-barrel mechanisms were developed.

name: Ten-Eyed Gonne
description: A remarkable Chinese gonne pushing repeated fire to its mechanical limit: each end of the weapon has touchholes for five separate charges, fired in sequence from the outermost inward, with damage and range increasing slightly with each successive shot as the barrel heats and fouls. Once one end's five charges are spent, the gun is flipped around with a Ready maneuver to fire the other five. European weapons of similar concept became known as 'Roman candle guns.' Reloading the inner charges is notably slower than the outer ones.

name: Summer Clothing
description: Lightweight, breathable garments suited to hot climates, such as the thin white Arabian thobe, the pleated linen kalasiris of ancient Egypt, an Indian cotton sari, a loincloth, or a grass skirt. Loose-fitting cuts allow air to circulate freely, keeping the wearer cool and comfortable. Such garments offer essentially no protection from weapons or weather extremes beyond sun exposure, but they are cheap, light, and practical for daily wear in warm regions. Cost is typically a small fraction of a person's cost of living, reflecting simple materials and construction.

name: Ordinary Clothing
description: Typical work wear or everyday dress for a temperate climate, made of heavier material than summer clothing or worn as an extra layer over it. This represents the standard outfit of a commoner or laborer: tunics, breeches, simple dresses, and similar sewn or wrapped garments fastened with pins, cords, or simple buckles. While it offers minimal protection from blades or arrows, it provides modest insulation against mild cold and shields the skin from sun, dirt, and minor abrasions during daily labor. Heavier ordinary clothing can increase fatigue costs in hot climates.

name: Winter Clothing
description: Heavy outdoor clothing for cold climates, consisting of extra layers, thick textiles, or furs designed to protect the whole body from heat loss, especially the feet, hands, head, and neck. In freezing temperatures it allows the wearer to resist fatigue loss from cold without penalty. Because of its bulk and dense weave, winter clothing is thick enough to provide a small amount of protection against cutting weapons. Common examples include fur-lined coats, wool cloaks, felted leggings, and heavy hoods, often layered over ordinary clothing for maximum effect in harsh environments.

name: Foot Wrappings
description: The earliest and simplest form of foot protection, consisting of large tough leaves, pieces of hide, or cloth wrapped around the foot and bound in place with lacing or cord. Foot wrappings keep the feet warm and provide a little cushioning for the soles, but wear out quickly and need replacing every few miles of travel. A minimal version covers only the foot itself, while a more complete wrapping extends up the lower leg, offering additional warmth and abrasion resistance for travelers who lack proper shoes or boots.

name: Mittens
description: Simple bags of fur or hide covering the hands to keep them warm, bound at the wrist and possibly lacking separate thumb compartments. The earliest examples date back to the second millennium B.C. and were sometimes lightly padded for use as boxing mitts. Mittens are clumsy to wear, reducing fine dexterity and grip strength considerably since the fingers cannot move independently, but they provide reliable warmth and a degree of protection against cutting injuries. A lightly padded boxing variant offers broader protection against blunt impacts as well as cuts.

name: Moccasins
description: Light, thin leather footwear favored by hunters, scouts, and others who need to move silently through wilderness terrain. Their soft soles and flexible construction allow the wearer's feet to flex naturally, improving balance and stealth on natural surfaces, granting a bonus to moving quietly comparable to going barefoot. The same basic design and statistics apply to similar lightweight footwear from other cultures, such as the Japanese tabi. Moccasins offer only token protection against sharp objects underfoot but excel at comfort and quiet movement.

name: Mukluks
description: Soft boots made from moose or caribou hide and lined with moss, traditionally worn by Arctic peoples. Their thick natural insulation protects the feet against frostbite even in extreme cold, and their soft construction reduces the noise and balance penalties normally suffered when walking on snow and ice. While not designed for combat or rough terrain, mukluks are prized for survival in frozen environments, providing a degree of cushioning against the cold ground as well as modest resistance to abrasion from icy surfaces.

name: Sandals
description: Open-construction footwear consisting of a hard sole, often made of wood, leather, or woven plant fiber, held to the foot with straps. Sandals are the footwear of choice in warm climates, allowing air to circulate around the feet to keep them cool while still protecting the soles from hot ground, sharp stones, and rough terrain. Their open design offers no protection to the top of the foot or ankle, making them unsuitable for combat or cold weather, but their low cost and minimal weight make them ubiquitous across hot-climate cultures throughout history.

name: Hobnailed Sandals
description: Footwear reinforced with hobnails, short metal-headed nails driven through the sole, a hallmark of Roman military sandals known as caligae. The protruding metal studs dramatically improve the wearer's footing on uneven, slick, or muddy ground, letting soldiers ignore penalties for bad terrain in combat. However, the hard nails make stealthy movement difficult, producing telltale clicks and scrapes on hard floors such as tile, cobblestone, or bare rock. Hobnailing can be applied to any footwear, adding cost and weight for the metal studs and the reinforced sole needed to hold them.

name: Gloves
description: Hand coverings with separate sheaths for each finger, allowing finer manual dexterity than mittens while still providing some protection from cold and minor cuts. Early Greek and Roman texts mention their use, though they were likely worn even earlier in colder regions. Standard gloves slightly hamper fine motor tasks and grip strength, while open-palmed variants restore grip at the cost of less warmth. Custom-tailored, high-quality gloves made for a specific wearer reduce the dexterity penalty, making them popular among archers, falconers, and craftsmen who need both warmth and manual precision.

name: Shoes
description: Light leather or textile footwear that covers the foot but does not extend up the leg to protect the ankle or shin. Low-tech shoes are not carefully tailored and lack distinct left and right pairs, with shapes varying by era and fashion: some are pointed, others square-toed. They may be simple slip-on slippers or fastened with laces or buckles. Shoes offer a modest layer of protection for the sole and upper foot against minor impacts and sharp debris, while remaining comfortable and practical for daily wear in towns and on roads.

name: Boots
description: Sturdy footwear made of thicker material than shoes, extending up to cover part of the lower leg for added protection and support. With the advent of the stirrup, riding boots sometimes incorporated a heel to prevent the foot slipping through. Boots are the standard footwear for soldiers, travelers, and riders, offering meaningful protection for the foot and shin against cuts, abrasion, mud, and impacts. Their thicker leather construction makes them more durable than shoes, though correspondingly heavier and more expensive, and they remain a practical choice across most temperate and cold environments.

name: Hat
description: A broad category of head coverings made from felt, straw, leather, fur, or cloth, found in nearly every culture and era. Originally invented to shield the wearer from sun, rain, and cold, hats quickly became fashion items and markers of social status, with shape, material, and decoration signaling wealth, occupation, or rank. While a basic hat provides little defense against weapons, it is essential for survival in extreme heat or cold, preventing sunstroke or frostbite. A hat specifically reinforced to resist blows is properly classified as a helmet rather than ordinary headgear.

name: Snow Goggles
description: Simple wooden eyewear carved with narrow horizontal eye-slits, worn to protect against snow blindness caused by intense sunlight reflecting off snow and ice fields. Traditionally used by Arctic peoples such as the Inuit, snow goggles drastically reduce the amount of light reaching the eyes, at the cost of significantly narrowing the wearer's field of vision. The carved wooden frame is light and durable, tied to the head with cord or leather thongs, and the goggles also provide a small amount of physical protection for the eyes from wind, ice particles, and debris.

name: Cloak
description: A versatile wrapped garment fastened about the neck with a cord or clasp, used for warmth, weather protection, and improvised shelter. Some cloaks are split for ease of riding, while others have armholes or sleeves resembling ponchos. A cloak can double as a sleeping blanket or makeshift tent, help conceal carried items, and even serve defensively when wrapped around an arm to block incoming blows or held outstretched to absorb the impact of thrown weapons. A heavier wool or leather cloak provides modest cut resistance at the cost of additional weight and expense.

name: Parka
description: A hooded, long-sleeved coat made from two layers of hide, with the inner layer's fur facing inward to trap body heat. The outer layer can be treated with waterproofing agents to shed rain and snow. Worn over winter clothing, a parka provides substantial protection against arctic cold, significantly aiding resistance to fatigue and injury from freezing temperatures. The combined layering is thick enough to provide a small amount of protection against all types of attack, though the bulk of the garment makes precise manual tasks somewhat more difficult for the wearer.

name: Poncho
description: A simple rectangular blanket with a hole cut for the head, worn either as everyday clothing or as an additional protective layer against cold. The loose, draping design hampers fine arm movements somewhat, but its bulk is excellent for concealing items carried on the body, much like a cloak. Ponchos are found across many cultures, especially in South America, and are valued for being quick to make, easy to don, and adaptable as a groundsheet, sunshade, or improvised stretcher in addition to their use as clothing.

name: Leather Apron
description: A flexible but thick protective garment worn by craftsmen such as blacksmiths and stonemasons to shield their bodies and clothing from sparks, hot metal, splinters, and abrasive debris during work. The apron covers the front of the torso, leaving the very top of the chest exposed, and extends down to protect the upper legs. While not designed as combat armor, its thick leather construction provides a meaningful degree of resistance to light cuts and impacts, making it a practical everyday item for any workshop where flying debris or sparks are a hazard.

name: Long Coat
description: A trench coat, duster, kaftan, or similar long garment covering the torso and extending to the knees or below. Its voluminous folds are excellent for concealing bulky items such as weapons or tools, though such a garment may draw suspicion in certain settings. A version made from leather or heavy felt provides meaningful cut resistance at increased cost and double the weight. Particularly heavy leather variants, sometimes called buff coats, were worn as genuine armor by cavalry and officers during the English Civil War and offer protection comparable to hide armor.

name: Undercover Clothing
description: Specially tailored clothing designed to hide items on the wearer's body, incorporating hidden pockets, loops, reinforced panels, or special cuts that disguise the presence of concealed objects. The quality of the work determines how effective the concealment is: a basic version offers a modest bonus to hiding small items, while a more elaborate version, requiring significantly more skilled tailoring and finer materials, offers a much greater bonus. Outwardly, undercover clothing looks like ordinary garments, making it invaluable for spies, smugglers, and bodyguards who need to carry weapons or tools discreetly.

name: Beekeeper's Outfit
description: A full-body protective garment depicted in medieval illustrations, consisting of an ankle-length robe of linen or hemp canvas with long sleeves and bloused gloves, topped with a hood that covers the head and shoulders and a circular mesh veil protecting the face. Together these provide complete body coverage against stinging insects. While the outfit is not heavy enough to offer meaningful protection against weapon blows, its tightly woven fabric and mesh effectively resist swarms of bees, wasps, or similar insects, making it indispensable for beekeepers and honey gatherers working with wild hives.

name: Fireproof Clothing
description: A long-sleeved, hooded garment of heavy wool treated with a fireproofing paste of vinegar, red clay, dissolved talc, fish glue, and sandarac, recorded in Moslem sources as protective gear for soldiers handling battlefield incendiaries. Some warriors reportedly coated themselves in this concoction, set themselves alight, and charged into the enemy to spread chaos. The thick, treated wool fabric closely resembles the protective garments used by firefighters into the 20th century, providing substantial resistance to burning damage while remaining flexible enough to wear in combat.

name: Lockpicks
description: A compact set of slender metal probes and blank keys of varying sizes, used to manipulate the internal components of a lock and open it without the proper key. A basic set is sufficient to attempt tumbler, rotary, and barb-spring locks, while warded rotary locks generally require both hands to manipulate. A higher-quality kit includes a more complete and finely made set of blank keys and probes, improving the user's chances of success. Lockpicks are small enough to hide easily and are considered evidence of criminal intent if discovered by authorities in many jurisdictions.

name: Housebreaker's Kit
description: A comprehensive burglary toolkit packed into a capacious sack, combining lockpicks, a small pry-bar, a mallet, a chisel, a small saw, ten yards of thin rope, a padded grappling hook, and a lantern. The sack itself is roomy enough to carry stolen goods after a successful break-in, making this kit a one-stop solution for a thief planning to enter a building, defeat its locks or barriers, and depart with valuables. Its bulk and variety of tools make it conspicuous and incriminating if found, but it equips an infiltrator for nearly any forced-entry scenario.

name: Padded Grappling Hook
description: A grapnel consisting of three or four sturdy metal hooks fixed to a rigid spine with an eyelet for attaching a rope, used to secure a climbing line to a ledge, windowsill, or wall by throwing it upward. When it strikes stone or concrete it normally rings out loudly, but a padded version wrapped in cloth or leather significantly muffles the noise, making it far less likely to alert nearby guards. The padded variant is slightly heavier and more expensive than the bare metal hook, but the reduction in noise is highly valued by anyone attempting a quiet, unauthorized climb.

name: Skytale
description: An ancient cryptographic device, apparently first used in classical Greece, consisting of a strip of leather or paper wound in a helix around a cylindrical wooden baton. A message is written horizontally across the strip so that each letter spans the width of the strip; once unwound, the writing becomes an unreadable jumble of characters. To read the message, the recipient must wrap the strip around a baton of exactly the same diameter as the original, realigning the letters into their correct sequence. This simple but effective transposition cipher device was used to transmit military orders securely between commanders.

name: Invisible Ink
description: A small vial of secret ink made from common kitchen ingredients such as lemon juice, onion juice, or other plant extracts that dry invisibly on paper but reveal writing when heat or a chemical reagent is applied. Ancient writers described various recipes, including crushed gallnuts revealed by a vitriol reagent, and spurge juice darkened by rubbing ashes over it. Using invisible ink effectively requires a steady, practiced hand, since too much pressure leaves visible indentations while too little leaves no readable trace once revealed, making it a favored tool for spies and secret correspondents.

name: Disposable Paper
description: A specially made sheet of rice paper or similar thin material that dissolves quickly in warm water or can simply be swallowed, allowing a secret message to be destroyed instantly once read. Suitable rice paper was invented in China early in the Tang Dynasty and became prized by spies, diplomats, and conspirators for transmitting sensitive information without leaving incriminating physical evidence behind. Each sheet is extremely thin, light, and inexpensive, making it practical to carry several at once for repeated covert correspondence with minimal risk of discovery.

name: Belladonna
description: A dose of toxin extracted from the deadly nightshade plant (Atropa belladonna), whose active ingredient is atropine. This poison can be administered as a follow-up agent applied to a weapon or as a digestive agent slipped into food or drink, with effects beginning after a short delay and then recurring repeatedly over several hours. Victims suffer ongoing internal damage and, once severely weakened, begin hallucinating with distorted perceptions. Belladonna is sold as a small vial or packet of prepared extract, valued by assassins and poisoners for its slow, debilitating, and difficult-to-trace effects.

name: Cantharides
description: Also known as 'Spanish fly,' this poison is derived from the dried and crushed bodies of the blister beetle (Lytta vesicatoria). It can be administered as a digestive poison mixed into food or drink, causing severe internal damage and nausea after about an hour, or applied directly to the skin as a contact agent, where it causes painful blistering almost immediately. Victims who are pushed to their physical limit by this poison may suffer violent convulsions. Sold as a fine powder in small packets or vials, cantharides has a long history of use both as a poison and, in folklore, as a supposed aphrodisiac.

name: Curare
description: A potent poison extracted from the sap of a South American vine (Strychnos toxifera), traditionally used by indigenous hunters to coat blowgun darts and arrows. As a follow-up agent applied to a weapon, curare takes effect within about a minute and causes repeated, severe internal damage over the following hours regardless of resistance, with failed resistance rolls causing paralysis and a critical failure risking death by choking. Sold as a small gourd or vial of thick, dark paste, curare is prized by hunters for swiftly immobilizing prey and by assassins for its reliable, paralytic effects.

name: Deathcap Mushroom
description: A dose of toxin prepared from the deathcap fungus (Amanita phalloides), one of the most lethal poisons available at low tech levels. Slipped into food or drink, it takes about an hour to take effect, after which it causes severe internal damage accompanied by hallucinations, with further waves of damage recurring over many hours. Failed resistance can cause unconsciousness or even a fatal heart attack, and the victim suffers escalating headache pain throughout the ordeal. Sold as dried, ground mushroom flesh in a small packet, deathcap is feared as one of the deadliest and least legal poisons available.

name: Fugu Toxin
description: A dose of poison extracted from the liver of the fugu, or Japanese pufferfish, whose active ingredient, tetrodotoxin, is among the most lethal natural toxins known. It can be used as a digestive poison or applied to a weapon as a follow-up agent, both causing paralysis on a failed resistance roll and the risk of fatal choking on a critical failure, along with skin tingling and severe weakening of the victim's strength and dexterity. Extracting the toxin safely is dangerous and requires great skill. Sold as a small sealed vial of pale extract, fugu toxin is extremely valuable and tightly controlled.

name: Hemlock
description: A prepared dose of poison from the hemlock plant (Conium maculatum), historically infamous as the substance used to execute the philosopher Socrates. Ingested in food or drink, it takes about an hour to cause weakness in strength and dexterity, followed by recurring internal damage over several hours. As the poison progresses, it causes creeping paralysis beginning in the feet and moving upward through the legs and into the torso, potentially leading to blindness or, in severe cases, a heart attack. Sold as a small vial of bitter greenish extract, hemlock has been used for both executions and assassinations since antiquity.

name: Monkshood
description: A prepared dose of poison from plants of the genus Aconitum, commonly called monkshood, blue rocket, or wolfsbane, whose active ingredient aconite attacks the nervous system. Used as a digestive poison, it causes a tingling sensation in the skin, tongue, and throat after a short delay, followed by recurring internal damage, nausea, and retching. As a follow-up agent applied to a weapon, it causes a slower onset of similar internal damage. Severely affected victims suffer escalating weakness and difficulty breathing. Sold as a small vial of dark extract or dried root powder, monkshood has long been associated with witchcraft and poisoning in European folklore.

name: Viper Venom
description: A dose of venom milked from a live viper (a snake of the family Viperidae), used as a follow-up agent applied to the points of weapons such as arrows, darts, or blades. After a short delay, the venom causes significant internal damage with each subsequent wound the victim receives, unless resisted, in which case the damage is reduced. A single viper can yield up to four doses, though extracting each one safely requires skill and carries the risk of a dangerous snakebite to the handler. Sold as a small sealed vial of yellowish fluid, viper venom is a classic poison for coating weapons used in assassination or hunting.

name: Lacquer (Toxic Sap)
description: A dose of raw sap tapped in spring from the lacquer tree (Toxicodendron vernicifluum), normally used to preserve wood and leather with a hard, glossy finish, but also usable as a poison. Applied to the skin as a contact agent, it causes painful blistering similar to poison ivy after a brief delay. When mixed with incense and burned, it acts as a respiratory poison, causing immediate coughing or sneezing and internal damage to anyone who breathes the fumes. Sold as a small jar of thick, dark sap, lacquer is more often legitimate craft material than poison, giving it a higher legality rating than most toxins.

name: Lime Powder
description: A pouch of powdered quicklime, an inexpensive caustic substance also used in mortar and mineral adhesives, repurposed here as a respiratory or blood-targeting poison, especially effective against the eyes. Thrown or blown into a victim's face, it causes immediate coughing and sneezing and, if not resisted, ongoing burning damage along with severe pain and potential blindness lasting until the affected area is thoroughly flushed with water. Lime powder loses its potency within days unless stored in a sealed, dry container. Its low cost and wide legitimate use as a building material make it one of the most accessible improvised poisons.

name: Bindings (Rope and Wire Restraints)
description: Lengths of rope, cord, leather strips, or metal wire used to tie a prisoner's wrists, ankles, or entire body to prevent escape. The amount of rope needed depends on the size of the captive, with additional coils making the bonds harder to break or slip out of. Wet leather strips contract as they dry, tightening further and making escape more difficult, while metallic wire bindings are even harder to work loose but can cut into the skin if the prisoner struggles. Bindings are cheap, lightweight, and universally available, making them the most common form of restraint throughout history.

name: Iron Shackles
description: Metal restraints for the wrists or ankles, locked or riveted closed so they cannot be untied like rope bindings. Forged from iron, shackles are far stronger than any human can break by main force, though a captive may attempt to slip out of them with great skill or pick the lock if one is fitted, albeit with extra difficulty when attempting to free oneself. Riveted shackles can only be removed with proper blacksmithing tools. Sturdy and nearly impossible to escape without specialized knowledge or tools, iron shackles were the standard restraint for dangerous prisoners, slaves, and condemned criminals throughout history.

name: Stocks
description: A restraint device consisting of a pair of hinged wooden boards with cut-out holes, either two for the ankles or three for the wrists and neck. Once a captive's limbs are placed in the matching holes, the boards are closed and locked together, immobilizing the victim while a punishment is carried out. Ankle stocks force the prisoner to sit on the ground with the soles of the feet exposed to abuse, while wrist-and-neck stocks allow the victim to remain standing or walk slowly while restrained. Built from thick timber and iron fittings, stocks are as difficult to escape as iron shackles.

name: Pillory
description: A punishment device built from stocks attached to a tall pole or wooden frame, designed to restrain a standing prisoner's hands and head while leaving the rest of the body exposed. Victims locked in a pillory were displayed in public squares, exposed to the elements and to projectiles, filth, and abuse thrown by hostile crowds, with prolonged exposure risking serious harm from exposure, hunger, or thirst. The pillory was also used as a whipping post, holding a criminal in place during corporal punishment, and was generally reserved for serious offenses due to its severity.

name: Barrel Pillory
description: A hinged wooden barrel fitted with a hole for the victim's neck, used as a portable and humiliating form of restraint and punishment, commonly applied to drunkards. One variant has a solid bottom, forcing the prisoner to crouch in their own filth inside the barrel, while another has an open bottom, allowing the victim to walk around while encased in the barrel and exposed to public ridicule. Made of wooden staves bound with iron hoops and fitted with a locking mechanism around the neck, the barrel pillory was a common feature of town squares and marketplaces in medieval and early modern Europe.

name: Punishment Whip
description: A flexible whip, light cane, or knotted rope specifically designed for corporal punishment and torture rather than lethal combat, dealing relatively minor crushing damage but causing escalating pain with repeated strikes. After being struck, the victim suffers moderate pain that, with successive blows over consecutive seconds, progresses to severe pain, terrible pain, and finally agony. Flogging traditionally involved pinning or tying down the victim and lashing them until agony set in, at which point interrogators could exploit the victim's suffering to extract confessions or information. Canes were more common in Asian punishment traditions.

name: The Rack
description: A heavy wooden torture frame fitted with wrist and ankle restraints attached to either end, with the upper restraints adjustable via a roller and ratchet mechanism. As the ratchet is tightened, the victim's body is slowly stretched, causing extreme pain, then dislocation of the joints, and ultimately separation of limbs from the torso if the process continues to its conclusion. Each ratcheting motion pits the strength of the device's mechanism against the victim's own toughness, with the victim suffering crushing damage to each limb and the spine on a loss. The rack was a centerpiece of formal interrogation chambers in many historical justice systems.

name: Iron Maiden
description: A grisly torture device, popularly but inaccurately attributed to medieval Europe and now believed to have been largely a Victorian-era fabrication. As traditionally described, it consists of a large iron cabinet shaped like a standing human figure, its two halves hinged and lined with adjustable, inward-pointing spikes. A victim placed inside would have the doors slowly closed, driving the spikes into the body while deliberately avoiding vital organs to prolong suffering rather than cause swift death. Constructed of heavy iron plate, the device is massive, ornate, and primarily intended to terrify and inflict prolonged agony rather than to kill quickly.

name: Torture Kit
description: A compact case containing a variety of small implements intended to inflict pain, including knives, pincers, hammers, metallic slivers or bamboo splinters, irons designed for heating in a fire, and vises for crushing bones such as thumbscrews. The kit's true purpose is limited only by the imagination of the torturer wielding it, and its mere presentation to a captive can be enough to instill dread and increase the effectiveness of interrogation before any implement is even used. Compact enough to be carried in a satchel, the torture kit was standard equipment for inquisitors, jailers, and interrogators in many low-tech justice systems.

name: Snow Saw
description: A wooden tool used for carving trapezoidal blocks of compacted snow when building an igloo. Roughly a long, flat wooden blade with a handle, sturdy enough to cut through dense snow without snapping. Any reasonably long, flat object can substitute, but a purpose-made snow saw is more durable and efficient. Used primarily by arctic hunter-gatherers and travelers needing to construct emergency shelters quickly from available materials. It is light and easily carried alongside other survival gear.

name: Bedouin Tent
description: A large residential tent made from breathable woolen cloth, designed for desert living. Its side walls stand five to six feet tall, with a flat or slightly peaked roof providing shade and shelter from sun and wind. The cloth's breathability helps keep the interior livable in hot, dry climates, and using it grants a bonus to desert survival skills. A standard example measures fifteen feet square and houses a family or small group, though it offers no real protective cover, only concealment from view.

name: Yurt (10-foot)
description: A round, collapsible structure built from a wooden lattice framework topped with a domed roof, all covered by a heavy felt shell. More durable than ordinary tents, a yurt resists collapse from a single blow to any support and offers modest protective cover against weather and attacks alike. Used widely across the steppes by nomadic herding peoples, the ten-foot-diameter version provides a snug shelter for a small family, packing down for transport by cart or pack animal during seasonal migrations.

name: Yurt (15-foot)
description: A larger version of the round, collapsible felt-covered yurt, offering more interior space for extended families or groups of travelers on the steppe. Its domed wooden lattice frame is reinforced for stability, and the heavy felt covering resists wind and cold. Like its smaller counterpart, it provides minor protective cover and cannot easily be toppled. Insulated variants lined with tapestries or extra felt layers improve cold-weather survival further, though at greater cost and bulk, making this the premier mobile dwelling of pastoral nomads.

name: Legionary Tent
description: A military-grade tent made from treated leather panels, far more resistant to water and wind than simple cloth tents. Covering a ten-foot-square area and standing six feet tall at its peak, it comfortably sleeps six to eight soldiers with room to stand in the center. Issued to Roman legionaries on campaign, this tent provided reliable shelter in varied climates and terrain, granting a bonus to general survival efforts. Its sturdier construction gives it modest resistance to damage compared to ordinary fabric shelters.

name: Portable Door
description: A framed wooden door designed to be fitted into an opening in a tent or temporary structure, giving travelers and nomads a sense of permanence and security. Because such doors often served as the focal point for visitors entering a dwelling, they were frequently carved, painted, or otherwise elaborately decorated to impress guests. Despite its portability, the door provides genuine protective cover, making it sturdier than most temporary shelter components and a valued possession passed between successive camps or homes.

name: Partition
description: A long panel of cloth or woven straw hung from ceiling beams or tent poles to divide a large interior space into smaller private rooms. Lightweight and quick to install or remove, partitions were common in tents, temples, and houses where flexible use of space mattered. They provide no protection against weapons or weather, serving purely to create visual privacy and define separate areas within a single structure. A typical example measures roughly six by ten feet.

name: Beaded Curtain
description: A series of cords strung with beads, bamboo segments, or shells, hung in a doorway or opening to visually divide a space without blocking airflow. While offering no real protection, the curtain provides light concealment for anyone standing behind it and creates a soft clattering noise whenever someone passes through, making it useful as a simple alarm. It also helps deter flying insects from entering a room, and its decorative rattling materials made it a popular furnishing across many warm-climate cultures.

name: Carpet
description: A thick, durable textile woven by tying tight knots on a loom, producing a dense pile suitable for use as a portable floor covering. Carpets insulated tents and stone or earthen floors against cold, added comfort underfoot, and often served as decorative status symbols when patterned elaborately. Produced across many cultures from wool, silk, or other fibers, a typical rug is priced and weighed by the square foot, making larger carpets significant investments of both materials and weaving labor.

name: Folding Screen
description: A set of hinged panels made from wood, or from wooden frames filled with paper or wicker, forming a freestanding barrier that can be folded flat for storage or transport. Folding screens divided rooms, blocked drafts, or provided modest privacy for dressing and bathing. They offer no real protection from attack, and any forceful blow simply knocks the screen over rather than damaging it meaningfully. A typical six-by-six-foot screen was a common feature in upper-class households across East Asia and beyond.

name: Wicker Fence Panel
description: A lightweight panel woven from flexible branches or reeds, fitted with wooden spikes along the bottom edge so it can be planted into the ground to form a temporary corral or boundary. Carried by herders and nomads, these panels assemble quickly into enclosures for livestock. They provide no real defense against determined intruders or predators, but domesticated animals generally respect the visual barrier and avoid pushing through unless panicked, making the fence useful for managing herds on the move.

name: Brazier
description: A footed metal dish designed to hold burning coals, fitted with a handle or chain for easy carrying between rooms or campsites. Braziers served double duty as cooking surfaces and portable heaters, capable of raising the temperature of a small room by several degrees. Their open design allowed for ventilation but also meant they posed a fire risk if tipped. Widely used before the advent of efficient furnaces, braziers were a staple of both humble homes and wealthy households throughout the ancient and medieval world.

name: Warming Pan
description: An almost fully enclosed metal brazier attached to a long handle, designed to be slid beneath bedcovers so that slowly burning coals warm the bedding through the night. Primarily a comfort item, the warming pan was essential in cold climates and could make a bed function as effective protection against cold exposure. Its enclosed design minimized the risk of sparks escaping into bedding, though care was still needed when handling the hot metal pan and its glowing contents.

name: Water Jug (Unglazed)
description: An unglazed earthenware jug whose porous walls allow water to seep slowly to the outer surface and evaporate, drawing heat away and cooling the contents inside. Although the vessel loses a small percentage of its water to evaporation each day, the cooling effect proved valuable in hot, dry environments, and using one improves a traveler's chances of surviving in deserts or jungles. A simple, inexpensive, and widely produced item, it was a staple of daily life in arid regions long before refrigeration existed.

name: Folding Fan
description: A hand-held fan constructed from thin wooden slats, sometimes covered with fabric or paper webbing, that folds flat for storage and opens into a wide arc for use. Fanning oneself with it creates a light, cooling breeze, offering simple relief from heat. Inexpensive and lightweight, folding fans were common accessories across many cultures and could also serve decorative or ceremonial purposes when elaborately painted or carved, becoming fashion statements among the wealthy.

name: Parasol
description: A collapsible canopy mounted on a stick, opened overhead to provide complete shade and protection from sunburn. Made of wood and plain cloth in a one-yard diameter, parasols originated in China by 1000 B.C. and spread to the Mediterranean centuries later. More expensive versions used bamboo and silk for reduced weight at double the cost. Larger two-yard versions, often carried by a servant to shade another person, were status symbols as much as practical sun shields.

name: Oil Lamp
description: A simple open stone or pottery bowl with a notch to hold a wick, burning a pint of oil for roughly twenty-four hours of light. The earliest designs date back tens of thousands of years and remained common throughout the low-tech era. Being completely open, an oil lamp is prone to spilling if moved quickly, and if knocked over it briefly burns where it lands, risking igniting dry surfaces. Despite the hazards, it remained the cheapest and most accessible source of artificial light for millennia.

name: Enclosed Oil Lamp
description: An improved pottery lamp design that fully encloses the oil reservoir, leaving only a spout to hold the wick exposed. This refinement greatly reduced the risk of spills compared to earlier open-bowl lamps, making the lamp safer to carry and move around a household. Becoming common in classical antiquity, these enclosed lamps were often mass-produced in molds and sometimes decorated with reliefs depicting gods, animals, or scenes from daily life, blending utility with modest artistry.

name: Torch
description: A bundle of dried rushes bound together to form a hand-held light source, providing about an hour of illumination when lit. An improved version is dipped in pitch before use, doubling its burn time and making the flame resistant to being extinguished even while running. Torches were the most basic portable light available across nearly all low-tech societies, cheap and easy to make from readily available materials, and useful in emergencies as both a light source and a makeshift weapon.

name: Pitch Torch
description: An improved torch made from a bundle of rushes dipped in pitch before lighting, giving it twice the burn time of a plain torch and the ability to remain lit even when carried at a run. The pitch coating made the flame more resilient against wind and movement, making this version preferred for travel through unlit areas, processions, or military use where reliable lighting mattered. Like ordinary torches, it could also serve as an improvised weapon, setting flammable targets alight.

name: Tallow Candle
description: A candle made from rendered animal fat, burning for approximately twelve hours and providing steady but modest illumination. Tallow candles produce noticeable smoke and a distinct, often unpleasant odor as they burn, a byproduct of the fat-based wax. Despite the smell, they were the most affordable candle option for common households, used for lighting homes, workshops, and religious spaces where flame-based light was needed through long nights.

name: Beeswax Candle
description: A candle made from refined beeswax, burning for about twelve hours with minimal smoke and a far more pleasant scent than tallow alternatives. The superior burning qualities and cleaner light made beeswax candles a luxury item, often reserved for wealthier households, churches, and special occasions. Their higher cost reflected the labor-intensive process of collecting and refining beeswax compared to simply rendering animal fat, making them a marker of status as well as practicality.

name: Covered Lantern
description: An oil lamp whose flame is shielded behind thin sheets of translucent bone, or glass in later periods, protecting it from wind and rough handling. Unlike open lamps, a covered lantern does not go out in a strong wind or when carried at a run, making it far more reliable for travel, military use, or work outdoors at night. The protective panes diffuse the light slightly while keeping the flame burning steadily, representing a significant practical improvement over earlier open-flame lighting.

name: Collapsible Bed
description: A substantial wooden bed frame held together with removable wooden pegs, allowing it to be quickly disassembled for transport or storage. The mattress rests on a network of ropes strung tightly across the frame, providing support and some give for comfort. Though heavy and bulky compared to simpler bedding, a collapsible bed offered a far more comfortable night's sleep than sleeping on the ground, and was favored by officers, nobles, and others who valued comfort while traveling.

name: X-Frame Chair
description: One of the earliest forms of portable furniture, the X-frame chair consists of a folding wooden frame with a cloth or leather seat stretched across it, essentially identical in design to a modern folding director's chair. Lightweight and quick to set up or break down, these chairs were favored by traveling nobles, military commanders, and officials who needed comfortable seating wherever they camped. Their simple, durable construction made them practical for centuries across many cultures.

name: X-Frame Table
description: A larger relative of the X-frame chair, this folding wooden table has neither arms nor a back, instead providing a flat surface supported by a collapsible crossed-leg frame. A typical example measures three feet square and comfortably seats at least four people for dining or work. Like other X-frame furniture, it could be quickly folded for transport, making it a practical choice for military camps, traveling merchants, and outdoor gatherings.

name: Headrest
description: A carved wooden support shaped to cradle the back of the head and neck during sleep, used by some societies as an alternative to pillows. Often elaborately carved with decorative motifs or symbolic designs, headrests kept elaborate hairstyles or headdresses from being disturbed during sleep, a practical concern in cultures where hair held social or religious significance. Despite being rigid, users became accustomed to the firm support, and the headrest's durability made it a long-lasting personal possession.

name: Mattress (Cheap)
description: A simple sleeping pad for one person, made by stuffing reeds into a cloth sack or weaving straw into a thick mat, similar to a Japanese tatami. More closely resembling a modern quilt than a modern mattress, this inexpensive bedding option provided basic insulation from cold ground and minor cushioning. Such bedding was notorious for harboring fleas, mice, and other vermin, and could occasionally contribute to the spread of disease through prolonged contact with unwashed bedclothes.

name: Feather Mattress (Fine)
description: A luxurious sleeping mattress filled with soft feathers, providing far greater comfort than reed- or straw-stuffed alternatives. Wealthy households often layered several such mattresses atop one another to maximize plushness. The fine feather filling required significant resources to produce and maintain, making this an item primarily affordable to the upper classes, and its softness marked a clear distinction in sleeping comfort between common folk and the wealthy.

name: Rope Hammock
description: A lightweight sleeping surface woven from rope into an open net, slung between two anchor points such as trees or posts. Originating with the Maya, rope hammocks allowed air to circulate freely around the sleeper, making them ideal for hot, humid climates, though their open weave left occupants exposed and cold in cooler conditions. Their light weight and ease of transport made them popular bedding for sailors and travelers in tropical regions.

name: Cloth Hammock
description: A variant of the rope hammock used in the Old World, made from a solid sheet of cloth rather than an open net. The solid fabric provided more even support and better warmth retention than the netted Mayan style, while remaining lightweight and easy to transport. Slung between posts, trees, or hooks aboard ships, cloth hammocks were a common sleeping arrangement for sailors and travelers where floor space was limited.

name: Straw Pillow
description: A coarse cushion stuffed with straw, providing basic head support during sleep at minimal cost. Common in households of modest means, straw pillows were simple to make and replace, though their rough texture and tendency to harbor pests made them less comfortable than finer alternatives. Despite their humble construction, they represented an improvement in sleeping comfort over using bundled clothing or bare ground as a headrest.

name: Feather Pillow (Top-Quality)
description: A finely made pillow filled with soft feathers, offering substantially greater comfort than coarse straw-filled alternatives. The high cost of quality feather filling and fine cloth covering made this an item primarily found in wealthier households. A feather pillow's softness and durability made it a desirable possession, often passed down or included among a household's prized bedding alongside feather mattresses and fine linens.

name: Bed Sheets
description: Fine but lightweight cloth used to cover a bed for a single sleeper, providing a smooth, comfortable layer between the sleeper and the mattress or blankets beneath. Sheets were considered a step up from sleeping directly on a mattress or straw bedding, and their quality often reflected a household's wealth and attention to hygiene. Regularly washed sheets also helped reduce the spread of pests and disease associated with older, unwashed bedding.

name: Cloth Bag (1 gallon)
description: A simple drawstring or tied bag made of woven cloth, sized to hold about a gallon of contents. Cloth bags are lightweight and flexible but offer no protection against crushing and are highly flammable, making them unsuitable for fragile goods but ideal for dry goods like grain, herbs, or personal effects. Their low cost and minimal weight made them the most common general-purpose container across nearly all low-tech societies, often produced at home from scrap fabric.

name: Earthenware Jar (1 gallon)
description: A fired clay jar with a fitted cover, sized to hold roughly a gallon of liquid or dry goods. Earthenware jars provided modest protection against impacts but were brittle and could shatter if dropped or struck. Their porous unglazed surface allowed slow evaporation, useful for cooling stored water, while glazed or stoneware versions could be made waterproof. Earthenware containers were a mainstay of food and liquid storage and transport throughout the ancient and medieval world.

name: Glass Bottle (1 quart)
description: A blown glass vessel with a stopper, holding about a quart of liquid. Glass bottles were prized for letting users see their contents and for being non-porous and easy to clean, but they were brittle and shattered easily under impact. Producing glass required advanced furnace technology, so bottles were costlier than equivalent earthenware vessels. They were primarily used for valuable liquids such as oils, medicines, perfumes, and fine beverages where preservation and visibility mattered.

name: Leather Pouch (1 gallon)
description: A flexible pouch sewn from tanned leather, sized to carry about a gallon of contents and typically closed with a drawstring or buckled flap. More resistant to impact damage than ceramic or glass containers, leather pouches were favored for carrying valuables, food, water, or tools while traveling, since they could withstand being dropped, bumped, or compressed in a pack without breaking. Their flexibility also allowed them to conform to a traveler's body or saddle for comfortable carrying.

name: Metal Box (1 gallon)
description: A sturdy box made of iron or bronze sheet metal, fitted with a hinged lid and sized to hold about a gallon of contents. Metal boxes offered far greater protection from damage than wood, cloth, or ceramic containers, including resistance to crushing, fire, and forced entry, making them ideal for storing valuables, important documents, or sensitive supplies. Their weight and cost were considerably higher than other container types, reflecting the value of the metal and labor required to fashion them.

name: Wicker Basket (1 gallon)
description: A container woven from flexible plant fibers such as reeds or willow withies, sized to hold about a gallon of contents. Wicker baskets are extremely lightweight and cheap to produce, but their loose, open weave makes them unsuitable for holding grain, soil, or other materials that could sift through the gaps. They neither protect their contents from crushing nor resist fire well, but their low cost and ease of repair made them ubiquitous for carrying produce, laundry, and household goods.

name: Wooden Box (1 gallon)
description: A simple box assembled from wooden boards or staves, sized to hold about a gallon of contents, often with a hinged or removable lid. Wooden boxes and barrels were used to store and transport everything from food and tools to coins and documents. Untreated wood is combustible and offers no resistance to crushing, but waterproofed barrels, available from TL2 onward, could safely hold liquids like wine, oil, or salted goods over long voyages.

name: Wooden Barrel (20 gallon)
description: A larger wooden cask made of curved staves bound with hoops, used to store and transport bulk liquids such as wine, beer, oil, or pickled foods, as well as dry goods. At twenty gallons capacity, it represents a substantial storage unit suited for warehouses, ships, and cellars. Waterproof versions, sealed with pitch or tight cooperage, became available at TL2 and could reliably hold liquids for extended periods without leaking, making barrels essential to long-distance trade.

name: Firebow
description: A bow drill adapted specifically for fire-starting, using a bow-strung cord wrapped around a spindle to produce friction against a dull-pointed base rather than drilling through material. Working the bow back and forth spins the spindle rapidly, generating heat that can ignite tinder in about two minutes. This method required physical effort, costing stamina with extended use, but was far faster and more reliable than rubbing two sticks together by hand, making it a valuable tool for travelers and survivalists.

name: Flint and Steel
description: A piece of flint paired with a small bar of metal or hard mineral, struck together to produce sparks capable of igniting tinder in about thirty seconds. This was one of the fastest low-tech fire-starting methods, but the loud striking noise could give away a person's position or ruin attempts at stealth. Compact, durable, and unaffected by weather in the way that friction methods are, flint and steel kits were a standard item carried by soldiers, travelers, and hunters.

name: Prepared Fire-Starting Block
description: A wooden shaft paired with a block containing resin-treated grooves; rubbing the shaft's tip rapidly within a groove generates friction and heat sufficient to produce an ember within about three minutes. The resin treatment improved the reliability of this friction method compared to plain wood-on-wood techniques. Lightweight and inexpensive, this kit was a practical fire-starting tool for hunters, travelers, and households without access to flint or more advanced methods.

name: Enhanced Tinder
description: Dried fungi soaked in a nitrate solution, prepared to catch fire more readily than ordinary dry wood shavings or leaves. Using enhanced tinder halves the time needed to start a fire, effectively counteracting the fire-lighting penalty imposed by damp conditions. Sold in single-use portions, this consumable item was valued by travelers who needed reliable fire-starting in unpredictable weather, representing an early chemical aid to what was otherwise a purely mechanical process.

name: Burning Glass
description: A handheld lens or mirror used to focus sunlight onto tinder for fire-starting, made from polished metal or natural quartz at earlier tech levels, or from ground clear glass later on. Burning glasses are fragile and expensive compared to flint or friction methods, and only function in clear, direct sunlight, limiting their reliability. Despite these drawbacks, they offered a fire-starting method that required no physical effort and left the user's hands free until the tinder ignited.

name: Fire Piston
description: A narrow shaft that fits tightly into a cylinder, with a small niche near the shaft's tip to hold tinder. Sharply slapping the shaft into the cylinder compresses the trapped air, heating it enough to ignite the tinder almost instantly, reducing fire-starting time to about thirty seconds. Originating in Southeast Asia, the fire piston represented a clever application of compression heating long before the principle was understood scientifically, and required precise craftsmanship to achieve an airtight seal.

name: Sulfur Matches (Bundle of 20)
description: Slivers of pine impregnated with sulfur, which catch fire quickly at the touch of any spark, dividing fire-starting time by four compared to unaided methods. First appearing in sixth-century China and spreading to Europe by the twelfth century, these matches were not self-igniting but functioned as excellent tinder that responded readily to flint sparks or embers. Sold in bundles of twenty, they were a cheap and convenient supplement to existing fire-starting kits.

name: Comb
description: A small grooming tool with a row of teeth, often carved from wood or bone, used to detangle and style hair. Combs were frequently left in the hair as decorative accessories as well as functional grooming aids, sometimes carved with elaborate patterns or symbols denoting status or cultural identity. Lightweight, cheap, and durable, combs were among the most universally owned personal items across nearly all low-tech cultures and time periods.

name: Razor
description: A blade designed for shaving hair, originally made from sharpened stone and later from metal in half-moon or oval shapes. Stone blades for hair-cutting date back tens of thousands of years, while metal shaving razors appeared around 3000 B.C. A basic personal grooming implement, the razor required regular maintenance to keep its edge sharp, and its small size made it easy to carry in a pouch or grooming kit.

name: Earthenware Bathtub
description: A small portable bathing tub made of fired clay, similar in size to an early modern hip bath, allowing a person to bathe while seated with limited water usage. Early examples originated with the Minoans. Earthenware construction made these tubs relatively affordable but heavy and prone to cracking if mishandled. They provided a basic but significant improvement in personal hygiene for households that could afford the water-heating and filling labor involved.

name: Metal Bathtub
description: A bathing tub formed from sheet metal, larger and more durable than earthenware versions, and able to hold more water for a fuller bathing experience. The high cost of metal and the labor required to shape and seal it into a watertight basin made metal bathtubs a luxury item, found primarily in wealthy households. Their durability meant they could last for generations, often becoming valuable family possessions passed down over time.

name: Brush
description: A grooming tool used for hair care, with the earliest Egyptian examples made from bound reed bristles resembling a small broom. Later versions used stiff animal hair bristles set into a wooden or bone handle, providing a softer and more effective brushing action. Brushes were valued for both practical grooming and for maintaining elaborate hairstyles, and their construction from natural materials meant they required periodic replacement as bristles wore down.

name: Strigil
description: A grooming tool resembling a dull knife with a curved, bent blade, used before the advent of soap to scrape oil and accumulated dirt from the skin after bathing. Though often associated with Greco-Roman bathing culture, examples date back to around 3000 B.C. Some strigils came in matched sets of different sizes, connected like keys on a ring, for cleaning different parts of the body, and were a standard fixture of bathhouse culture across the ancient Mediterranean.

name: Tweezers
description: A small pinching tool originating around 2000 B.C., likely first used to remove unwanted body hair. Typically made from a single folded strip of metal that provided spring tension, tweezers were a compact and lightweight addition to a personal grooming kit. Their precision made them useful for fine tasks beyond hair removal, such as handling small objects, splinters, or delicate materials, and they remained largely unchanged in design for thousands of years.

name: Liquid Soap
description: A semi-liquid cleansing substance made by mixing lye with oils, among the earliest soap formulations possibly appearing in the first century A.D. Harsher than later bar soap, liquid soap was nonetheless an improvement over scraping with a strigil for removing dirt and oils from the skin. Sold by the pint, it was used for both bathing and washing fabrics, gradually becoming more refined as soap-making techniques improved over the following centuries.

name: Bar Soap
description: A solid block of soap produced by processing liquid soap with salt water, which separates out harsher impurities and allows the purified solid soap to be pressed into convenient bars. This refinement, developed by Mediterranean soap-makers as early as the ninth century, produced a milder and more pleasant cleansing product than earlier liquid soaps. Bar soap was easier to store, transport, and ration for use compared to liquid alternatives, gradually becoming the standard form of soap.

name: Carrying Frame
description: A rudimentary backpack consisting of a broad board fitted with shoulder straps, used historically by Native Americans to carry loads on the back. The frame itself holds nothing directly, but gear, bundles, or game can be lashed to it with cord. Capable of holding up to one hundred pounds of equipment, the carrying frame distributed weight across the shoulders and back for easier overland travel, though tying and untying items took noticeably longer than using a modern pack.

name: Carrying Yoke
description: A wooden frame shaped like two curving hooks joined in the middle like a stretched letter W, balanced across one shoulder with baggage tied into the curve of the rear hook and resting against the bearer's back. Used historically by the Greeks among others, the carrying yoke could support up to eighty pounds of gear, with additional load or a free hand balancing the front. It required one hand on it at all times to keep it steady, though it could be dropped instantly if needed.

name: Hunter-Gatherer's Kit
description: A hide bag or small wicker basket containing a flakable stone core, two hammerstones, two foot-long bones or straight sticks, two tiny punches of bone, horn, or wood, and several yards of thin cord. Many of these items served multiple purposes: hammerstones could shape stone tools or crack open nuts and marrowbones, while the sticks could serve as digging implements or as shafts for fitted cutting tools. If the stone core wasn't flint, the kit also included fire-making sticks, making it a comprehensive survival toolkit for early peoples.

name: Pilgrim's Kit
description: A bundle of necessities carried by travelers passing through civilized regions but expecting poor accommodations and unpredictable food at inns or aboard ship. The kit includes a straw mattress, a blanket, a coat, a knife and whetstone, a jug of wine, a five-pound sack of flour or dried peas, and a pound of medicinal spices. Together these provisions gave a traveler basic shelter, warmth, sustenance, and minor remedies, making it a comprehensive package for anyone undertaking an extended journey through settled lands.

name: Luxury Kit
description: A compact case of luxuries carried by a traveling aristocrat, of little use for survival but indispensable for a wealthy person's comfort. It includes a full set of grooming equipment such as razor, brush, comb, soap, fragrances, and cosmetics, a writing box, and serving and drinking vessels for tea, coffee, or alcohol depending on the owner's culture, all neatly arranged in a purpose-built cabinet. A plain model with unremarkable contents represents the baseline; finer versions with brandy, ivory implements, and other refinements cost considerably more under luxury pricing rules.

name: Tobacco Pipe
description: A long wooden tube with a bowl at one end for holding smoldering tobacco, used for inhaling smoke through the mouthpiece. Early pipes were simple in form, made from carved wood, while later disposable versions were mass-produced from fired clay as smoking spread through Europe with the adoption of tobacco at TL4. Pipes were a common personal item for recreational smoking, and their style and material often reflected the owner's wealth and cultural background.

name: Water Pipe
description: A smoking device featuring a bowl for tobacco connected by a tube to the bottom of a water-filled reservoir, with a second tube above the waterline through which the smoker inhales filtered smoke. Originating in Persia or India around the first century A.D., water pipes were initially used to smoke medicinal plants before tobacco's introduction. The water filtration cooled and softened the smoke, making for a different smoking experience than a simple dry pipe, and the device's elaborate construction often made it a centerpiece of social smoking occasions.

name: Dolls
description: Small figurines fashioned by many societies from clay or other readily available, disposable materials, likely used primarily as children's toys though some may have served ceremonial or religious purposes. Clay dolls were more durable but heavier and fragile if dropped, while versions made of cloth, hair, or plant husks were essentially weightless and could be assembled quickly from scraps. Dolls represent one of the oldest and most universal forms of toy across human cultures.

name: Board Game Set
description: A wooden game board accompanied by clay or stone playing pieces, used for strategy and racing games. Evidence of board games dates to at least 2500 B.C., though they were likely played much earlier. Early Western games often involved racing pieces around the board while capturing opponents' pieces, similar to backgammon, while go developed independently and very early in China. Board games provided entertainment for people of all classes and were often elaborately decorated for wealthier owners.

name: Set of Dice
description: A small set of dice, typically up to five two-sided dice or two to three dice with more sides, used for games of chance. Early dice were carved from animal bones such as sheep's knuckles and may date back to 3000 B.C., with two-sided, four-sided, and six-sided shapes all known from antiquity. The Romans invented twenty-sided dice as early as the second century A.D. Compact and nearly weightless, dice sets were easy to carry and a common feature of gambling and recreational games.

name: Dominoes Set
description: A set of around thirty numbered tiles used for matching and scoring games, independently invented in both Egypt and China by 1400 B.C. The tiles, typically made of bone, ivory, or wood with marked pips, allowed for a variety of games. Larger sets of similar domino-like tiles were also used to play early card-like games resembling mah jong, requiring a bigger and heavier collection of pieces and correspondingly higher cost.

name: Kite
description: A lightweight flying toy made of paper or silk stretched over a wooden frame, appearing in eastern Asia between 1000 and 500 B.C. Beyond recreation, kites served practical purposes as signal flags visible over great distances or as a means to send small objects aloft and over obstacles. A kite about a yard across, flown with twenty yards of string, could lift up to half a pound in a favorable wind, making it a surprisingly versatile tool as well as a popular pastime.

name: Hand-Painted Playing Cards
description: An early deck of playing cards dating to the Middle Ages, with each card individually painted by hand before the advent of printing technology. The labor-intensive production made hand-painted decks expensive luxury items, generally affordable only to the wealthy. Despite the cost, playing cards quickly became popular for a variety of games once introduced, setting the stage for the much cheaper mass-produced decks that followed once printing technology matured.

name: Small Ball
description: A small ball intended for throwing games and light stick-and-ball sports. Made from materials such as wood, leather-wrapped cores, or similar substances depending on the culture, the small ball was an inexpensive and durable piece of sporting equipment used widely for casual recreation and children's games across many societies, requiring little maintenance and lasting through extensive play.

name: Large Soft Ball
description: A larger, softer ball suitable for games resembling soccer or rugby, made from leather or similarly flexible material often stuffed or inflated to provide bounce and resilience. This type of ball supported team sports involving kicking, throwing, and tackling, and its larger size and softer construction made it more forgiving for rough outdoor play compared to smaller, harder balls used in stick games.

name: Sport Stick
description: A wooden stick used for games involving knocking a ball through a goal, independently invented across many continents in various forms. Sticks were often shaped with a feature on the end suited to the specific sport, such as a curved blade for hockey, a paddle or net for tennis, or a mallet head for polo. These implements doubled as durable, all-purpose pieces of sporting gear and, in a pinch, as improvised weapons due to their solid wooden construction.

name: Maya Ball Game Ball
description: A large, heavy rubber ball used in the traditional Maya ball game, in which athletes wearing heavily padded loincloths knocked the ball around an I-shaped court without using their hands. The ball's substantial weight and solid rubber construction made it dangerous to strike with bare skin, necessitating the padded uniforms worn by players. This game held ritual as well as athletic significance in Mesoamerican cultures, and the ball itself was a specialized piece of equipment unlike anything produced elsewhere at the time.

name: Maya Ball Game Uniform
description: A set of heavily padded protective clothing, primarily a padded loincloth, worn by athletes competing in the Maya ball game to absorb impacts from the large, heavy rubber ball used in the sport. Variants of the game also had players wear additional arm and leg padding similar to leather limb armor. The uniform reflects the specialized protective equipment Mesoamerican cultures developed for their ritualized ball sport, distinct from typical low-tech clothing or armor.

name: Bronze Discus
description: A heavy disc-shaped throwing implement made of bronze, used in Greek athletic competitions. Although examples ranging from half to double the average weight and cost existed, a typical discus weighed around six pounds. Unlike a combat weapon, an athletic discus is not designed for point accuracy and has no aiming bonus, but its solid bronze construction made it a formidable improvised weapon if thrown at a person rather than for sport.

name: Firework Fountain
description: A tube of slow-burning gunpowder open at one end, producing a continuous fountain of flame and sparks for one to two minutes when lit. If held, it inflicts minor burning damage to the holder's hand each second, but it can also be aimed and used as a short-range jet of fire against a target, dealing the same burning damage per second. Static firework displays in the West often incorporated multiple fountains arranged on figurative frames for dramatic effect.

name: Ground Rat
description: A faster-burning gunpowder firework in an open-ended tube, essentially an underpowered rocket that skims unpredictably across the ground for twenty to thirty seconds while emitting sparks and noise. If held while active, it causes the same burning damage as a fountain. Ground rats were popular for their erratic, surprising movement, making them effective for startling crowds or animals during festivals and celebrations, particularly in East Asian traditions where noisemaking fireworks were especially prized.

name: Noisemaker Firework
description: Gunpowder packed into an enclosed paper tube, designed to explode with a loud bang rather than produce sustained flame or movement. If the noisemaker detonates in direct contact with someone, it can inflict minor burning damage. These simple firecrackers were widely used in celebrations, religious ceremonies, and to frighten away evil spirits or predators, becoming especially associated with festivals in China after fireworks technology spread there around the tenth century A.D.

name: Firework Rocket
description: A development of the ground rat with enough thrust to launch into the air, traveling up to seventy-five yards but entirely unguided, making it very difficult to aim at a specific target. Exploding versions, developed slightly later, include a separate compartment that detonates when the rocket reaches its peak height, scattering fragments and causing crushing explosive damage to anything fragile nearby. Rockets represented the merging of fireworks technology with early projectile weapon concepts, spreading from China along with gunpowder.

name: Bow Drill
description: A simple fire-making and hole-boring tool resembling a small bow and arrow, except the arrow shaft sits perpendicular to the bow's plane, its blunt top held steady in a socketed hand-block while the bowstring wraps around the shaft. By sawing the bow back and forth, the user spins the shaft rapidly, drilling holes in wood, bone, or shell, or generating enough friction heat to ignite tinder. Made of simple wooden parts and cordage, it requires only modest skill to use but steady technique to keep the point seated.

name: Pump Drill
description: A more advanced boring tool consisting of an arrow-like vertical shaft weighted near its pointed tip, a crossbar pierced to slide along the shaft, and cords linking the crossbar's ends to the shaft's top. Pushing the crossbar down spins the shaft, winding the cords; the shaft's momentum then rewinds them in reverse and lifts the crossbar for another stroke, creating a continuous reciprocating drilling action useful for boring holes in wood, bone, shell, or stone with minimal effort once set in motion.

name: Spindle
description: A simple, near-universal spinning tool consisting of a slender wooden rod fitted with a small weighted disc (the whorl) and tapering to a dull spike at the working end, onto which raw fiber such as wool or flax is wound into thread. The spinner twirls the spindle to add twist to the fiber while feeding more material from a held bundle, gradually building a spool of usable thread. Some spindles have a sharpened point sturdy enough to serve as a makeshift piercing implement.

name: Backstrap Loom
description: A simple loom consisting of a header board through which warp threads pass, a shuttle for wrapping weft thread, and a beater for packing it tightly, with one end tied to a fixed point and the other braced against the weaver's lower back via a strap, letting the weaver's body tension control the warp. Capable of producing cloth up to a yard wide, it is portable, inexpensive, and widely used by individual weavers across many pre-industrial cultures for household textile production.

name: Vertical Loom
description: A basic rope-and-wood loom that can be hung from a post, beam, or tree branch, allowing the weaver to work standing or seated below it. Suitable for producing cloth no larger than roughly six feet by three feet, it consists of little more than a wooden frame and warp-tensioning cords, making it cheap, easily transported, and simple to set up wherever a sturdy anchor point is available, though its size limits the dimensions of finished textiles.

name: Sewing Needle
description: A very thin, sharpened sliver of bone, thorn, or—at higher tech levels—metal, pierced or notched at one end to draw thread through fabric or leather. Indispensable for tailoring, mending, and leatherwork, sewing needles were among the most ubiquitous small tools of pre-industrial life, carried in cases or pouches to protect their delicate points. Sewing pins, which lack the eye for thread, cost half as much and serve for temporary fastening while garments are fitted.

name: Treadle (Flying Shuttle) Loom
description: A large, full-frame loom equipped with foot-operated treadles that automatically raise and lower the warp threads (sheds), greatly speeding up the weaving process compared to hand-operated looms. Capable of weaving fabric up to six feet wide, it represents a major advance in textile production efficiency, requiring a dedicated workspace due to its substantial size and weight, and forming the backbone of pre-industrial cloth manufacturing workshops.

name: Scissors
description: A cutting tool for cloth and fine materials, pre-modern scissors were forged from a single piece of metal bent into a U shape, with cutting blades at each end of the arms.
