Squeezing the arms together like tweezers brings the blades across each other in a shearing motion, cutting thread, cloth, or paper cleanly. Lighter and more precise than shears, scissors became an essential part of any tailor's or scribe's tool collection once metalworking allowed their manufacture.

name: Thimble
description: A tiny metal cup-shaped guard worn over a fingertip to protect it from being pricked while pushing a needle through tough fabric or leather. An inexpensive but essential accessory for tailors, seamstresses, and leatherworkers, the thimble's dimpled outer surface provides a stable bearing surface for the blunt end of the needle, allowing greater force to be applied safely during sewing.

name: Lathe
description: A workshop machine that spins a piece of wood back and forth on its axis so a craftsman can shave it down evenly or carve decorative patterns symmetrically around its circumference. Powered either by an assistant turning the workpiece or by a foot-operated treadle connected to a springy branch that automatically reverses the rotation, the lathe is large, heavy, and intended for permanent installation in a workshop, producing turned items such as bowls, spindles, and furniture legs.

name: Hand Saw
description: A single-person woodworking saw with a row of sharpened teeth along one edge of a flat metal blade, used with a back-and-forth pulling and pushing motion to cut through wood. Essential to carpentry, the hand saw allows controlled, relatively straight cuts in boards and beams, and its toothed edge can also inflict a nasty cutting wound if used in a fight, though it is far better suited to lumber than to combat.

name: Carpenter's Square
description: An L-shaped tool of wood or metal with two arms set at a precise right angle, used to verify and mark perpendicular edges and corners when cutting or assembling wooden components. A fundamental measuring aid for any woodworker, mason, or builder, the square ensures that joints fit cleanly and structures rise true, and its simple design has remained essentially unchanged across centuries of use.

name: Auger
description: A T-shaped hand drill with a long, broad bit designed to bore wide holes in timber, larger than those produced by a bow or pump drill. The user grips the crossbar handle and applies steady downward pressure while turning, slowly cutting away wood fiber to create holes for joinery, dowels, or fasteners. Its awkward grip makes it slow to use, but the size of hole it can produce makes it valuable for shipbuilding and heavy carpentry.

name: Brace and Bit
description: A hand-cranked, U-shaped drilling tool with an interchangeable metal bit, allowing a craftsman to bore holes by turning a crank handle that rotates the bit through a geared or cranked offset. Appearing at the end of the Middle Ages, the brace and bit offered improved leverage and control over earlier drilling methods, becoming a standard carpenter's tool for creating dowel holes, pilot holes for fasteners, and other precise borings in wood.

name: Alembic
description: A tall, narrow ceramic or glass jar with a tight-fitting, beak-spouted lid used in distillation, giving it a shape often likened to a penguin. When heated—usually in a sand or water bath to control temperature—vapors rise into the curved spout, where they cool, condense, and drip into a separate collection vessel. A staple of early alchemical and chemical laboratories, the alembic is delicate and prone to cracking under direct or uneven heat.

name: Aludel
description: A stackable, pear-shaped ceramic vessel open at both ends, used in the alchemical process of sublimation. Several aludels are stacked one atop another over the substance being processed; the assembly's base is heated, driving vapors upward where they condense as solids on the cooler inner walls of the upper vessels. Cheap and simple compared to an alembic, aludels were a common sight in any alchemist's workshop, used in sets for purifying substances like sulfur or mercury.

name: Crucible
description: A small, thick-walled ceramic pot, holding roughly one to two cups, with a spout or angled lip for pouring molten or heated contents. Built to withstand intense, direct heat from a furnace or brazier without cracking, crucibles were used by metalworkers, alchemists, and jewelers to melt metals, fuse glass, or carry out high-temperature chemical reactions. Their thick walls make them more durable than other laboratory glassware, though they remain vulnerable to thermal shock if cooled too quickly.

name: Cupel/Scorifier
description: Two related small, shallow vessels made from compressed bone ash, used in metallurgical assaying to separate precious metals from base ones. When heated with a sample, the bone ash absorbs oxidized base metals such as lead, leaving behind a button of purified gold or silver. The cupel is the smaller and more cup-shaped of the pair, while the scorifier is flatter and broader; both are consumed or degraded with use and must be periodically replaced.

name: Awl
description: A slender, sharply pointed hand tool used to pierce holes in leather and heavy fabric ahead of stitching, allowing thread or lacing to pass through material too tough for a needle alone. Early awls were fashioned from bone or horn, while metal versions appeared once basic metalworking became available, though the cheaper bone and horn types remained in common use for centuries. An essential companion to needle and thread for any leatherworker or cobbler.

name: Fish Trap
description: A basket-like trap, typically woven from reeds or withies, fitted with hinged, inward-opening doors that allow fish to swim in but prevent them from swimming back out. Anchored in streams, rivers, or tidal zones, fish traps let a fisherman work multiple sites or pursue other tasks while the trap passively gathers a catch. Larger installations, such as Pacific Northwest fish wheels using rotating baskets driven by river current, could harvest fish in great numbers when populations were dense.

name: Fishhook
description: A small, curved, barbed hook used to catch fish on a baited line, made from shaped bone at the earliest tech levels and from metal once basic smithing became available. Despite its tiny size and low cost, the fishhook was a transformative tool for subsistence, allowing a single line to passively catch fish with minimal effort and equipment, and remaining essentially unchanged in basic design across millennia of use.

name: Fishing Net
description: A woven mesh of cordage, sized by the square yard, used to entangle and capture fish in bulk from rivers, lakes, or the sea. Nets can be cast by hand, dragged between boats, or set as fixed traps across a channel, and represent one of the most efficient pre-industrial methods of harvesting fish. Made from plant fiber or, later, treated cordage, nets require regular drying and mending to prevent rot and tearing.

name: Chisel
description: A hand tool with a hardened, shaped cutting edge—ranging from a small point to a broad axe-like blade or scalloped form—designed to fit the hand and absorb the impact of a hammer blow on its rear end. Made of bronze or iron, chisels are used by miners, stonemasons, and carpenters alike to split, shape, and carve stone and wood. When struck with a hammer, a chisel converts a crushing blow into a focused piercing force ideal for working hard materials.

name: Large Crowbar
description: A heavy, five-to-six-foot metal bar used to pry apart stone, timber, or other obstacles by providing powerful leverage. Indispensable to miners and stonemasons for breaking loose rock and shifting heavy objects, the crowbar's length and rigidity also make it a serviceable improvised weapon, comparable to a crude polearm, in the hands of someone desperate enough to swing it.

name: Shovel
description: A flat-bladed digging implement on a long handle, used to move loose earth, sand, gravel, or other granular materials. Early shovels were carved entirely from wood, which doubled the time needed to dig compared to later designs; metal-edged versions cut digging time significantly, and all-metal shovels—though costly—were fastest of all and favored by professional excavators and miners.

name: Smith's Pliers
description: A sturdy pair of metal gripping tools, somewhat larger than a hand, used by smiths to hold small workpieces firmly while hammering, bending, or filing them. Pliers protect the user's fingers from heat and impact while providing precise control over awkwardly shaped or hot metal pieces during forging, a basic but essential tool for any metalworking station.

name: Metal Shears
description: Heavy, pincer-like cutting tools with long handles, used to cut softened or thin sheet metal after it has been heated or hammered to workable thinness. Operated like oversized scissors, shears allow a smith to trim metal stock into rough shapes before further forging, and their substantial cutting edges can inflict a nasty wound if used against flesh.

name: Smith's Tongs
description: A pair of long-armed metal gripping tools, roughly two feet in length, used to grasp heavy or red-hot objects and hold them firmly at a safe distance from the user's hands and body. Essential for moving workpieces into and out of a forge fire and holding them steady on the anvil during hammering, tongs are a basic fixture of every smithy.

name: Draw Plate
description: A flat stone or metal block pierced with a graduated series of holes of decreasing diameter, used to manufacture wire by repeatedly pulling a metal rod through progressively smaller holes, drawing it out into a thin, even strand. An essential tool for jewelers, wireworkers, and armorers producing chain mail, the draw plate turns crude metal stock into uniform wire through repeated, labor-intensive passes.

name: File
description: A flat metal plate with one or more deliberately roughened faces, used to grind down, smooth, and shape the edges and surfaces of metal, wood, or bone workpieces through repeated abrasive strokes. A versatile finishing tool found in smithies, jewelers' workshops, and toolkits across many trades, the file removes material gradually and precisely where a saw or chisel would be too coarse.

name: Anvil
description: A surface-hardened metal block, roughly six to seven inches across, tapered at the bottom so it can be wedged firmly into a hole in a tree stump or wooden base. The anvil provides a rigid, unyielding surface against which a smith hammers heated metal into shape; small holes and grooves on its face assist in producing nails, wire, and other specialized forms. Larger workshop anvils can weigh hundreds of pounds for heavy-duty forging.

name: Tailor's Kit
description: A complete portable toolkit for working with cloth or leather, comprising an awl, a pair of small knives or scissors, four sewing needles of different sizes, twenty pins, a measuring rod, a thimble, and a hundred feet of thread, all bundled together in a carrying roll or pouch. With this kit, a tailor can perform any garment-making or repair task without suffering the penalties of improvised or missing tools, making it essential gear for any traveling craftsperson.

name: Carpenter's Kit
description: A comprehensive set of woodworking tools comprising an adze, a bow drill, four chisels, a hammer, a hatchet, a level, a measuring rod, a saw, a square, and an abrasive sanding stone, typically carried in a wooden chest or canvas roll. This kit equips a carpenter to fell, shape, join, and finish wood for construction, furniture, and shipbuilding without the penalties imposed by missing or improvised tools.

name: Fletcher's Kit
description: A specialized toolkit for making and repairing arrows and crossbow bolts from semi-prepared parts in the field, comprising a small knife, a large knife, small pliers, an arrow-straightener (a grooved stone or bone used to check shaft straightness), and sanding abrasive. Producing arrows from raw materials additionally requires a carpenter's kit. With this kit and a supply of shafts, heads, feathers, and adhesive, a fletcher can keep an archer supplied with ammunition on campaign.

name: Smith's Kit
description: A minimal set of blacksmithing tools comprising three hammers, tongs, four chisels, shears, and a file, allowing a smith to work metal in the field provided a flat rock can serve as a makeshift anvil—though using a rock anvil risks breaking it and imposes a skill penalty. A deluxe version of this kit includes a portable iron anvil, eliminating these problems at much greater cost and weight, suitable for a traveling smith who can afford a wagon or pack animal.

name: Alchemist's Kit
description: A portable laboratory set comprising an alembic, two aludels, a brazier, two crucibles, four cupels or scorifiers, a large pot for use as a water or sand bath, several pieces of clean filtering cloth, tongs, a balance scale, and a small mortar and pestle. This kit equips an alchemist to perform distillation, sublimation, assaying, and other chemical operations away from a permanent workshop, though in many societies possessing one invites suspicion of fraud or sorcery.

name: Stoneworker's Kit
description: A heavy-duty toolkit for shaping and dressing stone, comprising a large hammer, a small hammer, six chisels of different shapes, a large crowbar, a small crowbar, a square, a level, and an auger. With this kit, a stonemason can cut, carve, and fit stone blocks for construction, monuments, and sculpture without suffering penalties for missing or makeshift tools, though its weight makes it impractical to carry far without a cart.

name: Eyeglasses
description: A pair of corrective lenses, invented in Italy around 1285 A.D., used to mitigate farsightedness with convex lenses or, by the mid-15th century, nearsightedness with concave lenses. Early eyeglasses are held before the eyes by a handle or frame (lorgnette style) or clamped onto the bridge of the nose (pince-nez style), the latter prone to falling off if the wearer moves quickly. Ground from glass and set in metal or horn frames, eyeglasses were a luxury item that dramatically extended the working lives of scribes and craftsmen with aging eyes.

name: Level
description: An A-shaped wooden frame with a plumb bob suspended from its apex, used to determine whether a surface is horizontal. When placed on a surface, the deflection of the plumb line from a marked center point on the crossbar indicates the degree and direction of any slope, making the level indispensable for construction, masonry, and surveying tasks where true horizontal or vertical references are required.

name: Surveyor's Cross (Groma)
description: A tall staff topped with a horizontally balanced cross, fitted with adjustable plumb bobs hanging from each of its four ends, and a sharp spike at the base for planting firmly in the ground. By sighting along the cross's arms, a surveyor can mark points at the same elevation, while sighting along the plumb lines establishes straight alignments. Widely used by Roman engineers for laying out roads, aqueducts, and field boundaries.

name: Chorobates
description: A long, narrow wooden bench—up to twenty feet in length—fitted with a water trough along its top and plumb bobs hanging from its underside, used to establish a precise level line over long distances. Both the water's surface and the angle of the hanging plumb lines confirm levelness, making the chorobates valuable for large-scale engineering projects such as road grading and aqueduct construction, though its size limits it to fixed work sites.

name: Cross-Staff
description: A short staff, three to four feet long, fitted with a sliding crossbar perpendicular to its length. The user sights along the staff at one reference point and slides the crossbar until its ends appear to align with another point, allowing the visual angle between the two points to be read off graduations on the staff. Used in surveying and early navigation to measure angular distances without complex instruments.

name: Dioptra
description: An adjustable sighting instrument consisting of a tube or set of sights mounted on a platform, with fine adjustment screws allowing the operator to measure both the vertical and horizontal angles from the observation point to a distant object. Each observation takes several minutes to set up and read accurately, restricting the dioptra to surveying stationary landmarks, but its precision made it valuable for mapping terrain, planning aqueducts, and astronomical measurements in the ancient world.

name: Astrolabe
description: A sophisticated brass instrument developed in the second century A.D. and refined in the medieval Muslim world, consisting of a flat plate (the mater) engraved with celestial coordinates for a given latitude, a rotating star-pointer grid (the rete), and a sighting pointer (the alidade) on the back, all held together by a central pin. Beyond measuring the altitude of celestial bodies, the astrolabe performs astronomical calculations, serving navigators, astronomers, and timekeepers alike. Some models offer interchangeable plates for use at different latitudes.

name: Kamal
description: A simple celestial navigation tool used by Muslim navigators, consisting of a small square board attached to a knotted cord. The user holds the board at arm's length, adjusting the distance until its edges just span the gap between a celestial body and the horizon; the length of cord played out indicates the body's angular height, from which latitude can be estimated. Cheap, portable, and effective despite its primitive appearance.

name: Quadrant
description: A quarter-circle-shaped instrument of wood or metal, its curved edge marked off in degrees. The user sights along one straight edge at a celestial body while a plumb bob hangs freely from the apex, indicating the body's elevation above the horizon on the degree scale. Beyond celestial observation, a quadrant can be used with trigonometry to estimate the height of distant objects such as towers or walls, making it a versatile surveying and navigational tool.

name: Measuring Rod
description: A standardized rod marked off in units of length, such as the Egyptian royal cubit—a 21-inch granite rod divided into 28 digits with fractional gradations down to a sixteenth. As trade and bureaucracy grew, standardized measuring rods became essential for ensuring fair transactions, construction accuracy, and consistent record-keeping, with master rods kept by authorities against which other rods could be checked and calibrated.

name: Odometer
description: A mechanical distance-measuring device fitted to a cart or chariot wheel, in which the wheel's rotation drives a gear mechanism that drops a pebble into a collection box after every mile traveled, giving a running tally of distance covered. Described by Vitruvius around 15 B.C. and independently devised in China, the odometer allowed remarkably accurate distance records for overland expeditions, such as those compiled by Alexander the Great's chroniclers.

name: Surveyor's Kit
description: A complete equipment set for land surveying, comprising a surveyor's cross, a dioptra, two ten-foot poles, a hundred and twenty feet of wax-stiffened cord for accurate length measurement, and twenty marker posts for staking out points on the ground. With this kit, a surveyor from the Roman era through the Renaissance could measure and map land for construction, boundary disputes, and taxation purposes.

name: Measuring Basket or Jug
description: A basket, cup, jug, or jar manufactured to hold a precisely standardized volume, with that volume often marked on the exterior for ease of reference during trade. Used to measure dry goods like grain or liquids like oil and wine by filling and emptying the container a counted number of times, measuring vessels ranged from small cups to enormous thirty-five-cubic-foot barrels known as tuns, the origin of the word 'ton.'

name: Balance Scale (Small)
description: The original weighing device, consisting of two pans suspended from opposite ends of a beam that pivots freely on a central support. The item to be weighed goes in one pan while standardized counterweights are added to the other until the beam balances level, at which point the counterweights' total equals the item's weight. Small portable balances with lead counterweight sets became symbols of fair trade and justice across the ancient world, though they cannot weigh anything heavier than their full set of counterweights.

name: Large Balance Scale
description: A larger version of the classic two-pan beam balance, intended for weighing heavier goods such as merchandise in a marketplace. As with smaller balances, the object to be weighed is placed in one pan and standardized lead weights in the other until equilibrium is reached, with the maximum weighable load limited by the total of the available counterweight set. Larger balances were a fixture of markets, customs houses, and warehouses throughout the ancient and medieval world.

name: Steelyard Balance
description: A weighing device similar to scales found in old-fashioned doctor's offices, in which the object or person being weighed rests on a platform or in a pan while a sliding counterweight is moved along a graduated beam until its leverage balances the load. The counterweight's final position is read against numbered gradations to give the weight directly, requiring far smaller counterweights than a simple balance for a given load by exploiting leverage. A steelyard was found among the ruins of Pompeii.

name: Clepsydra (Water Clock)
description: A vessel filled with water that drains slowly through a small hole in its base, with lines marked on the inside walls indicating the passage of hours as the water level falls. Invented in Egypt around 1550 B.C., the basic clepsydra measures fixed-length hours, though tapered sides can compensate for the slowing flow as the water level drops, and different scale markings allow it to track the variable-length hours used in some calendars. Accurate to roughly ten minutes, it was the first device to measure time independent of sunlight.

name: Sundial
description: A timekeeping device consisting of a vertical projection, called a gnomon, that casts a shadow onto a marked surface as the sun moves across the sky; the shadow's position indicates the time of day. First developed in Egypt around 1500 B.C., the sundial measures hours of variable length that shift with the seasons, and is nearly perfectly accurate for the latitude at which it was made, but is useless at night or under overcast skies.

name: Portable Sundial
description: A compact Greek refinement of the sundial, small enough to be carried in a pouch or pocket and used while traveling. Before use, the portable sundial must be aligned to the local noonday sun to read accurately at a new location, after which it functions like its larger stationary cousins, casting a shadow onto graduated markings to indicate the time of day.

name: Regulated Clepsydra
description: An advanced water clock devised by the Greek inventor Ctesibius, which uses a float valve—similar to that in a modern toilet tank—to maintain a constant water level in a supply tank, ensuring a steady outflow rate regardless of how full the tank is. The outflow is measured by the rising water level in a second receiving tank, achieving an accuracy of about two minutes, a significant improvement over earlier unregulated water clocks.

name: Graduated Candle Clock
description: A timekeeping set consisting of six twelve-inch candles, each designed to burn down completely in four hours and marked into twelve twenty-minute sections, kept burning inside a protective case with translucent horn sides to shield the flame from drafts. First described in Chinese writings of the sixth century and later used in Alfred the Great's England, the candle clock measures fixed-length hours by the candle's steady, predictable burn rate.

name: Weight-Driven Clock
description: An early mechanical clock powered by the slow descent of hanging weights, whose fall turns a shaft connected to a gear train within the clock's mechanism. Lacking a pendulum or other speed regulator, it is accurate only to within an hour, signaling the passage of time by ringing a bell. Some models featured dials, though these served as astronomical displays rather than precise timekeeping. Each such clock was an individually crafted, prototype-like creation, often built into a tower or large frame.

name: Miniature Clepsydra
description: An ultra-precise variant of the water clock invented by Chinese artificer Li Lan in 450 A.D., crafted from jade and using liquid mercury rather than water as its working fluid for greater consistency. It holds enough mercury to run for about twenty-nine minutes and can measure intervals as short as one-twentieth of that period, making it remarkably precise for its era, suitable for timing rituals, watches, or short tasks.

name: Sandglass
description: A timer consisting of two glass bulbs joined by a narrow neck, through which fine granular material—typically marble dust rather than ordinary sand—flows at a steady rate from the upper bulb to the lower one. The standard half-hour sandglass was a vital navigational tool because, unlike water clocks, it remains unaffected by the rocking and tilting of a ship at sea, and was also used to time watches and tasks ashore.

name: Cylinder Seal
description: A small cylindrical piece of carved semiprecious stone, originating in ancient Sumer, engraved with a design or inscription in reverse relief. When rolled across a strip of moist clay or wax, it leaves a continuous impression of its carving, serving as a personal signature or mark of authenticity on documents, jars, and sealed containers. Carrying one's cylinder seal was equivalent to carrying one's legal identity in many ancient Near Eastern societies.

name: Signet Ring
description: A ring with an image or inscription carved into the flat face of its stone or metal bezel, performing the same authenticating function as a cylinder seal but worn constantly on the finger for convenience. To seal a document, the wearer presses the ring's face into a blob of wax on the letter or container, leaving an impression that signifies the owner's authority or identity—forgery or theft of a signet ring could have serious legal consequences.

name: Wax Tablet
description: A shallow wooden frame holding a thin layer of wax, written upon with a pointed stylus and erased by smoothing the wax surface again, making it ideal for notes, drafts, and lessons that need not be permanent. Standard equipment for Roman clerical workers, wax tablets were sometimes hinged together in pairs or sets for longer documents, and wealthier owners had tablets backed with ivory rather than plain wood for added prestige.

name: Stylus (Writing)
description: A rigid pointed tool, typically of reed or wood, used to press characters into soft writing media such as clay tablets or wax. One end is sharpened for writing while the opposite end is blunt, allowing the user to smooth out and correct mistakes by rubbing the surface flat again. A later metal version can double in a pinch as an improvised stabbing implement, though its primary purpose remains scribal.

name: Brush (Writing/Painting)
description: A simple writing and painting implement consisting of a wooden or bamboo stick with a bundle of animal-hair bristles bound to one end. Dipped in ink or pigment, the brush allows fine control over line thickness and stroke style, making it the primary writing tool in East Asian calligraphy traditions as well as a fundamental tool for artists working in any culture that uses ink or paint on flat media.

name: Ink (Liquid, Western)
description: A water-based writing fluid containing a pigment, such as soot or lampblack, suspended with a binder like gum arabic or lacquer to prevent it from settling and to help it adhere to writing surfaces. Sold and stored in liquid form by the pint, Western inks are typically black or brown by default, with other earth tones, reds, or rarer colors like violet commanding higher prices due to the cost of exotic pigments.

name: Ink Sticks (Asian)
description: A solid block of dried ink, typically made from soot bound with animal glue, used by grinding a corner of the stick against a wet ink stone to release pigment into water until the desired darkness is achieved. This method, central to East Asian calligraphy and painting traditions, allows the artist to mix ink fresh for each session and to control its consistency, while the solid sticks are far more compact and durable to transport than liquid ink.

name: Ink Stone
description: A shallow stone dish used in conjunction with solid ink sticks: the scribe pours a small amount of water into the dish and grinds an ink stick against the wet surface in circular motions until the resulting ink reaches the desired darkness. A fundamental tool of East Asian calligraphy and painting, the ink stone's flat grinding surface gradually wears smooth with use but remains functional for a very long time.

name: Pen (Reed/Quill/Metal)
description: A writing implement formed as a hollow tube with a slit nib and a small reservoir near the tip to hold ink by capillary action. At the earliest tech levels pens are made from reeds; metal pens appear once basic metalworking allows fine nib shaping, and quills cut from large bird feathers become common later. Cheap reed or quill pens wear down after about twenty pages of writing, higher-quality quills can be resharpened repeatedly for up to a hundred pages, and metal pens never wear out at all.

name: Pumice Eraser
description: A piece of lightweight, porous volcanic stone used to abrade and remove writing or marks from solid or flat media. By gently rubbing the pumice across a written surface, a scribe can erase mistakes on materials like papyrus or parchment, though repeated use gradually wears away the writing surface itself, limiting how many times a given sheet can be corrected.

name: Metal Stylus (for Tracing)
description: A pointed implement of lead, copper, silver, or gold used to trace faint, permanent lines onto flat writing media such as paper treated with clay or organic primers, useful for ruling lines or making marks that won't smudge like ink. Silver styluses are especially prized because the lines they leave cannot be rubbed off, making them popular among scribes who need durable guide marks or under-drawings.

name: Egyptian Scribe's Palette
description: A flat wooden case used by ancient Egyptian scribes, featuring two shallow depressions for holding cakes of different colored ink—usually black and red—and a slotted compartment for storing several reed pens. While writing, the scribe slung the palette's cord over one shoulder so the ink wells rested against his chest, keeping his writing tools organized and within easy reach during long sessions of record-keeping.

name: Medieval Scribal Kit
description: A set of tools used by medieval and Renaissance European scribes to keep their handwriting straight and consistent, including a ruler for drawing guide lines, a square for checking right angles in page layouts, and adjustable calipers for precise measurements when ruling margins and columns. This kit reflects the increasing standardization of book production as European scriptoria and early print shops sought more uniform page designs.

name: Printing Block
description: A flat sheet of wood, most commonly pear wood, into which the mirror-image design of an entire printed page—text, illustrations, or both—is carved in relief. To print, the carver rubs ink onto the raised portions with a brush, lays paper over the block, and rubs the back of the paper with a dry brush to transfer the ink, a method capable of producing up to 1,500 copies per day. Both faces of a block may be carved with different page designs to economize on materials.

name: Abacus
description: A calculation aid consisting of a wooden frame holding beads strung on a series of parallel wires or rods, with the beads' positions representing numerical values according to a positional system built into the device's structure. By sliding beads back and forth, a trained user can add, subtract, multiply, and divide far faster than working with pencil and paper, even when the user's own number system—such as Roman numerals—is not positional.

name: Cube Root Extractor
description: A mechanical calculating device invented by ancient Greek engineers in the third or fourth century B.C. to solve a specific problem in catapult design: finding the cube root of a stone projectile's weight to determine the proportions of the engine. The device consists of several rods set at angles to one another, one of which slides; by making an initial estimate and adjusting the rods' positions, the operator can read off an increasingly accurate cube root.

name: Merkhet
description: An ancient Egyptian astronomical sighting device made from a slitted palm leaf, used in clear weather to observe stars crossing a plumb line, helping the observer determine direction more accurately than by eye alone. Although extremely fragile and easily broken, it is normally carried inside a protective hardwood case, and its use significantly reduces the difficulty of navigating by the stars when no compass is available.

name: Windrose
description: A rectangular wooden box marked with thirty compass points around its exterior, each corresponding to the rising or setting position of one of fifteen fixed reference stars used by ancient navigators. Separate models were required for the northern and southern hemispheres due to differing star visibility. Using a windrose in good weather lets a navigator orient by the stars with greater precision than unaided observation.

name: Sunstone
description: A piece of naturally polarizing mineral, such as cordierite, used according to interpretations of Norse sagas to locate the sun's position in the sky even through cloud cover, fog, or shortly after sunset by analyzing the polarization pattern of skylight. Associated with the era of Viking expansion and their famously skilled long-distance navigation, the sunstone is a small, easily carried crystal that requires no maintenance but only functions under specific lighting conditions.

name: Stick Chart
description: A navigational training aid developed in the Marshall Islands, constructed from curved and straight sticks lashed together to represent ocean swell and current patterns, with cowry shells marking the positions of islands. Stick charts were not carried aboard vessels but were used ashore to train navigators to memorize wave patterns and routes by heart, a tradition that allowed Pacific Islander navigators to cross vast stretches of open ocean without instruments.

name: Periplus / Rutter
description: A reference document describing coastal destinations, landmarks, and the approximate distances between them along a shore, used by sailors since Phoenician, Greek, and Roman times. The earliest form, the periplus, takes the shape of a scroll; its medieval successor, the rutter, is a bound book. Either reduces the difficulty of navigating toward an unfamiliar destination, with higher-quality examples providing even greater benefit, though price and weight vary considerably depending on length and material.

name: Sounding Pole
description: A long pole, typically about twelve feet, used in ancient Egypt and beyond to gauge water depth in shallow rivers, lakes, or coastal areas by thrusting it straight down from the bow of a boat until it touches bottom. A simple but vital tool for avoiding groundings in shallow or unfamiliar waters, the sounding pole remains useful even alongside more advanced navigational techniques and instruments.

name: Lead Line
description: A fifty-yard line fitted with a wax-coated lead weight at one end, thrown over a ship's side to measure water depth by reading length markings along the rope as it sinks to the bottom. The wax coating picks up samples of the seabed material, which can be examined and compared against reference descriptions to help identify the ship's location. Developed in the ancient Mediterranean, it remains a staple of navigation even alongside more sophisticated instruments.

name: Dividers
description: A geometric compass consisting of two pointed rods joined by a stiff hinge at the top, which can be opened to a specific angle and used to trace circles and arcs or to transfer distances accurately between a chart and a measuring scale. An essential tool for dead-reckoning navigation, dividers let a navigator measure off distances traveled and plot a ship's estimated position on a chart with precision.

name: Compass (Floating Needle)
description: A navigational instrument using a magnetized needle floating on water in a small bowl or dish, which aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field to indicate north (or south, in early Chinese designs). First developed in China, the floating-needle compass was the earliest practical form of magnetic compass, allowing sailors to maintain a heading even when landmarks, sun, and stars were obscured, though it requires care to keep the water bowl steady and unspilled.

name: Compass (Pivoted Needle)
description: An improved magnetic compass in which the magnetized needle is mounted on a pivot rather than floating in water, allowing it to swing freely and settle pointing toward magnetic north regardless of the vessel's motion. This design, which spread from China to the Near East and Europe, proved more reliable at sea than the floating-needle type and became the standard form of compass for serious navigation, fitted in a small protective case.

name: Sun Shadow Board
description: A crude precursor to the quadrant developed by the Vikings, consisting of a semicircular piece of wood mounted on a handle, marked to allow rough measurement of the sun's elevation above the horizon for celestial navigation. While far less precise than later instruments, the sun shadow board provided Norse sailors crossing the North Atlantic with a simple means of estimating latitude during long open-ocean voyages.

name: Bone Skates
description: Among the earliest skates, made from curved pieces of animal bone strapped to the feet with leather straps, developed in Finland around 3000 B.C. Lacking sharp edges, they glide over ice rather than cutting into it, so the skater cannot push off with the feet alone and instead relies on hand-held wooden poles for propulsion. They are slow and offer poor traction, making them tricky to use on rough or uneven ice, but they represent humanity's first attempt at efficient travel across frozen ground.

name: One-Man Sledge
description: A small wooden platform mounted on two long runners, designed to drag heavy loads across snow, ice, grass, or hard ground without lifting them off the surface. The runners spread the weight over a wide area and reduce friction, effectively halving or further reducing the load's apparent weight when hauled by a single person. Simple and cheap to build from available timber, this device was an early and widespread solution for moving goods in regions without wheeled transport, especially useful in colder climates where snow and ice make runners more effective than wheels.

name: Skis
description: Long, narrow runners strapped to the feet, allowing a traveler to glide across snow at speeds comparable to running on bare ground. The oldest known skis date to Scandinavia around 5000 B.C., where they enabled hunters and travelers to cross snowfields that would otherwise be impassable on foot. Skiing downhill builds speed rapidly, while uphill travel is slow and tiring. Skilled skiers can brake sharply to avoid obstacles, and a fast descent can even spray snow into the eyes of anyone following too closely behind.

name: Snowshoes
description: Elliptical frames, larger than the wearer's foot and typically woven from wood and rawhide netting, strapped to the feet to distribute body weight over a wider area when walking on snow. Used by tribal peoples across the cold regions of both the Old and New Worlds since the Paleolithic era, snowshoes allow travel atop deep snow that would otherwise cause a walker to sink with every step. Though they slow a traveler slightly compared to normal walking, they make long winter journeys across snowfields possible where none would otherwise be feasible.

name: Travois
description: A hauling aid made of two notched poles lashed together at a raised forward end, with their rear ends dragging separately along the ground, supporting a flexible platform of basketry, leather, or netting slung between them. Loads carried on a travois are effectively much lighter to drag than if carried directly, especially over snow, ice, or soft ground. Versions exist sized for a man, a dog, or (at TL1) a horse to pull, the larger animal-drawn versions carrying substantially more weight and being common among nomadic peoples such as the Plains tribes of North America.

name: Ice Skates
description: Modern-style ice skates with steel blades developed in the Netherlands between 1300 and 1400 A.D., once good steel became widely available. Unlike earlier bone skates, the sharpened steel blade actually cuts into the ice, giving the skater far better traction, control, and the ability to push off for greater speed. Strapped or bound to ordinary boots, these skates turned ice skating from an awkward gliding technique into a genuinely fast and maneuverable form of winter travel and recreation across frozen lakes, canals, and rivers.

name: Blanket (Horse)
description: A moderately heavy cloth laid over a horse's back beneath a saddle or before a rider mounts bareback. The blanket cushions the rider's weight and prevents chafing of both the horse's sides and the rider's legs during long rides. Simple and inexpensive, it was among the earliest pieces of riding equipment developed, improving the comfort and endurance of both horse and rider on extended journeys and reducing the fatigue that comes from constant friction and pressure during travel.

name: Bridle
description: A band of leather straps that fits around a horse's nose and head, developed in Ukraine around 4000 B.C. as one of the earliest pieces of equine equipment. It provides a secure attachment point for reins, allowing a rider or handler to direct the animal's movements, and can also be used to lead the horse on foot. The bridle partially compensates for the difficulty of controlling a mount through leg pressure alone, making it a foundational piece of gear for any rider working with horses, donkeys, mules, or similar animals.

name: Bridle and Bit
description: A standard leather bridle augmented with a metal mouthpiece that fits into the natural gap between a horse's teeth, resting on the sensitive gums. By applying gentle pressure to the bit through the reins, a rider gains far more precise and immediate control over the animal's direction and speed than with a plain bridle alone. This combination became the standard arrangement for controlling riding and draft horses across most of the ancient and medieval world, vastly improving a rider's ability to guide a mount in combat or travel.

name: Halter
description: A simple piece of harness resembling a bridle, but designed specifically for tying up or leading a horse or other domesticated animal rather than for riding control. Made of leather straps fitted around the head and nose, a halter provides a secure point for a lead rope and is far safer for tethering an animal than a bridle, which can injure a struggling horse's mouth. Halters were made for many species of working and pack animals across the ancient world, forming a basic part of any handler's equipment.

name: Riding Crop
description: A short cane, typically two to three feet long, wrapped in braided leather with a flexible leather lash at the tip. Used to tap or strike a horse's sides to encourage it forward or guide its direction, the riding crop can be held in the same hand as the reins, leaving the rider's other hand free. Though simple, it gives a rider noticeably better control over a mount and became a common accessory for riders of all classes, later acquiring associations with equestrian sport and aristocratic horsemanship.

name: Cushioned Saddle
description: Developed by the Scythians around 400 B.C., this saddle consists of a pair of cushions, one for each side of a horse's back, joined together by wooden arches at the front and rear. It distributes the rider's weight more evenly across the horse's back than riding bareback, reducing fatigue for both animal and rider on long journeys. The stable, padded seat also helps the rider stay mounted, and was often sold together with a horse blanket for additional comfort and protection.

name: Horned Saddle
description: A rigid-framed saddle with vertical protrusions, or horns, at all four corners, used by the Celts around 100 B.C. and later adopted by the Roman army. The horns brace a rider's thighs firmly in place, giving an exceptionally secure seat that even allows an unconscious rider to remain mounted. This stability came at the cost of making it difficult to dismount quickly. Sold with a horse blanket, the horned saddle represented a major step toward the combat-ready saddles that would follow at later tech levels.

name: Riding Saddle
description: First used by the Thracians around 300 B.C., the standard riding saddle has a rigid wooden frame providing a far more stable seat than a simple cushion, featuring a low pommel at the front and a low cantle at the rear. It greatly improves a rider's ability to remain mounted and control the horse over long distances, removing penalties associated with carrying heavy loads while riding. Sold together with a horse blanket, this saddle design became the basis for most later European riding saddles.

name: Saddlebags
description: A pair of leather pouches designed to drape over a horse's back behind the saddle, allowing a rider to carry food, supplies, tools, or personal belongings without holding them by hand or burdening the rider's own pack. Each set can hold around forty pounds of goods, making them indispensable for travelers, messengers, merchants, and soldiers on long journeys where self-sufficiency was essential. Saddlebags became a standard accessory wherever riding saddles were used.

name: Spurs
description: A Roman invention dating to the first century B.C., spurs are metal devices worn on the heels of a rider's boots, used to prod a horse's sides and encourage it to move faster or respond to commands. In the later Middle Ages, spurs became symbols of knighthood and nobility, often crafted ornately in gilded or silver finishes and ceremonially awarded to new knights. Functionally, they give a rider improved ability to direct and motivate a mount, especially in combat situations.

name: Horseshoes
description: Curved metal plates, developed around 1000 A.D., that are nailed to the underside of a horse's hooves to protect them from wear and damage on hard surfaces such as rock or paved roads. A set of horseshoes greatly reduces the risk of a horse going lame or developing sore feet during long journeys or heavy labor, and also improves the animal's stamina. Their introduction allowed horses to be worked harder and travel further on rough terrain than was previously practical.

name: War Saddle
description: A development of the riding saddle featuring a pommel at the front and a high cantle at the back, allowing a mounted warrior to brace himself firmly during combat without the dismounting penalty of a horned saddle. This design gave cavalry riders the stability needed to wield weapons effectively from horseback, particularly when bracing a couched lance against the cantle. Sold with a horse blanket, the war saddle became standard equipment for medieval knights and other shock cavalry.

name: Stirrups
description: A pair of foot supports suspended from straps on either side of a saddle, most likely invented in Central Asia and shown in Chinese art dated to 322 A.D., reaching Western Europe by 700 A.D. Stirrups allow a rider to mount a horse easily, stand up in the saddle for better visibility or to strike downward at an enemy, and brace firmly when using a couched lance. Their introduction revolutionized cavalry warfare by giving riders dramatically improved stability and leverage in combat.

name: Sidesaddle
description: Invented at the behest of Catherine de Medici, the sidesaddle allows a woman wearing a full skirt to ride facing forward rather than sideways. The rider's right leg curls around a pommel so it can dangle over the horse's left side, braced by a secondary pommel on the saddle's right side, and the design includes a single stirrup. While safer and more dignified than earlier sideways-facing arrangements, mounting and dismounting quickly remains awkward, and the design requires the horse to compensate for an unbalanced rider.

name: Ankus
description: An elephant goad consisting of a wooden shaft tipped with a sharp metal hook, used by a mahout to control an elephant by tugging at sensitive points on its head and ears, or by reversing the tool to strike the animal. The ankus gave handlers reliable control over animals far too large and powerful to restrain by force, and was essential equipment wherever elephants were used for transport, labor, ceremony, or war. In a pinch, its hooked metal head could also serve as a weapon.

name: Howdah
description: A boxlike platform strapped to an elephant's back with ropes, providing seating for up to four passengers behind the mahout, who rides on the elephant's neck. Howdahs were used both for ceremonial transport of nobles and kings, and in warfare, where occupants could shoot bows or wield weapons from an elevated vantage point. Many howdahs included a large umbrella as a sunscreen for the riders. Roughly five feet long, three feet wide, and two feet deep, the howdah was an iconic feature of South and Southeast Asian elephant transport.

name: Camel Mats
description: An early form of camel gear consisting of several thick mats piled in front of the camel's hump to create a high, flat platform. Originally intended for carrying cargo rather than passengers, this simple arrangement could also accommodate a rider, though it provided an unstable seat. The considerable bulk and weight of the stacked mats represented a significant burden for the animal, but the design's simplicity made it an accessible early solution for using camels to transport goods across desert trade routes.

name: Camel Bridle and Bit
description: A bridle and bit adapted for the different mouth structure of camels, developed once these animals came into use as riding mounts. Functioning similarly to equine versions, this gear gives a rider substantially improved control over a camel's direction and pace, whether the reins are held in one hand or two. As camels became important pack and riding animals across Arabia and Central Asia, specialized control gear like this became essential for both everyday travel and military use.

name: Camel Stick
description: A simple stick used by riders seated behind a camel's hump to reach forward and tap or strike the animal's sides, encouraging it to move or change direction. Functionally similar to a riding crop for horses, the camel stick gave handlers a basic but effective means of directing their mounts on long desert journeys and trade caravans, complementing bridles and saddles in the overall control of these valuable pack and riding animals.

name: Cushion Camel Saddle
description: A purely riding-oriented camel saddle consisting of a padded loop that encircles the camel's hump, held in place by wooden poles at the front and rear. This design provided a more stable seat than simply sitting atop the hump unaided, helping riders remain mounted during long journeys across desert terrain. Lightweight and relatively simple to construct, it represented an accessible option for travelers who needed basic riding stability without the cost of more elaborate framed saddles.

name: Early Riding Camel Saddle
description: Developed in southern Arabia around 1200 B.C., this is the oldest known design for a camel riding saddle. A wooden saddlebow positioned in front of the camel's hump supports a cushion placed behind it, on which the rider sits, while cargo can also be lashed to the saddlebow itself. This arrangement provided an early standardized way to ride camels comfortably and securely, laying the groundwork for the more elaborate framed saddles that would follow centuries later.

name: Framed Camel Saddle
description: The most elaborate and familiar type of camel saddle, developed in northern Arabia around 500 B.C. and credited with enabling the use of camels in warfare. Wooden saddlebows at front and rear, supported by cushions, are linked by side frames that hold a platform atop the hump where the rider sits. By transmitting the rider's weight to the camel's ribs rather than the unsupported hump, this saddle provides an exceptionally secure and stable seat suitable for combat and heavy loads alike.

name: Shoulder Camel Saddle
description: A North African camel saddle that places the rider on the camel's shoulders rather than over the hump. A high pommel and cantle hold the rider securely in place, while the design allows the rider to use their toes against the camel's neck for additional steering control. This unusual seating position offered riders a different balance of stability and control compared to hump-mounted saddles, reflecting regional variation in how different cultures adapted camels for riding.

name: Litter
description: The simplest passenger-carrying device, consisting of a stretcher made from two long wooden poles with leather or heavy cloth fastened between them to form a bed. The passenger lies down between the poles, which two bearers lift onto their shoulders and carry across virtually any terrain that can be walked over. Litters were used throughout history to transport the sick, wounded, elderly, or otherwise immobile, requiring no roads or animals, only human strength and stamina.

name: Sedan Chair
description: A passenger conveyance consisting of a seat mounted on two long poles that extend front and back, carried on the shoulders of two bearers. The basic version is an exposed seat, but more ornate models add curtains, walls, and doors for privacy and weather protection, making them especially popular among the wealthy. In Chinese tradition, brides traditionally rode to their weddings in enclosed sedan chairs, reflecting the sedan chair's association with status, ceremony, and comfort for those who could afford to be carried rather than walk.

name: Palanquin
description: A larger and more luxurious form of sedan chair used in ancient India, long enough for the rider to recline on a cushioned floor and always fully enclosed for privacy and shade. Its poles are spaced more widely apart and supported by four bearers, with parties of six porters often employed so that pairs could rest in rotation during long journeys. The palanquin represented the height of comfort in human-powered transport, reserved for royalty, nobility, and other high-status travelers.

name: Horse Litter
description: Developed by the Normans around 1100 A.D., this device resembles an oversized stretcher but is carried between two horses harnessed to its shafts rather than on the shoulders of human bearers. Wider than a hand-carried litter and built with longer poles, it allowed the wounded or infirm to be transported more quickly across the countryside than human bearers could manage. Controlling the two horses required skilled handling, and a passenger trying to fight from within the litter found their footing precarious.

name: Dogsled
description: The classic arctic vehicle used by Inuit tribes, made of bone and leather rather than wood and long enough for a man to lie down on, or alternatively to be loaded with gear while the owner runs alongside. Drawn by a team of fourteen dogs, each harnessed by its own leather trace, the dogsled was the primary means of overland transport across snow and ice in the far north, capable of covering long distances efficiently where wheeled vehicles could never function.

name: Fifty-Man Sledge
description: A massive sledge used for hauling construction materials and other heavy loads, similar in principle to the one-man sledge but on a far larger scale. The load rests on a flat wooden platform that sits directly atop two long runners, requiring dozens of laborers to haul it across the ground using ropes. Such sledges were essential for moving the enormous stone blocks and timbers used in monumental construction projects before the widespread use of wheeled transport for heavy cargo.

name: Oxcart
description: One of the world's oldest utility vehicles, found across most of Europe and Asia, where it has hauled farm products to market for millennia. A two-wheeled cart pulled by a pair of oxen yoked together, with a driver typically walking alongside to lead the animals using the Teamster skill. Oxcarts move at a slow walking pace and are limited to about five hours of travel per day, but their low cost and reliance on oxen rather than horses made them accessible to farmers and merchants throughout the ancient and medieval world.

name: Heavy Chariot
description: A large, massive war chariot drawn by four ponies and carrying three men: a driver, a warrior, and a shield carrier. A U-shaped wooden screen rises to waist height at the front and sides, protecting the riders from attacks by foot soldiers. Favored by the Hittites of Anatolia and used in China during the Warring States period, heavy chariots were designed to charge directly into infantry or other chariots, breaking enemy formations through sheer momentum and the threat of mounted attack.

name: Light Chariot
description: A two-man chariot designed as a mobile shooting platform for an archer wielding a powerful composite bow, carrying a driver and an archer and pulled by two ponies. It features a waist-height screen made of leather or basketry over a light wooden frame, light enough that the entire vehicle could be carried by one or two men over rough terrain. The standard tactic was to ride past enemy formations while shooting arrows, a hit-and-run technique used widely across the ancient Near East and Eurasian steppe.

name: Straddle Car
description: An early precursor to the chariot, drawn by an onager rather than a pony, offering the driver no protective screen and no floor at all. The driver sits just above the axle with legs dangling on either side of the central pole, perched on a seat resembling a low-tech bicycle saddle. Straddle cars were not driven into combat directly; instead, they ferried warriors to the battlefield, where the occupant would dismount and fight on foot, representing one of the earliest uses of wheeled vehicles in warfare.

name: Battle Car
description: An Irish light chariot variant weighing even less than the typical Near Eastern light chariot, and lacking any protective screen for its two riders. The warrior aboard carries several javelins rather than a bow, throwing them at enemies or running out onto the yoke between the ponies to strike at foes directly. Like other light chariots, the battle car was primarily used to transport a warrior into position, who would then typically dismount to continue fighting on foot.

name: Wagon
description: A heavier four-wheeled vehicle drawn by two draft horses, featuring a seat in front for the driver and a substantial cargo bed behind. Wagons represented a significant step up from two-wheeled carts in carrying capacity, becoming the backbone of overland freight transport across medieval and early modern Europe and Asia. Their greater size and capacity made them indispensable for moving goods, settlers, and military supplies over long distances on roads capable of bearing their weight.

name: War Wagon
description: Known as the tabor or hradba vozova in Czech, this armored wagon was developed by Jan Zizka during the Hussite revolts of the early 1400s, turning an ordinary wagon into an early armored personnel carrier. Drawn by four draft horses, it has a twenty-foot rectangular body with heavy wooden sides three to four feet high, above which hinged boards with firing slits can be raised to shelter soldiers armed with bows, crossbows, or early firearms. War wagons were typically deployed in defensive squares of ten vehicles chained wheel-to-wheel, forming a mobile fortress that could be assembled almost anywhere, crewed by drivers, gunners, crossbowmen, and melee troops.

name: Carriage
description: A small vehicle used for city transportation, suspended on leather straps over its axles rather than mounted directly upon them, providing a far smoother ride than earlier wheeled vehicles by absorbing shocks from rough cobblestone streets. Known as a hackney carriage, this two-horse vehicle formed the basis of urban taxi fleets in cities such as London and Paris, with London's hackney carriage trade dating back to 1605, offering paid rides for hire to city dwellers and travelers.

name: Coach
description: A large four-horse passenger vehicle, also known as a coach-and-four, that entered use around 1640 and became one of the major types of stagecoach. Like the carriage, the body is suspended by leather straps rather than mounted directly on the axles, smoothing out the bumps of travel over rough roads. An advanced harness arrangement allows a single driver to manage all four horses, making coaches the premier long-distance passenger and mail vehicles of the early modern period before the railway era.

name: Surfboard
description: Developed in Hawaii prior to European contact, the surfboard is a long wooden board used to ride ocean waves, a pastime traditionally reserved for chiefs and comparable in cultural significance to jousting for medieval Europeans. A nobleman's board measures roughly fifteen feet long, eighteen inches wide, and five inches thick, while a commoner's board is smaller, typically around ten feet long. Riders can reach considerable speeds on good waves, though paddling out to catch them is far slower.

name: Float Bridge
description: Described in a fourth-century Roman military text as the ascogefyrus, this contraption consists of animal skins worked into flattish air sacs, inflated with bellows, then rolled up and carried to a river crossing where they are unrolled and tied into place to form a four-foot-wide walkway. Footing on the unsteady surface is treacherous, similar to walking on a raft, but the float bridge allowed armies to cross rivers quickly without waiting to build a permanent bridge, each section providing substantial buoyancy per yard of length.

name: Inflated Skin Float
description: A buoyancy aid made from an animal skin sealed and inflated with air, used by swimmers to support themselves in water or to construct simple rafts. Among the lightest and most buoyant float materials available at low tech levels, inflated skins provided a cheap and portable way to cross rivers, support a load on the water, or assist a struggling swimmer. Such floats formed the conceptual starting point for hide boats and other watercraft, exploiting the simple principle that air-filled skins are far lighter than the water they displace.

name: Reed Bundle Float
description: A bundle of dried reeds bound tightly together to form a buoyant mass that floats on water, used both as a personal swimming aid and as the basic building block of reed boats and rafts. Reed bundles are heavier and less buoyant than inflated skins but far more durable and easier to obtain in marshy regions where reeds grow abundantly, such as ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia. Over time, reed floats become waterlogged and lose buoyancy, but tight binding extends their useful life considerably.

name: Dugout Canoe
description: A very basic log boat suitable for one man, made by hollowing out a log roughly eight feet long and two and a half feet in diameter using fire or cutting tools, leaving a roughly U-shaped rigid shell. Heavier and more durable than a bark canoe, with walls two to three inches thick, dugout canoes are seaworthy enough that ancient Polynesians crossed the Pacific Ocean in similar craft. They can be produced anywhere good-sized trees grow, making them one of the most widespread early watercraft designs.

name: Long Dugout Canoe
description: A larger dugout canoe made from a sizable log thirty feet long and three feet in diameter, wide enough to seat additional paddlers alternately on the left and right sides for its length. This design allowed dugout canoes to scale up substantially in passenger and cargo capacity while retaining the rigid, single-piece-hull construction of smaller dugouts, making them suitable for transporting groups of people and significant amounts of cargo on rivers, lakes, and coastal waters.

name: Outrigger Canoe
description: A long dugout canoe fitted with an outrigger: a smaller log fifteen feet long, attached to the main hull's midsection by several poles about three feet long. The outrigger provides significant added stability in rough water, making such craft well suited to lengthy ocean voyages, including the Polynesian expansion across the Pacific Ocean. The outrigger is treated as a separate structural component from the main hull, able to be damaged independently in combat or storms.

name: War Canoe
description: A very large dugout canoe, exemplified by the Maori war canoe of New Zealand, carved from a single massive kauri pine log whose sides are expanded outward to provide room for two paddlers seated side by side. Measuring sixty feet long with a five-foot beam, war canoes carried large crews of paddlers and warriors into battle along coastlines and rivers. Similar large dugouts were built in the Pacific Northwest, sometimes by joining two trees end to end where individual trees were not large enough.

name: Large Bark Canoe
description: A large but comparatively light canoe, twenty feet long and three feet wide, holding four men seated in a single row. Made from a single piece of bark stripped from a tree such as birch, elm, hickory, eucalyptus, or spruce, bent into a semi-cylindrical shape with curving ends sealed by sewing, grass, or clay. Construction is very light, with walls averaging only half an inch thick, making bark canoes fast and easy to carry overland between waterways, though less durable than dugouts.

name: Oblong Hide Boat
description: A craft comparable to the Irish coracle, fairly round but somewhat longer than it is wide, typically about five feet long and two-thirds as wide. The same statistics describe Vietnamese fishing boats made of bamboo matting sealed with resin. Propelled by paddling, oblong hide boats are simple, lightweight vessels that one person can carry, well suited to fishing and short-distance travel on calm waters near shore.

name: Round Hide Boat
description: A circular watercraft made of hides stretched over a light wooden frame, such as the Plains Indian bull boat or the bamboo-framed parical of South India; the Mongols used a similar boat called pi. The same statistics also represent the ancient Mesopotamian quffa, a basketry boat with an external coating of tar for waterproofing. Roughly five feet in diameter, these simple round craft were used for ferrying people and goods across rivers and along calm waterways, particularly where larger trees for dugouts were scarce.

name: Large Hide Boat
description: A substantial craft framed with heavy timbers and covered with several large hides, exemplified by the Inuit umiak, the similar Siberian baidara, or the Irish currach in which legend claims Saint Brendan voyaged across the Atlantic. Typical dimensions are thirty-six feet long, six feet wide, and three feet high. These boat-shaped vessels have curved sides, are steered by a stern oar, and can be propelled by oars or sail, making them capable of substantial open-water voyages despite their relatively simple hide-and-frame construction.

name: Double Canoe
description: A sailing vessel similar to those used by the Polynesians who colonized the Pacific, consisting of two long dugout canoes held side by side, ten feet apart, by a frame supporting a fifteen-foot-square mat platform. A mast above the platform carries a distinctive proa sail that allows the craft to beat upwind by shunting. Half a dozen paddlers can sit in front of and behind the platform, while the space beneath it under each canoe is used for cargo storage, making this a versatile vessel for long ocean voyages.

name: River Barge
description: A fairly large, flat-bottomed rectangular vessel suited to hauling bulk cargo up and down rivers, or ferrying freight and passengers across them. Effectively a big open box forty feet long, seven and a half feet wide, and one foot deep, very slightly tapered toward the ends, the river barge is poled across rivers by four men on each side, while travel upriver requires towing from the bank. Its simple flat-bottomed design maximizes cargo capacity for its size on calm inland waterways.

name: Sampan
description: The starting point for East Asian boat and ship design, a flat-bottomed boat made from one bottom plank and two side planks, with the side planks converging in front to form a pointed prow while the stern is squared off. Typical dimensions are fifteen feet long, four feet wide, and one and a half feet high. Sampans feature watertight bulkheads dividing the interior into segments, making them very hard to sink, and are usually propelled by single-oar sculling with a yuloh, or poled in shallow water.

name: Sewn-Plank Riverboat
description: A boat in the Egyptian style, assembled from planks of acacia or expensive imported woods such as cedar, averaging three feet long and sewn together edge to edge. Dimensions are thirty feet long, seven feet wide, and two and a half feet high, with both ends tapering to points. Propelled by paddles wielded by four pairs of crewmen, a lookout in the bow uses a sounding pole to feel for underwater snags while a helmsman in the stern steers with a paddle held in the water.

name: Fowling Boat
description: A papyrus raft boat built for pharaohs and nobles to use for duck hunting along the Nile, suitable for travel over still or slow-moving water anywhere. The sixteen-foot-long body tapers from a three-foot beam at the midsection to a blunt prow and a sharp stern, both curved up out of the water. Two crewmen pole the craft along while a passenger, typically the hunter, rides at the front, making this a lightweight pleasure and hunting craft for the Egyptian elite.

name: Fishing Boat
description: A boat constructed in the shell-first style of the ancient Mediterranean, with planks joined edge to edge and pegged together, and minimal internal framing for light construction. Dimensions are twenty-seven feet long, seven and a half feet wide, and four feet high, with a pointed bow and squared-off stern. Propelled by two pairs of oars, the fishing boat is primarily used for fishing but can be adapted to carry cargo or up to ten passengers, making it a versatile small working vessel of the classical world.

name: Square-Rigged Sailboat
description: A Romano-Celtic craft of the British Isles dating to the later Roman Empire, with planks laid edge to edge but not fastened together directly; instead, they are nailed to internal framing timbers and the gaps between them are caulked watertight. Dimensions are thirty-seven and a half feet long, ten feet wide, and three feet high, with both bow and stern pointed. A single twenty-five-foot mast, positioned a third of the way back from the bow, carries a square sail, and construction is sturdy enough for use in bays and coastal waters.

name: Faering
description: A boat constructed much like the square-rigged sailboat but propelled by three to four pairs of oars, used in the Viking era, though the same statistics can represent a variety of medieval oared boats. Typical size is twenty feet long, four feet wide, and two feet high. The faering can be used in coastal waters for fishing or transport, or carried aboard a larger ship to serve as its tender, providing a versatile small craft for short trips ashore or local fishing.

name: Sewn-Plank Sailboat
description: A boat of the design traditionally used in the Indian Ocean, built from long planks stitched together with little or no internal frame, giving the hull flexibility that proves advantageous in coastal waters. A single mast carries a large lateen sail, efficient for sailing into the wind but too heavy for quick tacking, so the vessel relies on the wearing technique to change tack. At twenty-two feet long and five feet wide, this is a comparatively small craft, well suited for fishing or local travel.

name: Diving Stone
description: A simple weighted aid to diving, consisting of a stone with a cord tied around it. The diver thrusts one foot into the cord as though into a stirrup, and the stone's weight carries him quickly downward without requiring active swimming effort, while he can still swim horizontally to some degree. A companion in a boat can pull the stone back up by its attached rope for reuse, making this an inexpensive and reusable tool for divers seeking to reach depth quickly without expending energy fighting their own buoyancy.

name: Breathing Tube
description: An early snorkel analog developed by ancient Egyptian fowlers to help them sneak up on waterfowl: a hollow papyrus reed used like a huge straw to inhale air while the body remains submerged. A two-foot tube allows submergence to about sixteen inches below the surface; any deeper and water pressure prevents the lungs from drawing breath through it. The device let hunters approach prey almost invisibly, as only the small tube breaks the water's surface, making the swimmer very difficult to spot.

name: Air Bladder
description: A diving aid shown in use in an Assyrian relief dated to the eighth century B.C., consisting of an animal-skin bladder filled with air before the diver enters the water, providing several breaths' worth of reserve air to extend a dive considerably. Because an inflated bladder is also a strong float, the diver must carry additional weight to remain submerged while using it. This device represents an early attempt at extending underwater endurance beyond what a single held breath could achieve.

name: Diagnostic Manual
description: A book or collection of scrolls cataloging medical conditions, visible symptoms, recommended treatments, and likely outcomes. Owning one lets a healer make an unmodified Diagnosis roll; without it, a practitioner facing an unfamiliar condition suffers a penalty. A large, comprehensive manual amounting to a medical encyclopedia (or set of volumes) provides an even greater bonus for known conditions. Such works were copied by hand before printing, making the comprehensive versions rare and costly. Printed editions become available at higher tech levels, while hand-copied scrolls remain the norm for early physicians and itinerant healers.

name: Comprehensive Diagnostic Manual
description: An expanded medical encyclopedia or multi-volume reference set compiling diagnostic and treatment knowledge for a wide range of conditions. It grants a significant bonus to Diagnosis rolls for conditions described within it, effectively serving as a portable medical library for a physician's practice or traveling kit. Such works represent the accumulated case histories and theories of generations of practitioners, often produced by religious or scholarly institutions that supported hospitals and centers of learning. Their bulk and cost made them the province of well-funded infirmaries rather than individual healers.

name: Urine Flask
description: A small glass vessel resembling a modern test tube, used by TL3-4 diagnosticians to collect and examine urine specimens for signs of blood, sugar, or sediment. It is standard equipment for the era's most advanced physicians, who relied on visual inspection of bodily fluids as a key diagnostic technique. Without one, a healer attempting to diagnose conditions affecting the urinary tract works at a disadvantage. Its glass construction makes it both a mark of medical sophistication and a fragile item requiring careful handling and storage in a physician's bag.

name: Tourniquet
description: A length of sturdy cord, long enough to be tied tightly around a wounded limb to restrict blood flow and allow a wound's surface to clot. Functionally similar to a garrote, it can be made from rope, string, leather thong, or other suitable cordage. Available at the most primitive tech levels, it represents one of the oldest emergency interventions for serious bleeding. While effective at stopping blood loss, improper or prolonged use risks tissue damage to the limb below the tie point, a danger well understood even by early practitioners of field medicine.

name: Bandages (basket of precut cloth)
description: A basket of precut, clean cloth strips, typically cotton, linen, or silk, sufficient to dress about half a dozen wounds. Used to treat burns, cuts, impaling and piercing injuries, and abrasions, bandages help control bleeding, keep dirt out of wounds, and reduce the risk of infection. They entered systematic use with ancient Egyptian linen wrappings and remain a cornerstone of first aid through every later tech level. A tight bandage can even substitute for a tourniquet in an emergency, making this basic kit indispensable equipment for any healer or soldier.

name: First Aid Kit
description: A satchel containing bandages plus medicinal substances: raw materials for poultices, and infusions or decoctions for compresses. At higher tech levels it also includes ointments and soap for cleaning wounds. This well-stocked kit grants a noticeable bonus to First Aid attempts compared to working with bare hands or improvised materials, reflecting the value of having the right herbal preparations and dressings ready to hand. It is the standard equipment carried by traveling healers, military medics, and prudent adventurers heading into dangerous territory.

name: Arm Cast
description: A rigid support made by tightly wrapping a broken arm with bandages and then applying plaster over the wrappings, which hardens to hold the bone in place during healing. More effective and durable than a simple splint, the cast distributes support evenly around the limb and resists shifting. Casting represents an advance over splinting available from TL1 onward, requiring plaster-working knowledge in addition to bandaging materials. Once set, the rigid plaster shell must be cut away when the bone has sufficiently healed.

name: Leg Cast
description: A rigid plaster shell formed by tightly wrapping a broken leg with bandages and then applying plaster over them, hardening to immobilize the limb during healing. Larger and considerably heavier than an arm cast due to the size of the leg, it provides the structural support necessary for a major fracture to mend correctly. This technique, available from TL1, represents a significant improvement over crude wooden splints, though it requires more material, time, and skill to apply properly.

name: Barber's Kit
