description: A modest collection of tools, including a knife, razor, scissors, small whetstone, and at higher tech levels a spoon and tiny file, primarily intended for shaving beards and cutting hair. In a pinch, the same sharp implements make it usable for minor surgery, though its tools are not purpose-built for the task. Historically, barbers often doubled as surgeons in many low-tech societies, performing bloodletting, tooth extraction, and minor procedures alongside their grooming trade, blurring the line between the two professions.

name: Forceps
description: A pair of pincer-like tools used for grasping objects or body parts with a firmer grip than unaided fingers can provide. Surgeons rely on forceps to hold tissue steady during incisions, retrieve foreign objects, or manipulate delicate structures without slipping. They also let a surgeon work in tight or awkward spaces, such as wounds or natural body cavities, without penalty. Basic forceps appear at TL1 and form the foundation for many specialized variants developed at higher tech levels, from dental tools to fixation clamps.

name: Dental Forceps
description: A specialized variety of forceps designed specifically to grip a tooth firmly and pull it free from the jaw. Using them effectively requires a strength-based surgical effort; with a good grip the procedure goes more smoothly, though a critical success extracts the whole tooth cleanly while failure can leave splinters behind or the tooth in place entirely. Introduced at TL2, dental forceps reflect the growing specialization of surgical tools as practitioners began developing instruments tailored to specific procedures rather than relying on general-purpose implements.

name: Dental Splinter Forceps
description: A fine-tipped variant of dental forceps used to extract the small root fragments left behind when a tooth breaks off during an extraction attempt. Unlike standard dental forceps, using this tool to remove splinters requires no additional skill roll, making cleanup of a botched extraction more reliable. Its narrow jaws are designed to grip tiny fragments embedded in the gum or socket, a task that would be impossible with bulkier instruments. It is a small but essential addition to any TL2+ dental practitioner's kit.

name: Fixation Forceps
description: Forceps fitted with a sliding ring mechanism that locks the jaws shut, allowing them to grip and hold a body part or piece of tissue securely without the surgeon needing to maintain manual pressure. This free-standing grip is invaluable during lengthy procedures where the surgeon's hands are needed elsewhere, or when steady, prolonged traction is required. Introduced at TL2 alongside other specialized forceps variants, fixation forceps represent an early step toward instruments that could function semi-independently during an operation.

name: Staphylagra
description: A specialized form of fixation forceps fitted with toothed jaws, used to firmly crush chronically inflamed uvulas or hemorrhoids so they can be removed without excessive bleeding. The locking mechanism inherited from standard fixation forceps allows the surgeon to clamp the tissue and maintain pressure throughout the procedure. This grim but practical TL2 instrument illustrates how low-tech surgeons adapted general clamping designs to address specific, painful chronic conditions that had no other effective treatment.

name: Surgical Hook
description: A simple rod fitted with a sharp or blunt hook at one end, used by surgeons to pull back the edges of a wound or incision, or to manipulate a piece of tissue during an operation. Its design gives the surgeon a way to hold tissue out of the way without using fingers, which is especially useful in deep or awkward wounds. Available from TL1, the surgical hook is one of the most basic specialized instruments, found in nearly every surgeon's kit regardless of size or quality.

name: Surgical Needle
description: A fine, pointed needle designed to pull thread or sinew through flesh when stitching up a wound. Ordinary sewing or leatherworking needles can substitute in a pinch, but they count as improvised gear and impose a penalty on the overall surgery. A proper surgical needle is shaped and sized specifically for closing incisions and lacerations with minimal additional trauma. Available from TL1, it is among the cheapest yet most essential items in any surgeon's small kit, used in nearly every operation that closes with sutures.

name: Surgical Probe
description: A long, flexible rod, usually made of bronze, used by surgeons to locate foreign objects lodged within a wound or to assess the body's internal state by touch. By gently exploring a wound's depths, a probe reduces the severe penalty surgeons face when operating on an undiagnosed internal injury, such as an arrow or bullet buried in tissue. Available from TL1, the probe is a vital diagnostic aid in an era without imaging technology, letting a surgeon plan an operation with at least some idea of what lies beneath the skin.

name: Scalpel
description: A small, extremely sharp blade used to make precise incisions during surgery. Its fine edge allows a surgeon to open skin and tissue with minimal additional trauma, an essential capability for everything from lancing an abscess to performing amputations. Available from TL1, the scalpel is the most iconic surgical instrument and a standard component of every surgeon's kit, small or large. Roman smiths were known to carburize the cutting edges of such small tools, giving them superior, steel-like sharpness that improved a surgeon's results.

name: Arrow Spoon
description: A specialized surgical instrument shaped to cradle and extract an embedded arrowhead from a wound without causing further injury during removal. Its spoon-like form slides alongside the shaft or head, shielding surrounding tissue from the barbs as the projectile is withdrawn. Introduced at TL2, the arrow spoon reflects the practical needs of battlefield surgeons dealing with the era's most common combat injuries, and represents a significant improvement over simply pulling an arrow free, which could tear additional flesh and worsen bleeding.

name: Catheter
description: A narrow tube that can be inserted into the bladder to displace a bladder stone and drain urine, providing temporary relief from blockage without curing the underlying condition. Using it correctly requires medical training, as improper insertion risks injury to delicate internal tissues. Introduced at TL2, the catheter addressed one of the more agonizing chronic conditions of the era, bladder stones, for which the only permanent cure was the dangerous surgical procedure known as cutting for the stone.

name: Speculum
description: An instrument used to dilate a body cavity, giving a surgeon or diagnostician a clearer view for examination and significantly reducing the awkward-reach penalties normally incurred when operating on natural orifices or deep wounds. Different body cavities required differently shaped specula, so a complete set might include several variants. Introduced at TL2, the speculum represented an important advance in gynecological, dental, and general diagnostic practice, allowing physicians to see and work more effectively without relying purely on touch.

name: Trephine
description: A specialized drill used to cut a circular plug of bone out of the skull during the ancient surgical procedure known as trepanning. Formed as a hollow metal tube with saw-like teeth at its working end, the trephine is rotated against the skull to remove a disc of bone, exposing the membranes beneath. Evidence of trepanning dates back to the Stone Age, with healed skulls showing patients survived the operation, but the trephine itself as a dedicated metal instrument appears at TL2, refining a procedure once performed with crude stone tools.

name: Small Surgeon's Kit
description: A portable set of essential surgical tools, typically including forceps, hooks, needles, probes, and scalpels, along with a supply of thread or sinew for stitching wounds and material for bandages. This compact kit represents the basic equipment a traveling surgeon would carry, sufficient to perform amputations, set bones, and close wounds in the field. Introduced at TL1, it forms the baseline against which more elaborate surgical equipment is measured, and its contents form the core of every larger surgical kit as well.

name: Large Surgeon's Kit
description: An extensive surgical kit typically kept in an infirmary or a surgeon's house, equivalent to two small kits combined with more specialized versions of the basic instruments, plus bone chisels and small hammers. At TL2 it expands further to include arrow spoons, catheters, cauteries, and specula. The superior craftsmanship and breadth of this kit give a meaningful quality bonus to surgical attempts, reflecting the advantage of a well-equipped operating room over a field surgeon's traveling pouch. Its size and weight make it impractical to carry, restricting it to a fixed medical facility.

name: Cautery
description: An instrument for controlled burning of human tissue, consisting of a sharp metal point at the end of a long rod with an insulated grip, designed to be heated in a brazier before use. Made of iron for its heat resistance, cauteries are sometimes called irons. A heated cautery can stop bleeding that resists ordinary first aid by sealing the wound through burning, and destroys bacteria along with flesh, potentially arresting an infection. Most surgeons regard cauterization as a last resort given the severe burns it can inflict if mishandled.

name: Cataract Needle
description: A very fine, sharp piece of metal designed to pierce the eyeball with minimal injury during eye surgery. Skilled use allows a surgeon to push a cataract away from the pupil, sever pieces of it, or press it down to fix it permanently out of the line of sight, restoring some vision to a patient suffering from clouded lenses. This delicate TL2 instrument exemplifies the specialized tools eye surgeons developed to work on one of the body's most sensitive organs without causing the crippling damage that ordinary surgical tools would inflict.

name: Eyelash Cautery
description: A fine iron needle fitted with a handle, heated and used to burn out the root of an ingrown eyelash after the offending hair has been plucked. This prevents the eyelash from regrowing inward and continuing to irritate the eye, a chronic and painful condition with no other reliable cure at low tech levels. A specialized application of general cautery technique, this TL2 instrument's small, precise tip allows a surgeon to target the tiny follicle without damaging the surrounding eyelid tissue.

name: Eyelash Forceps
description: A tiny set of grippers designed to seize and pull out an ingrown eyelash before the follicle is cauterized to prevent regrowth. Their small, precise jaws allow a surgeon to grasp a single hair without injuring the eyelid or eye itself. Working alongside the eyelash cautery, this TL2 instrument forms part of a specialized pair of tools developed specifically for treating chronic eyelid irritation, illustrating the increasing specialization of surgical equipment as tech level advances.

name: Traction Bench
description: A heavy bench, first recorded in ancient Greece around 500 B.C., that supports a patient and applies mechanical traction to a broken limb, allowing bonesetting to proceed independently of the surgeon's own physical strength. By providing a powerful, steady pulling force equivalent to a very strong surgeon, the bench enables proper realignment of severely displaced fractures that would otherwise be impossible to set. This device is considered an ancestor of the rack, a torture device built on similar principles, highlighting the uncomfortable overlap between early medical and punitive technologies.

name: Artificial Eye (Bitumen)
description: An early prosthetic eye made of bitumen paste coated with a thin layer of gold, worn purely for cosmetic and social purposes since it does not restore any sight. The oldest known example was worn by a woman in ancient Persia around 2900 B.C. Its brightly reflective surface would not have closely resembled a real eye and tended to cause chronic irritation to the socket. Despite these drawbacks, such prosthetics allowed people who had lost an eye to avoid the social stigma of an empty socket in eras with no functional alternative.

name: Wooden Hand
description: A purely cosmetic prosthetic replacement for a lost hand, elaborately carved to resemble the real thing but entirely nonfunctional for grasping or manipulation. Such prosthetics allowed amputees, often soldiers, laborers, or accident victims, to present a more typical appearance and avoid some of the social difficulties associated with visible disability. Introduced at TL2, the wooden hand reflects the skill of artificers who developed increasingly sophisticated carved replacements for lost limbs, even before functional prosthetics became possible.

name: Wooden Leg
description: A prosthetic leg that lessens the detrimental effects of having lost a leg, allowing a wearer to move about more easily than with no replacement at all. Herodotus wrote of a man with a wooden foot around 500 B.C., demonstrating the ancient origins of this technology. Its hard surface gives an unexpected secondary use: kicking with a wooden leg inflicts additional crushing damage compared to a normal kick. Introduced at TL2, the wooden leg represents one of the earliest genuinely functional, rather than purely cosmetic, prosthetic limbs.

name: Moxa Bundle
description: A small cone of dried mugwort leaves, burned on the skin at acupuncture points in the practice known as moxibustion. The cone is placed over a chosen point and ignited, with the heat believed to stimulate the body's vital energy much as needle insertion does. Practitioners can gather and prepare moxa bundles for free if mugwort can be found in the wild, requiring only a successful search and a simple preparation step. Though often associated with Japan, moxibustion is practiced throughout East Asia as a complement to acupuncture.

name: Cup (bloodletting cup)
description: A small horn or metal cup, heated and pressed against the skin over a shallow incision as part of the bloodletting practice known as cupping. As the trapped air cools, a partial vacuum forms, sealing the cup to the skin and drawing out blood through the incision. An older TL0 variant features a small hole through which the user sucks out air before sealing it with wax, achieving the same vacuum effect without heating. Cupping was practiced widely in Western and Eastern medical traditions as part of the broader theory of bleeding to balance bodily humors.

name: Lancet
description: A specialized small knife designed for opening a vein during bloodletting, known as venesection. Its narrow, precise blade allows a practitioner to make a controlled incision into a blood vessel, a procedure that requires careful skill to avoid disastrous complications. A botched cut can result in nothing but useless superficial bleeding, while a serious error risks opening an artery entirely, leading to dangerous, hard-to-control blood loss. Introduced at TL2, the lancet was a fixture of Western medical practice for centuries, used routinely as a treatment for countless ailments under humoral theory.

name: Massage Supplies
description: A collection of equipment for therapeutic massage, including a small brazier, vessels for heating oil and water, a towel that can be warmed and applied either dry or wet, and a stock of consumables such as oils and lotions for lubrication, scents, skin-stimulating compounds, and charcoal fuel for heating. Massage has been used for pain relief, particularly for tense or strained muscles, since the Stone Age, and these supplies represent the basic toolkit of a professional masseur. Replacement consumables must be purchased after each day of active use, reflecting their consumable nature.

name: Massage Table
description: A table large enough for an adult to lie on at full length, featuring a smooth surface and typically fitted with a pillow or cushion to support the ankles when lying prone or the knees when lying supine. This dedicated piece of furniture provides a stable, comfortable platform for therapeutic massage, which has been practiced around the world since TL0 for pain control and relief of strained muscles. Without such a table, any flat surface can serve as improvised equipment, though at a penalty to the masseur's effectiveness.

name: Massage Chair
description: A specialized chair designed for sitting in while receiving a massage, providing optimal exposure of the body to the masseur and adjustable to fit different body sizes and postures. The typical arrangement has the subject leaning forward with the back exposed, allowing focused treatment of back and shoulder tension. Its purpose-built design provides a quality bonus to massage treatment compared to improvised seating. Introduced at TL2, the massage chair reflects increasing specialization of furniture for therapeutic purposes alongside the rise of dedicated bathhouses and treatment facilities.

name: Olive Oil (medicinal, per pint)
description: A high-quality oil pressed from olives, used around the Mediterranean since the Neolithic for cleaning, healing, and ritual anointment. As a medicinal item, it serves as a lubricant during massage, a carrier medium for herbal preparations applied to the skin, and a soothing treatment for dry, irritated, or burned skin. Its quality and expense set it apart from ordinary fuel oils, which can substitute only as inferior, improvised equipment. A pint represents a practical working quantity for a healer's or masseur's supplies.

name: Lanolin (per pint)
description: A waxy substance extracted from sheep's wool by washing it in water, valued for its ability to naturally penetrate human skin. When mixed into creams and ointments, lanolin improves their quality, and applied to skin injuries it aids the body's natural recovery from wounds. Introduced at TL1, lanolin represents an early example of refining a byproduct of animal husbandry, specifically wool-washing, into a valuable medicinal ingredient, foreshadowing later cosmetic and pharmaceutical uses of the same substance.

name: Lotion (per pint)
description: An emulsion prepared from water and some form of fat or oil, with herbal additives providing texture, scent, or therapeutic effects. Basic lotion provides the same soothing and lubricating benefits as olive oil, while finer grades give greater bonuses to the quality of treatments using it, at correspondingly higher cost. Introduced at TL1, lotion represents a refinement of simple oils into a more sophisticated cosmetic and medicinal preparation, used for skin care, massage, and as a vehicle for delivering herbal remedies topically.

name: Backpack, Frame
description: A large rigid-framed pack worn on the back, designed to carry heavy loads of gear over long journeys. The internal or external frame distributes weight onto the hips and shoulders, making it far more comfortable than a simple sack for carrying bulky supplies such as food, bedding, tools, and camping equipment. Standard issue for adventurers, soldiers, and travelers who need to be self-sufficient on the road. Holds up to about 45 kilograms of gear, making it the workhorse choice for extended overland expeditions where every item must be carried by hand.

name: Backpack, Small
description: A compact soft pack worn on the shoulders, suitable for carrying a modest amount of personal gear without the bulk of a full frame pack. Useful for travelers who want to keep their hands free while carrying rations, a change of clothes, small tools, or personal valuables. Less cumbersome than a frame pack and easier to conceal under a cloak, but holds considerably less. A common possession for scouts, messengers, students, and anyone who needs quick access to a modest amount of belongings during day trips or short journeys.

name: Blanket
description: A thick woven blanket made of wool or similar heavy fabric, used for warmth while sleeping outdoors or in unheated quarters. It can be rolled and tied to a pack for travel, used as a makeshift cushion, or thrown over a shoulder for warmth on cold nights. While not as effective as a dedicated sleeping bag, a good blanket is an inexpensive and versatile piece of survival gear that every traveler in a low-tech world is likely to carry, doubling as an improvised stretcher, sunshade, or bundle wrap in a pinch.

name: Bottle, Ceramic
description: A fired-clay or earthenware bottle sealed with a stopper, used for storing and transporting liquids such as water, wine, oil, or medicine. Ceramic bottles are cheap and easy to produce but fragile compared to skins or metal containers, and they shatter if dropped or struck hard. Common throughout pre-industrial societies as household and travel containers, often stamped or marked to indicate contents or origin. A quart-sized bottle is a standard size for personal use, fitting easily into a pack or saddlebag.

name: Candle, Tallow
description: A simple candle made from rendered animal fat with a fiber wick, providing a small but steady light source for roughly twelve hours of burning. Tallow candles produce a notably smoky, greasy-smelling flame compared to beeswax candles, but they are far cheaper to produce and widely available. Used to light rooms, read by, or provide a portable light source when carried in a lantern or holder. A staple item for households, inns, and travelers throughout the medieval and early modern periods, often bought in bundles.

name: Climbing Gear
description: A bundled kit of equipment for scaling cliffs, walls, and rough terrain, including a small hammer, metal spikes for anchoring ropes, and simple metal loops (carabiners) for attaching lines. Used together with rope by anyone attempting a serious climb, this kit provides the basic tools needed to secure handholds and lifelines on a difficult ascent. Compact enough to be carried in a pack, it is essential gear for explorers, scouts, and anyone who expects to encounter steep terrain such as mountains, towers, or fortress walls during their travels.

name: Cord, 3/16-Inch
description: A thin length of braided or twisted cord, much lighter and weaker than full climbing rope but useful for a wide range of everyday tasks such as tying bundles, lashing gear to a pack, binding a prisoner's wrists, repairing equipment, or setting simple snares. Sold by the length, it supports a modest load before snapping and is carried in coils for convenience. Because it is thin and lightweight, a traveler can carry a large quantity without much added bulk, making it a versatile, low-cost item for camp chores and improvised repairs.

name: Fishhooks and Line
description: A small kit of metal hooks and lengths of fishing line, providing the basic tackle needed to catch fish from a riverbank, lake, or coastline when paired with a pole. Compact and lightweight, this kit is considered essential gear for anyone relying on the Fishing skill to supplement their food supply during extended travel or survival situations. The hooks come in a range of sizes for different catches, and the line can also serve double duty as light cordage in an emergency, making it a practical inclusion for any wilderness expedition.

name: Group Basics
description: A shared set of communal camping equipment intended to support a group of three to eight travelers using the Cooking and Survival skills together. The kit typically includes a large cook pot, lengths of rope, a hatchet, and other essentials needed to set up camp, prepare meals, and handle routine outdoor chores for the whole party. Rather than each person carrying duplicate gear, one or two members of a group can carry this kit to outfit everyone, making it an efficient and cost-effective choice for parties traveling together through the wilderness.

name: Iron Spike (Piton)
description: A sturdy iron spike with a ring or eye at one end, hammered into rock, wood, or masonry to anchor a rope, secure a line for climbing, or jam a door shut from the outside. Climbers drive pitons into cracks in a cliff face to create secure anchor points for a safety line, while adventurers might use the same spikes to wedge doors closed against pursuers or to gain purchase while scaling a wall. Cheap, durable, and endlessly reusable, a handful of these spikes is standard equipment for anyone expecting to climb or need quick improvised security.

name: Lantern
description: An enclosed light source consisting of a small oil reservoir, a wick, and a metal-and-glass housing that shields the flame from wind and rain while still letting light shine through. A single pint of oil keeps a lantern burning for roughly a day, making it far more efficient and reliable than open torches or candles for extended use. Lanterns can be hung from a hook, carried by a handle, or set on a surface to illuminate a room or campsite, and their enclosed flame makes them much safer to use around hay, paper, or flammable supplies.

name: Oil, Lantern (per pint)
description: A pint of refined oil suitable for burning in a lantern, providing roughly twenty-four hours of steady illumination per pint when used with a standard lantern. Typically derived from rendered animal fat, vegetable sources, or mineral oil depending on the setting's technology, this fuel is sold by volume and stored in small flasks or skins for travel. Anyone carrying a lantern for extended journeys needs to budget for additional pints of oil to keep their light source running through multiple nights of travel or camping.

name: Personal Basics
description: A small bundle of everyday personal items considered the bare minimum for camping and self-care while traveling, including eating utensils, a tinderbox or flint and steel for starting fires, a towel, and similar small necessities appropriate to the era. Without this kit, a character attempting to survive in the wilderness suffers a penalty to Survival rolls due to lacking basic conveniences. Lightweight and inexpensive, this is the sort of unglamorous gear that any sensible traveler packs before setting out, ensuring they can eat, wash, and start a fire without improvising every time.

name: Pole, 6-Foot
description: A simple wooden pole roughly six feet in length, useful for pitching tents, testing the depth of water or mud ahead of the traveler, fishing, or prodding suspicious objects from a safe distance. Cut from a straight sapling or shaped from milled lumber, the pole is light enough to carry lashed to a pack and sturdy enough for moderate leverage tasks. Travelers and campers often keep one or two on hand for setting up shelter or as a walking aid over rough or uncertain ground.

name: Pole, 10-Foot
description: A long wooden pole roughly ten feet in length, used for tasks requiring greater reach than a shorter pole allows, such as probing for pit traps, testing unstable floors, fording deep water, or holding something at a safe distance from the user. Heavier and more cumbersome than the six-foot version, it is typically carried lashed along the side of a pack or across a saddle. A classic piece of dungeon-delving gear, the ten-foot pole has become emblematic of cautious adventurers checking for hazards before stepping forward.

name: Pouch or Purse, Small
description: A small drawstring bag made of leather or sturdy cloth, worn on a belt or carried by hand to hold coins, small valuables, herbs, or trinkets. Holding a few pounds of contents, it is the standard container for carrying money and small personal effects when a full pack is unnecessary or impractical. Its small size makes it easy to conceal under clothing, though this also makes it a tempting target for pickpockets and cutpurses in crowded places such as markets and taverns.

name: Sleeping Fur
description: A large cured animal pelt used as bedding, providing warmth through insulation even when conditions are damp, unlike some woven blankets which lose their insulating value when wet. Common among hunters, herders, and travelers in cold climates, a sleeping fur can be rolled up and strapped to a pack or saddle for transport. Beyond sleeping, it can serve as a seat cover, a makeshift cloak in an emergency, or a barrier between a sleeper and cold, damp ground, making it a valued possession in any northern or mountainous region.

name: Traveler's Rations
description: A single meal's worth of preserved food suitable for carrying on long journeys, typically consisting of dried or salted meat, hard cheese, dried fruit, or similar foods that resist spoilage for extended periods without refrigeration. Compact and lightweight compared to fresh food, rations are the standard fare for soldiers, sailors, and travelers who cannot rely on finding meals along the way. While not particularly appetizing, a supply of rations can mean the difference between a successful expedition and a hungry, exhausted party stranded far from civilization.

name: Wineskin
description: A flexible container made from a treated animal hide, sewn and sealed to hold liquids such as water, wine, or oil without leaking. Holding about a gallon, a wineskin is lighter and far more durable than a ceramic bottle of similar capacity, able to survive being dropped, squeezed, or packed tightly without breaking. Travelers sling wineskins over a shoulder or attach them to a saddle, squeezing the contents out through a narrow spout or tied opening. Its flexibility lets it collapse as it empties, taking up less space over the course of a journey.

name: Scribe's Kit
description: A compact kit containing everything needed to write and prepare documents by hand: quill pens, small bottles of ink, a penknife for sharpening quills and scraping errors, and a supply of paper or parchment. Essential equipment for clerks, scholars, monks, and adventurers who need to copy texts, draft letters, forge documents, or record findings during their travels. The kit is compact enough to fit in a small case or pack pocket, making it practical for anyone whose profession or hobbies require regular writing while away from a proper desk or study.

name: Hip Quiver
description: A leather or wooden quiver worn on a belt at the hip, holding up to twenty arrows or crossbow bolts within easy reach of an archer's drawing hand. Designed for quick access during sustained shooting, a hip quiver lets the user grab fresh ammunition with minimal movement, making it popular among hunters and skirmishers who need to reload rapidly without breaking stance. It is somewhat less convenient than a back-mounted quiver for carrying very large numbers of arrows, but its position keeps the contents from shifting awkwardly during movement.

name: Shoulder Quiver
description: A larger quiver slung over the shoulder and across the back, holding up to a dozen arrows or crossbow bolts in a position that keeps them out of the way while moving, climbing, or fighting in melee. Favored by traveling archers and soldiers who need to carry ammunition securely over long distances, the shoulder quiver distributes weight more evenly than a hip-mounted version, though drawing an arrow requires reaching back over the shoulder. Often made of leather or stiffened fabric with a reinforced opening to protect fletching from damage.

name: Lanyard, Leather
description: A length of leather cord tied between a weapon's hilt or grip and the wielder's wrist, allowing a dropped weapon to be quickly retrieved with a sharp tug and a moment's effort. Popular among soldiers and duelists who fear losing their weapon in the chaos of battle, particularly when fighting on horseback, in water, or on unstable footing. The cord is thin enough to be severed by a sharp blow if an enemy targets it deliberately, but under normal circumstances it provides a cheap, simple safeguard against an embarrassing and dangerous loss of arms.

name: Wheelbarrow
description: A single-wheeled hand cart consisting of a wooden tray or basin mounted between two handles and a front wheel, used to transport heavy or bulky loads short distances with much less effort than carrying them by hand. Capable of holding roughly 160 kilograms of material, a wheelbarrow effectively divides the felt weight of its load by five for the person pushing it, making it indispensable for construction, farming, mining, and moving supplies around a camp or worksite. Its simple design has remained largely unchanged for centuries across many cultures.

name: Padded Training Weapon
description: A wooden weapon, typically a sword, staff, or polearm substitute, wrapped in cloth or other soft padding for safe practice. The padding converts any attack into crushing damage at a significant penalty, making it suitable for sparring without risking serious injury. It is cheap to produce since it requires only a wooden core and inexpensive wrapping material. Used by warriors, soldiers, and martial arts students throughout history to rehearse forms and bouts without the lethality of edged or pointed weapons, this remains a staple of training halls and military drill yards across all tech levels.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Wooden Training Weapon
description: A hard wooden replica of a metal weapon, such as a sword, axe, or mace, carved to the same shape and balance as its steel counterpart but lacking a sharpened edge or point. Despite being unsharpened, a wooden weapon of this kind is sturdy enough to deliver crushing blows capable of breaking bones, making it dangerous in earnest combat as well as useful for drilling. Such practice weapons, like the Japanese bokken, have long been used by soldiers and duelists to rehearse techniques cheaply, sparing costly metal blades from the wear of constant training.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Barbed Chain
description: A cinematic kusari (weighted chain weapon) adorned with sharp edges, spikes, and barbs along its links, common in fantasy art and sword-and-sorcery depictions. Functionally similar to a normal kusari, it adds crushing damage from the embedded barbs and makes it far harder for an entangled victim to escape, as the barbs catch on clothing and flesh. The many sharp protrusions are hazardous to the wielder as well; a fumbled swing can lacerate his own hands. Priced at roughly double an ordinary kusari of the same length due to the elaborate, dangerous construction required to fit a chain with so many cutting edges.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Double Crossbow
description: A cinematic ranged weapon formed from two ordinary crossbows bolted back-to-back, allowing a wielder to fire one bolt and then flip the entire assembly over as a free action to bring the second loaded crossbow to bear instantly. This ingenious arrangement gives the effective firepower of a two-shot weapon without the mechanical complexity of a true repeating crossbow, at the cost of considerable extra weight. The standard version pairs two ordinary crossbows, while a more expensive variant uses two composite crossbows for greater power and range, both retaining all other handling characteristics of their base weapons.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Double Composite Crossbow
description: An upgraded form of the double crossbow, built from two composite crossbows joined back-to-back so the wielder can flip the weapon over to instantly present a second loaded bow. Composite limbs give each half greater draw weight and range than the standard double crossbow, at significantly higher cost and weight. As with its plain counterpart, this device lets a hero deliver rapid follow-up shots without the complexity of a repeating mechanism, trading practicality for dramatic firepower in cinematic engagements.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Double-Ended Sword
description: A cinematic weapon consisting of two broadsword-length blades joined hilt-to-hilt by an elongated central handle, wielded like a quarterstaff using two-handed sword or staff techniques. Either end can strike independently, delivering cutting damage on swings and impaling damage on thrusts, and a skilled wielder can attack opponents on both sides simultaneously by striking with both blades at once. Its dramatic double-bladed silhouette makes it a popular design in fantasy media, though its great length and the danger of the trailing blade make it impractical for real combatants.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Spiked Plate Armor
description: A suit of plate armor studded with short spikes across its surface, an exaggeration found mainly in legend and fantasy art rather than genuine military history. The spikes make unarmed and grappling strikes from spike-covered limbs noticeably more damaging, turning gauntlets and knee guards into improvised weapons. However, the protrusions disrupt the smooth, deflecting surfaces that make plate armor effective, reducing its protective value, and they snag on equipment, clothing, and bystanders, making the wearer clumsy outside of close combat. It is best suited to arena duels or fights against grappling creatures rather than open battlefield use.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Studded Leather Armor
description: Leather or heavy cloth armor decorated with rows of metal studs or rivets, a design ubiquitous in fantasy illustration but never used historically as genuine armor reinforcement. In reality, the studs serve no protective function and may even reduce the armor's ability to deflect blows; true historical studding was decorative, or used to rivet together layered fabric or to secure hidden metal plates beneath the surface (as in a coat of plates or brigandine). When added deliberately to a glove or elbow piece, the rigid studs can increase the damage dealt by unarmed strikes from that body part, at extra cost and added weight.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Basket-Hilt Weapon Guard
description: A metal cage-like guard fitted to a weapon's hilt that wraps around and protects the wielder's hand, commonly seen on Scottish broadswords and similar blades. An enclosed basket hilt provides substantial protection to the gripping hand at all times, while a lighter open-frame or partial basket offers protection only some of the time but adds less bulk. Either version slightly increases the punching power of a strike made with the hilt itself, though the altered balance takes a fighter time to get used to. This upgrade can be retrofitted to any hilted weapon, adding modest weight and cost.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Spiked Shield
description: A shield fitted with a long offensive spike in place of its central boss, turning every shield bash into a piercing attack rather than a blunt one. The spike adds to the force of a bash and changes its damage type to impaling, making the shield a genuine secondary weapon. However, the protruding spike can become lodged in a target like a pick, and there is a chance the spike snaps off entirely after a block. Popular among aggressive shield-fighters who want their defensive equipment to double as an offensive tool, this modification adds noticeably to the shield's weight and cost.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Shield with Disarming Spikes
description: A shield whose rim has been fitted with two or more short spikes designed to catch and entangle an opponent's weapon during a block. After successfully blocking an attack with such a shield, the defender gains a brief advantage when attempting to wrench the weapon from the attacker's grip. The spikes are dangerous to the wielder as well, since a badly fumbled block can drive a spike into the user's own arm. This modification adds modest weight without increasing the shield's hit points, and is favored by defensively-minded fighters who want to punish enemies who engage their shield directly.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Rim-Bladed Shield
description: A metal-rimmed or fully metal shield with a portion of its edge ground into a sharpened blade, allowing the wielder to make a cutting attack with the shield itself in addition to its normal bashing and blocking functions. Only part of the rim is typically sharpened to reduce the risk of self-injury, but a badly failed block can still cause the wielder to cut himself on his own shield. This customization turns a purely defensive item into a viable offensive weapon for fighters who favor aggressive shield techniques, at a modest increase in cost.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Ditch and Rampart
description: The earliest known fortification design, dating to the Neolithic period, consisting of a dug ditch with the excavated earth piled into an adjacent mound, or rampart, on the defender's side. A typical rampart stood 4-6 feet tall with a ditch of similar depth, presenting attackers at the ditch's bottom with an 8-12 foot obstacle. The rampart's base thickness scales with its height, roughly thickness equal to height. Freshly built earthworks offer modest protection, but within a couple of years the soil settles and compacts, becoming tougher and equivalent to a hard earth wall while losing some height.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Dry Stone Wall
description: A wall built by stacking loose, uncut stones on top of one another without any mortar to bind them, relying purely on careful placement and gravity for stability. Because such a wall cannot safely exceed its own width in height, historical dry stone fortifications rarely topped 10 feet. A more advanced TL1 form, ashlar construction, uses stones cut to interlock tightly with one another, allowing far greater heights; Incan ashlar walls reached 30 feet and Mycenaean Cyclopean walls up to 40 feet, and offer notably better protection than simple dry stone.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Hard Earth Wall
description: A wall built by ramming earth, clay, and aggregate into wooden forms in successive layers, each compressed with heavy rams before the next is added and the forms raised again, a technique used to build sections of the Great Wall of China. Unfired mud bricks, made from mud or clay bound with straw or rice husks and dating back to the eighth millennium B.C., are considered equivalent construction. Such walls range from 6 to 30 feet tall and hold up best in dry climates, deteriorating more quickly when exposed to rain. A settled earthen rampart eventually becomes equivalent to this type of wall.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Defensive Hedge
description: A thick wall of thorny shrubs or thickets, strategically planted and trimmed over years to form a living barrier. While offering little protection against weapons fire, a mature thorn hedge is enough to dissuade casual intruders and snags or injures anyone who tries to force their way through or climb it. Its effective height depends on the species of plant used and how long it has been allowed to grow. Being organic, a hedge is highly flammable and easily destroyed by fire compared to constructed walls, but costs almost nothing beyond the time needed to cultivate it.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Wooden Palisade
description: A defensive wall formed from a row of wooden posts driven vertically into the ground close together, often with sharpened tips, quickly raised in wooded areas to create an immediate barrier. Palisades are frequently combined with other works, such as being planted atop an earthen rampart; when the stakes are laid horizontally pointing outward instead, the resulting obstacle is called a fraise. Typical palisades stood 8-12 feet tall, limited mainly by available timber length, and were often used as a stopgap measure while more permanent stone or earth fortifications were under construction. Like the hedge, it is vulnerable to fire.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Brick Wall
description: A wall constructed of fired bricks, ceramic blocks made from molded clay baked in a kiln until hardened, first appearing in the third millennium B.C. Bricks are laid in courses much like cut stone, either dry-stacked or bonded with mortar, and can be built to heights comparable to equivalent stone walls. The kiln-firing process makes brick more uniform and weather-resistant than unfired mud brick, giving it noticeably better protective qualities than hard earth construction while remaining cheaper and lighter than solid stone.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Cribwork Reinforcement
description: A construction technique that reinforces an earthen, brick, or stone wall by tying its courses together with a secondary material, such as transverse log ties running through an earthen rampart or courses of brick binding a stone wall. The Romans encountered Celtic settlements fortified this way and called the log-reinforced version Murus Gallicus, or 'Gallic wall.' Applicable to any qualifying wall at least two feet thick, cribwork measurably improves the wall's structural resilience and resistance to battering without significantly altering its basic protective value against weapons.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Mortared Stone Wall
description: A stone wall similar to dry stone construction but with its stones bound together using a cementing agent such as bitumen, lime, or plaster, the latter first developed in the Neolithic. This was the most common construction method for medieval fortresses; the largest wall of Constantinople was 16 feet thick and 40 feet high, the keep at Pembroke Castle had walls 19 feet thick and 75 feet tall, and Rochester Castle's walls reached an extraordinary 13 feet thick and 113 feet tall. The bonding mortar gives this construction substantially greater strength and protective value than unbonded dry stone of the same thickness.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Piled Turf Wall
description: A wall built by digging out slabs of turf or sod and stacking them on one another until reaching the desired height, a method used by Roman legionaries to quickly fortify marching camps each evening. It was commonly used to reinforce a wooden palisade, or, where manpower allowed, two parallel turf walls were raised with rubble from the surrounding ditch packed into the gap between them. This produced a surprisingly effective fortification using nothing more than digging tools, offering moderate protection comparable to a fresh earthen rampart.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Roman Concrete Wall
description: A wall built from the Roman formula of wet lime, pozzolana (volcanic ash), and gravel combined in carefully measured ratios, shoveled into wooden forms and packed tightly with rams in a process similar to rammed earth construction. This drier mix than modern concrete proved remarkably durable, exemplified by the Colosseum, which stood about 150 feet tall and survives today without the steel reinforcement that modern concrete depends on. Roman-style concrete walls offer excellent protection against both impact and projectile weapons, representing one of the most advanced fortification materials available at its tech level.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Embossed Wall
description: A defensive wall, made of stone or brick and at least one foot thick, into which large stones are set to protrude at regular intervals across its face, similar in concept to the log-reinforced Murus Gallicus but using stone knobs instead of timber. These projecting stones help spread and dissipate the impact of siege weapons such as battering rams and catapult shots across a wider area of the wall, reducing localized damage. The technique was an evolutionary refinement of earlier cribwork methods, applied specifically to improve a wall's resistance to crushing impacts from siege engines.
book: Low-Tech Companion II - Weapons and Warriors (4E)

name: Wooden Temple
description: A small but complete house of worship, roughly 15 by 30 feet and 12 feet tall, consisting of a single large room. Suitable as the sole church in a small town or as a minor center of worship within a larger settlement. Built primarily from wood with a thatched or shingled roof, it represents the cheapest formal religious structure described in the book, lacking the durability and prestige of stone construction but still serving as a recognized communal gathering place for rites, festivals, and modest congregations.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Stone Temple
description: A house of worship of the same modest size as the Wooden Temple but constructed mostly from rough stone, finished on the exterior with fine dressed stone facing. The added masonry greatly increases its durability and resistance to fire compared to wooden construction, making it a far more permanent religious landmark. Such buildings were common upgrades for communities that could afford skilled masons, and their stone facades often served as canvases for inscriptions, carvings, and religious iconography reflecting local beliefs.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Monastic Dormitory
description: A rough but durable stone building containing fourteen small cells, each about five by seven feet, intended to house monks or other religious residents. As religious institutions grew from simple shrines into self-sufficient communities, dormitories like this became central to monastic life, providing private sleeping quarters for ascetics who spent their days in prayer, labor, and study. Its compartmentalized layout reflects the partitioned design typical of communal residential architecture, with thick stone walls providing both insulation and security.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Big Temple
description: A fairly large church, roughly 80 by 150 feet and 40 feet tall, with a mostly open floor plan punctuated by a few small rooms used as chapels or offices along the sides. Representing the grand cathedrals and major shrines of history, such a building was a massive undertaking requiring skilled labor, abundant stone, and significant wealth, often funded by donations, endowments, or royal patronage. Its scale allowed it to host large congregations, processions, and elaborate ceremonies, becoming a focal point of civic and religious life.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Palace
description: An impressive urban structure roughly 90 by 90 feet and 30 feet tall, built from fine stone and appropriate as the residence of a prince, bishop, or imperial governor, or as the public palace of a self-governing city. It combines large chambers suited for official events, audiences, and receptions with smaller rooms for use as private apartments and administrative offices. While not on the scale of the greatest temples, a palace represents a substantial investment in prestige architecture, signaling the wealth and authority of its occupant to visitors and subjects alike.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Wooden Cult Statue
description: A large figurine carved from wood, sized roughly to a typical human body's volume of about 2.5 cubic feet, used to depict gods, saints, heroes, or important figures within temples and shrines. As the cheapest and earliest statuary material available, wooden statues were common in less wealthy communities or as interim images before a society could afford stone or metal replacements. They could be painted, gilded, or otherwise decorated to enhance their religious or political impact, granting reaction bonuses based on the value of their adornment.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Terracotta Statue
description: A human-sized figure molded and fired from clay, representing a step up from carved wood in both durability and detail. Terracotta statues were used widely across ancient civilizations for funerary art, temple decoration, and votive offerings, since clay could be shaped into fine features before firing into a hard ceramic. Though more fragile than stone or bronze, terracotta was far cheaper to produce in quantity, making it popular for armies of figures such as the famous tomb guardians of ancient China, as well as smaller devotional images in shrines and households.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Stone Statue
description: A human-sized figure carved from solid stone, the most durable and prestigious common statuary material in the ancient and medieval world. Stone statues adorned temples, tombs, public squares, and palaces, depicting deities, rulers, and honored citizens. Their permanence made them ideal for political propaganda and religious veneration alike, from Egyptian colossi to Greek and Roman portrait sculpture. Carving required significant skilled labor and good-quality stone, often transported from distant quarries, making fine stone statues a notable expression of wealth and power.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Hollow Bronze Statue
description: A human-sized figure cast in hollow bronze, representing the height of metallurgical statuary available before TL5. Bronze statues were prized for their fine detail, resistance to weathering, and ability to be polished or gilded to a brilliant shine, making them favorites for honoring emperors, gods, and victorious generals throughout the Mediterranean and Asia. Casting such a statue required sophisticated foundry techniques, including complex molds and large quantities of metal, making bronze statuary among the most expensive and politically significant forms of public art in low-tech societies.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Hand-Copied Codex Library (Basic)
description: A basic library's worth of books (about ten linear feet of shelving) produced entirely by hand-copying onto bound codex pages rather than printed. Hand copying takes far longer than printing and costs roughly ten times as much as an equivalent printed library, while the bulkier handwritten pages also quadruple the weight and shelf space compared to printed equivalents. Before the spread of movable type, virtually all books -- legal codes, scriptures, philosophical works, and chronicles -- existed only in this form, each copy the product of months of a scribe's painstaking labor.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Scroll Collection
description: A set of roughly two dozen papyrus or vellum scrolls equivalent in content to a single modern book, filling about six linear feet of shelving. Scrolls were the dominant format for written records and literature in many ancient civilizations, including Egypt, Greece, and Rome, before the codex became standard. Their long, rolled format made them bulkier and heavier to store than bound books, and reading required unrolling and re-rolling, but they remained the primary medium for important documents, religious texts, and literary works for centuries.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Clay Tablet Archive
description: A set of roughly 1,200 inscribed clay tablets, equivalent in content to a single modern book but occupying about 100 linear feet of storage. Clay tablets were the writing medium of choice for early Mesopotamian civilizations, used for everything from temple tax records and legal codes to epic literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh. Although extremely heavy and bulky compared to later media, fired clay tablets are remarkably durable, with many surviving intact for thousands of years, making them an invaluable archaeological resource despite their impracticality for everyday use.
book: Low-Tech Companion I - Philosophers and Kings (4E)

name: Lever (Construction)
description: A simple but essential tool of low-tech engineering, consisting of a sturdy log up to 20 feet long used to shift heavy weights over short distances. By resting the beam on a fulcrum near the load, workers could multiply their effective strength by up to a factor of ten, making it possible to budge stones, timbers, and other massive objects that would otherwise be immovable. Levers were indispensable on construction sites throughout history, from raising standing stones to positioning blocks during the building of pyramids and temples.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Lightweight Winch
description: A small winch consisting of an axle turned by a crank or handles, mounted on posts spanning an open space such as a well or mineshaft. As the operator turns the crank, a rope winds onto the axle, lifting loads with mechanical advantage up to eight times the operator's effort. This lightweight model, rated for loads up to 1,000 pounds, was a common fixture at wells, small construction sites, and workshops, providing a simple and portable way to raise buckets, tools, and modest building materials.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Construction Winch
description: A heavy-duty version of the basic crank winch, built with reinforced timbers and a thicker axle to handle far greater loads than the lightweight model. Rated to lift up to 18 tons, construction winches were essential equipment on major building projects, used to hoist massive stone blocks, timbers, and other materials into place during the construction of fortifications, cathedrals, and other monumental architecture. At TL2, built-in ratchet catches prevented loads from suddenly dropping if an operator lost their grip, greatly improving safety on dangerous worksites.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Block and Tackle
description: A set of compound pulleys that multiplies lifting power at the cost of requiring the rope to be pulled a proportionally greater distance. The basic version halves the effective load that must be lifted, while additional pulley sets can double this advantage repeatedly, up to an eightfold reduction, at increasing cost and weight. Rated for loads up to 1,000 pounds in its base form, with heavier versions available for loads up to 18 tons, block and tackle rigs could be combined with cranes to dramatically increase the weight that a small crew could raise.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Crane (25-foot)
description: A basic wooden crane built as a leaning triangle of two long beams fastened together at the top, braced by shorter beams and guy ropes, with the vertical legs set a few feet apart and fitted with brackets that double as a ladder. Workers at the base pull a rope running through a pulley at the top to lift loads at a rate of about one yard every four seconds. This 25-foot crane could raise up to six tons, and additional cable lines or attachments such as block and tackle could be added for greater capacity, making it a versatile tool for construction and dock work.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Crane (50-foot)
description: A larger version of the basic wooden crane, twice as tall as the 25-foot model and proportionally heavier, used for the most demanding lifting tasks on major construction sites such as cathedrals, fortifications, and large harbor installations. Despite its increased size, its maximum actual load remains six tons per cable line, though additional lines, winches, or block and tackle attachments could be fitted to multiply its effective lifting power. Such large cranes were impressive landmarks of medieval engineering, often permanently installed at busy ports and quarries.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Crane Treadle
description: A large circular treadwheel, eight yards in diameter and four yards wide, attached to an axle wound with cable. Humans or draft animals walk inside the wheel on internal risers, their weight and motion turning the axle and reeling in the cable at one yard per second. Acting as a powerful mechanical advantage device with a load divisor of two, a crane treadle could be attached to a crane to enable a small crew to lift extremely heavy loads, and was a common sight at major construction sites, quarries, and ports throughout the medieval period.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Pile Driver
description: A massive one-ton weight, raised by a crane and dropped onto logs to pound them into the ground as foundations for buildings, docks, and bridges. The falling weight delivers a tremendous crushing blow -- enough to do serious damage to anything caught beneath it -- and was essential for establishing stable footings on soft or wet ground. Pile drivers were widely used in harbor construction, bridge-building, and the foundations of large structures, allowing builders to create solid platforms even on marshy riverbanks or tidal flats.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Shadouf
description: A simple water-lifting device consisting of a long pole balanced on a pivoting post, with a bucket on one end and a counterweight on the other. The operator dips the bucket into a water source, and the counterweight eases the effort of lifting it, allowing the water to be swung over and dumped at a higher point. Capable of moving up to 1,000 gallons of water per hour to a height of about three yards, the shadouf was simple to build and maintain, and remained in widespread use across the Near East and Egypt for irrigation for thousands of years.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Archimedean Screw (Agricultural)
description: A broad-bladed screw housed within an angled cylindrical shaft, turned by a hand crank at the top. As the crank is operated, the rotating screw draws water steadily upward from its lower end. The agricultural model is designed to irrigate fields from adjacent canals, capable of moving up to 5,300 gallons of water per hour, though it can only lift water about two feet. Despite its limited lift height, its high throughput made it valuable for flooding fields during planting season in river-valley agriculture across the ancient Mediterranean and Near East.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Archimedean Screw (Mine-Draining)
description: A heavier-duty variant of the Archimedean screw, built to drain water from mineshafts rather than irrigate fields. It moves a more modest 400 gallons of water per hour but can lift it ten feet, far higher than the agricultural model, making it suitable for pumping standing water out of deep excavations. Flooding was one of the most persistent obstacles to mining at depth, and devices like this -- often arranged in series -- allowed miners to keep shafts dry enough to continue extracting ore well below the water table.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Saqiya
description: An animal-powered water-lifting wheel, often described as a waterwheel run in reverse. A yoked draft animal walks in a circular path, turning an axle connected to a large wheel fitted with buckets around its rim, their open ends facing the direction of motion. As the wheel rotates, the buckets dip into a water source, fill, and empty into a trough at the top. A saqiya can move up to 3,900 gallons of water per hour to a height of four yards, and was a staple of irrigation in Egypt, Mesopotamia, and other arid regions for centuries.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Bucket Chain
description: A ladder-like loop of connected buckets secured at the bottom by an axle and driven by an attached treadmill or waterwheel. As the chain rotates, buckets dip into a body of water at the bottom and dump their contents at the top, ten yards above. Capable of moving up to 4,800 gallons of water per hour, bucket chains were used for irrigation and drainage, and occasionally to haul small quantities of building materials such as earth or rubble up to elevated construction sites, making them a versatile labor-saving device.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Large Two-Man Saw
description: A six-foot saw fitted with handles at both ends, requiring two workers to operate. Often used to cut logs placed over a pit, with one worker standing above and another below, the large saw made fast, deep cuts through timber that would be impractical for a single sawyer with a smaller blade. This tool was a mainstay of pre-industrial lumber yards and shipyards, enabling teams to produce planks and beams for construction, shipbuilding, and furniture-making long before mechanized sawmills became common.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Oil Press
description: A device for extracting oil from olives and other oil-rich plant materials. Crushed paste from a mortar, millstone, or edge crusher is placed in coarse fiber bags within a shallow trough, and a heavy stone or wooden block is lowered onto it -- sometimes aided by a lever, winch, or screw -- to squeeze out the oil through a spout for collection. Capable of processing up to 100 pounds of material per session, oil presses were vital to the economies of olive-growing regions around the Mediterranean, producing oil for cooking, lighting, religious anointing, and trade.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Edge Crusher
description: A heavy stone wheel up to four feet across, mounted on its edge on a circular track and connected to a pivoting central axle. Driven by animal power walking the circuit, the wheel rolls around its track, crushing material placed in a trough beneath it. Edge crushers processed roughly thirty pounds of material per hour, with each full rotation taking ten seconds or more, and were used for a wide range of materials from olives for oil production to iron ore for smelting, making them a versatile piece of pre-industrial heavy machinery.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Animal-Powered Grain Mill
description: A scaled-up rotary quern, larger than a portable household mill, designed to be turned by a draft animal walking in a circuit attached to a central shaft. A single-animal mill of this type could grind about 25 pounds of flour per hour, with larger versions using multiple animals producing proportionally more. Such mills were a common feature of villages and towns throughout the ancient and medieval world, often run as commercial operations where farmers brought their grain to be ground for a fee, freeing households from the laborious task of hand-grinding.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Water-Powered Grain Mill
description: A grain mill driven by a one-horsepower waterwheel rather than draft animals, capable of processing about 175 pounds of flour per hour -- seven times the output of a single-animal mill. Water-powered mills represented a major advance in food-processing efficiency, allowing a single installation on a river or stream to supply flour for an entire town. Their construction required not only the milling machinery itself but also a waterwheel and millrace, making them a significant capital investment typically owned by lords, monasteries, or municipal authorities who charged fees for their use.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Waterwheel (5-foot)
description: A wooden wheel mounted vertically in a stream or millrace, turned by the flow or fall of water to provide rotational power for attached machinery such as grain mills, sawmills, or trip hammers. The base model is five feet in diameter and delivers a strength rating of 40, sufficient to drive a single small mill. Larger wheels scale up in diameter and power output. Horizontal wheels were the simplest design but less efficient; undershot and overshot wheels, introduced later, could deliver substantially more power and became central to medieval industrial development.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Water-Powered Sawmill
description: A set of saw blades driven by a waterwheel, mechanizing the laborious work previously done by two-man hand saws. A powered sawmill blade cuts rapidly through timber, and installations could mount up to eight blades for high-throughput lumber production. First appearing in the 13th century, water-powered sawmills were sometimes also used near quarries to cut stone blocks. They dramatically increased the speed and scale at which lumber could be processed, supporting the construction booms of late medieval Europe and the expansion of shipbuilding industries.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Small Trip Hammer
description: A waterwheel-driven hammer weighing about 150 pounds, mounted on a see-saw arrangement so that the turning wheel pushes down the haft end, raising the head, before releasing it to fall under gravity. Small trip hammers could strike as fast as 200 times per minute, making them useful for processing textiles -- such as fulling cloth -- and for lighter metalworking tasks. Their rapid, repetitive action made them far more efficient than hand-hammering for repetitive tasks, representing an early form of mechanized industrial labor.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Large Trip Hammer
description: A massive waterwheel-driven hammer of up to three tons, operating on the same see-saw principle as its smaller counterpart but striking only about once every two seconds due to its size. Large trip hammers were central to early industrial metallurgy, used to pound impurities and slag out of iron blooms during the bloomery process, gradually refining the metal as workers progressed from large, slow hammers to smaller, faster ones. Their thunderous operation was a defining feature of medieval ironworking centers and an early step toward mechanized heavy industry.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Windmill (9-foot)
description: A wind-driven wheel of sails mounted on a tower or post, used to power attached machinery such as grain mills or sawmills, which are not included in its cost. The base model is nine feet in diameter and provides a strength rating of 40, equivalent to the smallest waterwheel. Larger windmills scale up in both diameter and power, with maximum strength ratings increasing at later tech levels. Horizontal windmills, an early and simpler design, deliver reduced power but require no more material or expense, making them an accessible option in regions lacking reliable flowing water.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Wire Mill
description: An apparatus that creates a back-and-forth pulling motion via tongs attached to a shaft or rope, used to draw metal wire through a perforated draw plate. A metalworker grips the wire as the tongs move back, drawing it through the plate, then releases as he leans forward to grasp it closer to the plate again. Some wire mills mounted the worker on a swing for a broader range of motion, increasing the wire drawn per cycle. Wire mills mechanized a previously exhausting manual process, enabling more efficient production of wire for chainmail, fasteners, and decorative work.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Miner's Hammer-and-Chisel Set
description: The basic toolkit used by miners and quarrymen for thousands of years: hammers (often with one flat end and one pointed end, similar to modern rock hammers), chisels of various sizes for cutting grooves into stone, and crowbars for splitting off sections of rock once a groove was cut. These tools varied little across cultures and eras, reflecting the universal physical requirements of breaking and prying apart stone by hand. A set like this was essential equipment for anyone excavating mineshafts, quarrying building stone, or extracting ore from rock veins.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Mining Derrick
description: A pile-driver-like rig used to bore narrow shafts, typically for wells, up to a foot in diameter. The derrick repeatedly pounds a pointed bit into the ground, loosening soil and rock that is then hauled up by a bucket on a rope. This pounding technique allowed ancient engineers, notably in China, to dig wells several hundred feet deep, though progress could be agonizingly slow -- sometimes only an inch of excavation per day in hard rock -- making the construction of a single deep well a project spanning years.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Hard Earth (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: The cheapest class of permanent building material, encompassing mud brick (mud packed into wooden forms and dried for months), rammed earth (dirt shoveled into forms and forcibly compacted), and sod (blocks of turf cut directly from the ground, bound together by grass roots). Despite its humble origins, hard earth construction is extremely cheap, naturally fire-resistant, and surprisingly long-lasting even in temperate climates, making it the foundation of vernacular architecture for much of human history, from ancient ziggurats to medieval cottages and frontier homesteads.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Rubble (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: Unshaped or only lightly shaped stone, piled and fitted together rather than precisely cut, forming the most basic and ancient type of stone construction. Despite its rough appearance, rubble construction is extremely durable -- the walls of Jericho include a partial tower roughly ten thousand years old -- and far cheaper than dressed stone. Rubble walls were used for everything from simple field boundaries to massive fortress curtain walls, often serving as a sturdy core that could later be faced with finer ashlar stone for a more polished appearance.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Thatch (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: Bundles of reeds and grasses, or thin wooden slats woven into wicker panels, used to cover wooden frames and provide inexpensive walls and roofing. On its own, thatch makes a poor structural material, but when attached to a frame and often coated with mud for windproofing, it produces cheap and serviceable -- if flammable and flimsy -- shelter. Thatched roofs and wattle-and-daub walls were ubiquitous in peasant housing across medieval Europe and beyond, so flimsy in some cases that a thief could break in simply by forcing an opening through the wall.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Ashlar (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: Neatly squared-off and polished stone blocks, cut with metal tools to fit together far more tightly than rough rubble. Ashlar construction is extremely expensive but also attractive, exceptionally sturdy, and necessary for the most sophisticated architectural techniques such as vaulting. Because of its cost, ashlar was often used selectively, as a fine facing applied over cheaper earth or rubble cores, giving important buildings -- temples, palaces, fortifications -- an impressive and durable exterior appearance while controlling overall expense.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Brick (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: Mud brick taken a step further by firing it in a kiln to produce a hard ceramic block, which can then be laid in courses much like cut stone. Cheaper than quarried stone but considerably more durable than unfired hard earth, thatch, or wood, brick became a staple of urban construction across many civilizations. Even where full brick construction was too costly, thin brick facings were often used to cover and protect less-desirable building materials. To modern eyes, many ancient bricks resemble thick tiles, being notably longer and wider than they are deep.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Concrete (Building Material, per inch-foot)
description: A mixture of aggregate and binding agent that hardens into a solid, monolithic mass, sometimes dismissively described as little more than rubble fill between sturdier walls, but in practice a major architectural advance. Concrete allows for rapid construction of durable buildings, with strength and durability comparable to stone but at lower cost, and can be poured into complex shapes that would be difficult to achieve with cut blocks. The Romans famously exploited concrete for domes, aqueducts, and harbor structures, many of which survive intact two thousand years later.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Badan
description: A small dhow-style cargo vessel under 50 feet long, pointed at both bow and stern, rigged with a single mast and a fore-and-aft sail. Like other dhows, its planked hull is sewn together with cords rather than nailed, giving it a flexible but seaworthy shell. Badans were common workhorses of Indian Ocean coastal trade, used by Muslim merchants to move modest cargoes between ports, fish, and ferry goods along the shore. Their light construction and shallow draft made them maneuverable in coastal waters and easy to beach when needed.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Boum
description: A larger dhow, starting at 50 feet long and pointed at both ends like its smaller cousin the badan, but built with heavier framing timbers in addition to its sewn or fitted planked shell. A boum may carry one or two masts rigged with fore-and-aft sails, giving it greater cargo capacity and range for longer voyages across the Indian Ocean. Boums were workhorses of the medieval Arab and Swahili trading networks, carrying goods such as spices, textiles, and timber between East Africa, Arabia, and India along the monsoon trade routes.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Cog
description: A 60-foot North European cargo ship that, after 1000 A.D., was built with a true keel borrowed from Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian ship designs, giving it slanted stem and stern posts and a sharper prow than its keelless predecessors. Rigged with a single large square sail, and later fitted with a bowsprit and additional lines for better control when sailing upwind, the cog became the dominant merchant vessel of the Hanseatic League, carrying bulk goods such as grain, timber, wool, and wine across the North and Baltic Seas.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)

name: Hulk
description: A keelless, flat-bottomed 60-foot cargo ship whose timbers curve upward at both bow and stern, giving the hull a distinctive U-shape like half an eggshell. Its flat bottom allowed a hulk to navigate shallow river waters and be beached easily, while its rounded shape made it extremely stable and gave it substantial cargo capacity for its size. Rigged with a single large square sail near the prow and steered by two side rudders, hulks were originally developed by Frisian traders and became specialized river cargo carriers as cogs took over ocean routes.
book: Low-Tech Companion III - Daily Life and Economics (4E)
